- - "THE LAND OF NOD." Last night I went to the Land of Nod; What do you think I saw there? Why, all the babies in the world; - Yellow haired, dark haired, light haired, and curled, Some black, some tawny, some fair. i ." What is the way there ?" On and on • Over the velvety sod; Firstyou go up, then you go down, And then you come into Shut-eye town, Away in the Land of Nod. The houses are made of jujube paste, And the doors of plum-cake sliced; And if you are hungry by day or night, You may go to the door and nibble a bite, All plummy and iced and spiced. The fountains, you know, run lemonade, And their playing, it never stops; And wkenever it rains in that wonderful town, Torrents of honey ond cream come down, And lemon and chocolate drops. Oh, it snows white sugar and pink ice-cream, And it freezes lemon ice; Tall sugar-loaf hills all around you see, And cookies and tarts grow on every tree, And they taste remarkably nice. °Tell you some more ?" Oh, I haven't the time, But maybe, if each little elf Will run and climb into mamma's lap, And cuddle right down for a forty-winks nap, He may see the land himself. .--The Fireside.

"OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM" In bleak December, when the icy blast Such keenness had that ruddy lips and cheeks Grew grey and shrivelled, on my way I passed A squalid court, where pallid hunger keeps A bony hand, and flaunts with sin and shame. Though warmly clad, yet such the piercing cold Perforce I shuddered. To the court there came A toddling mite of three or four years old, With tangled curls like wavelets touched with gold By westward-drooping sun. Bare-legged she stepped, Bareheaded too, while all about her swept The cruel wind, yet bravely onward trudged, Undaunted all. Firm by the hand she clasped Another mite, whose baby-face was smudged By many a tear. The bitter, wintry blast Around them fluttered, and the younger child Sobbed louder still, chilled by the biting wind. Her sister stooped with loving byok and smiled: "There, Polly dear, don't cry—here, talce-rny shawl We ain't got fur to go, and I don't mind." With that the baby-angel two feet tall, From off her shw'ring shoulders quick unrolled, A ragged cloth—the thing she called a shawl, Her sole protection 'gainst the freezing cold, And round the trembling infant gently wrapped it o'er, Then clasped her hand, and onward trudged once more. I stood as one entranced, all else forgot • In silent worship,—for I felt the spot A holy aiscp. A ray of love divine Within me shone. A flood of unshed tears Surged to my heart. Oh, baby heroine! Oh, toddling angel! in that deed of thine, That Christ-like deed, such depth of love appears, 'That all my noblest thoughts, poetic dreams, And vain aspiring,s, pass and fade away, As the dim light which in a sick-room gleams, Pales into darkness with the dawn of day. Thoughts fade and poems die, but in God's heaven above, Eternally shall shine that simple deed of love. BY .1. CouLsos KER/uxuar. —Sunday Aragazine.

Tim FEAST OF Asses.—One of the most singular and ludicrous mediteval ceremonies of the season was held, at Beauvais, France, in the fourteenth centultY; called ' the Feast of Asses. The flight into Egypt was repre- sented in church. A beautiful young woman, with an infant in her arms, was seated upon an ass elegantly adorned. Entering the church, the girl and ass were placed near the altar, on the Gospel side. High mass was then begun, and the Introit, Kyrie, Gloria, Credo, etc, all terminated with an imitation of the ass's bray— hiss-hew ,or he-hatrn. At the end of the mass, when the priest turned to the people, saying, "Ite, .11fissa set," he actually he-hawned, or brayed, twice, as ordained by the rituaL And instead of the usual response, "Dee Graiias,'! the people he-hawned, or brayed, thrice, in like manner. A Latin hymn was sung during the mass. A transla- tion of a stanza or two will give an ideas of it : " In an Eastern region Chanced an Ass to be. Beautiful and bravest, Fittest loads to bear. atGrus. He-hawn, sire Ass, you sing; Fierce mouth you grin. Hay enough you'll have, Oats enow to plant. " Here he is with big ears, Primitive clod-hopper, . t Ass as big as ever, Lord of all the asses. Chorus. He-hewn. etc. A TREBUTR TO PROFESSOR FAWCEFT.—Even at this distance of time it is impossible to think without tear- ful sympathy of the bright-eyed, splendidly-gifted youth, who went out with his father for a day's sport in the fields to return wounded and blind, shut out for evermore from the chief avenue of knowledge, never to look again on the beautiful world he loved so well. How strange are the caprices of imagination! For tragic situations to exercise our profoundest emotions we go back to the shadowy ages of mythic story, and the ad- ventures of impossible things. Yet, at any one hour of contemporary time there are always a hundred homes in which the struggle of patience, hope,. and devotion inst adverse destiny is grander than in any woes of Thebes or Pelops' line," though it finds not a singer to set it forth. But the sublime courage of this young man found better expression than that even of 2Eschy- lus. It found voice in a life the fruit., of which will be immortal. For some few terrible hours, physical suffer- ing and weakness, combined with the agony of sudden and hopeless darkness, threatened to paralyse all reso- lution, and to make the future a blank. But the man was too strong, too great, too noble, to succumb to such a trial. Oh, well for him whose will is strong! He suffers, but he will not suffer long. He suffers, but he cannot suffer wrong For him not moves the loud word's random mock; Nor all Calamity's hugest waves confound; Who seems a promontory of rock That, compassed round with turbulent sound, In middle ocean meets the surginz, shock, Tempest-buffeted citadel-crowned. No career ever recorded in history is a nobler living , comment upon these lines than the life and work Of ' Henry Faweett—J. A. Picton, 31.. P., in " Good Words. PLANTS USED IN NEW 'YEAR CELEBRisTIQNs 75Y TEE JAPANESE.—The most striking feature of NOW Year's Day in Japan is the decoration placed with more or less completeness before every portal. Every object of which the decoration is composed has, as might be sup- posed, a symbolic meaning. Suppose the spectator to face the green arch—on his right will be a Me-matsu (Pinus densiflora) with its reddish stem, and on his left will be the black trunk of the Omatsu (Finns Thimbergii or Massonia.na). Immediately behind the pines rises on each side the graceful stem of the bamboo, of which any kind that is convenient is selected. Its erect growth and succession of knots marking its increase during succeeding seasons, render it a symbol of hale life and a fulnsss of years. The distance of usually about six feet between the bamboos is spanned by a grass rope (natoa). Although convenience obliges this rope to be sufficiently high to allow of passage beneath, it should, to accord with its symbolic meaning, debar all bad and unclean things from crossing the threshold. In the centre of the arch thus formed of pines, bamboos, and rope, is a group of several objects. The most conspicuous is the scarlet yebe, or lobster, whose crooked body betokens the back of the aged bent with the weight of years. The lobster is embowered amongst YRS= branches. In the Yusuri (Melia japonica), when the young _leaves have budded, the old leaves yet remain unshed. Se; may the parents continue to flourish, while children and grandchildren spring forth. In the centre also are the graceful fronds of the Shida, or Urajiro, the Polypodium dichotomum. This fern symbolises conjugal life because the fronds spring in pairs from the stem. These uniform graceful leay.es Might suggest dangerous ideas of the equality of the sexes, but the simile has not in Japan been pushed to so desperate a length. Between the paired leaves nestles, as offspring, the little leaf-bud. Here and there are quaintly-cut scraps of white paper, the gohei, or offering to the gods; the form of the paper is said by some to be a conventionalised representation of a human form—that of the offerer—devoting himself thus in effigy to the deities. The New Year arches are out down in Tait:, on January 7, and in some places on January 3. AMERICAN INDlANS.—According to statistics of the Indian Bureau there were three'years ago about 376,000 Indians in the United States, distributed as follows: Citizens, 67,000; the Six Nations, the remnant of the Iro- quois, 7,000; the five partly civilised nations in the:ln- dian territory, 58,000; other Indiane,in reservations, es- timated at 1.98,000; wandering tribes, 15,000; and in Alaska 31,000. Of Indians then; on the reservations, 56,000 were supported by the Government,. 47,000 re- ceived large appropriations, 95,000 were supported by fishing and hunting, farming, and other small industry, and the proceeds of the sale of their land. The land under cultivation by Indians increased fr0m1.157,000 acres in 1879 to 205,000 in 1881, while the number in- creased 5,724 during the years 1880-81, leaving out In- dians who were citizens and those of Alaska. There were 60,000 children among the Indians of school age; the education of the Six Iroquois Nations was managed by the Sta,te of New York; that of the Five Nations Of the Indian Territory was in their own hands; that of the Indians on the Reservations was left to missionaries of religious bodies, with some help from the Govern- ment, amounting in 1881 to 365,000 dole. The New York Indians had a special allowance from the State of 9,000 dols. a year and teachers, and a.Teachers' Institute of their own, with 1,175 out of their 1,600 children in the schools. The Five Nations in the Indian Territory had or 6,000 children in their 198 day and 11 boarding schools, educated in their own Cherokee alphabet with 'its 85 letters, invented by one of their, own members in 1827. For the children of the other and wilder Indians there were schools at various places, including Hamp- ton, Va., Carlisle, and Philadelphia, in this State, and Forest Grove, Oregon, where industrial training is made a useful element in fitting these Indians to return home ready to be instructors to their tribes. There were 4,000 Indian youths of both sexes in boarding schools andit,ooo in day schools, established among their own Western homes, and of these the Santee Normal School and St. Paul's School in Nebraska were reported to be the best; while a newspaper in the Dakota language was printed at Chicago for their benefit. The Indians show a real zeal for education of their children' and the Oma- has of Nebraska sold part of their lands to the Winne,- bagos for the purpose of raising money for schools.— Philadelphia Public Ledger. THE BAD BOY AND SANTA CLAUS.—" Well, what did you get from Santa Claus?" asked the groceryman of the bad boy as he came in the grocery with a big blue neck- tie, on which was pinned a piece of beer glass cut in imitation of a diamond. "Santa Claus must, have re- membered you splendidly," and the groceryman handed the boy a• sour orange. "Oh, don't talk to me about Santa Claus," said the boy, as he bit into the orange, and then went to the vinegar barrel and drew some vinegar in a glass and took a swallow to sweeten the taste of the orange. "Do you know I wonder there is a boy in this whole world that does not grow up to be a first-class liar, when they have their parents lie to them the first seven years of their lives phout Santa Claus? What can a child think when told it is wicked to lie. and then find out that its parents have been lying to it about the Santa Claus business? Do you know I have watched for Santa Claus to come down chimneys, and when I asked how a big fat fellow could come down such a small hole, and crawl through a stove pipe, pa would tell me that Santa Claus was made of India- rubber, and was blowed up, and all he had to do was to let the wind out, and then he would be small enough to get into a gimlet-hole, When I found that Santa Claus was a fraud, and accused pa of deceiving me, he got hot and said I was too smart for my boots." "Oh, that is all right, but what did you get ?" said the groceryman. "I got nice enough things but I haven't got them now. ,I traded off a lot of my things for presents for some boys down our way that didn't get anything. I made a change in the Christmas-tree business at our church. You see, they have been in the habit of getting all the children together the night be- fore Christmas, and having a Christmas-tree, and it is cruel on the poor children. The rich parents put expen- •sive presents on the trees for their children, and the poor children get a ten cent whistle, or a popcorn ball, or an orange. The poor children began to think Santa Claus showed partiality, and that he was in the employ of the rich folks, and they were beginning to get sour on Santa Claus, but this time me and my chum sold all the pre- sents we got at home, and went and bought a whole lot of nice things for the poor boys, and when the man began to distribute the presents, and the poor boys had their mouths made up for popcorn balls, and they got club skates and fur caps, and nice warm mitt-ens, they yelled so the minister was afraid the church would disorderly house. I never had so ‘nch

Why is the horse the most humane of all animals ? "Because he gladly gives the bit out of his mouth, and listens to every woe. What is that which everyone wishes to have, and arhich everyone wishes to get rid of directly he obtains it ?—A good appetite. " What is a curiosity, ma ? " asked little Jamie. " ouriosity is something that is very strange, my " son. "If pa bought you a sealskin sacque this Christmas would that be a curiosity?" "No, my son; that would be a miracle." An Irishman went into a shop and said he—" Faith, a& did you put in the papers that you wanted a man ?" Yes," said the shopkeeper. "And I distinctly stated that all applications must be made by mail.' "An' faith an' it's myself that's a male, sure,' says Pat; and he was engaged. At Mrs. D.'s cooking' ecture the other evening, Lady, solliquising—" Now that she's got it cooked, I wish she'd tell us how to use up cold mutton." Next lady over- hears, and remarks—" I have some infallible receipts." First lady, alert with pencil and notebook—" will you -please favour me ?" Second lady—" Six boys !" HaNes DOWN.—For simplicity and fun this game has few equals. It is as old as the historic period. Sides taken, generally the ladies against the gentlemen. Any mall object, as a thimble, is won by a toss, and the party in possession, opposite their opponents at a table, at the cry of "hands down" work it among their fingers under the table till it is at last lodged in some hand. At the cry of "hands up," all hands are held up, and those opposite must guess in which hand the thimble is held, Clever players can tell by the face of the holder almost without a mistake. " What is your theory concerning the remarkable weather we have been having of late?" asked one great scientist of another. "Well," was the response, "I am inclined to think it comes largely about through the ineterological influence of the red sunset." "My idea is much the same as yours, although there is a remote passibility—" Here the great scientist's little boy spoke out. "I know what's the reason of the wet weather, papa." "Hush, my son! You mustn't inter- '-P t people when they are talking." "I know the canes of the wet weather just the same," insisted the boy. "Well, what is it ? " "Rain." A STATE or INNOCENCE. —While we were sitting in. th" 'Tillage square, waiting for luncheon, we were amused to see a troop of children scantily clad, one or two being minus garments of any kind whatever, playing at bull- fighting. A friend who was with us told me that until lately many of the children never wore any clothes at all till they were twelve or fourteen years old, and that she and some other ladies had formed a little club in order to modify the crudity of this state of innocence, and had been for several years employed in making the most 1 e-isential garments for the children of the poor—Lady Brassey's New Book. "Fiasr-roorom."—This is a New Year custom pecu- liarly Scottish. As soon as twelve o'clock has struck and the New Year has made its appearance, the person who first calls at the house is styled its "first-foot,' and much depends upon the circumstance of this visit. As a rule, but without previous knowledge or consent, friends make a practice of " first-footing " friends, and M order that their presence may not only be welcome in itself but propitious to the household, they arm them- selves with cake, fruit, and the like. It is considered by no means a fortunate thing to be your own "first-foot," and cases are common in which paterfamilias, returning home after twelve but before any visitor has looked in, has been detained outside until a " first-foot"laas arrived First-footing" is generally practised between the hours of twelve and one or two in the morning.—" Little Folks"

Magazine far January. Tam:toms FOR THE Iticw YEAR.—We are standing on the threshold of a new year. Behind us is the old year t, and worn out, and done with. Whatever it -10 rt 7 give us it has given us. We know all about it. It has come and gone. It is like an empty basket, all the contents of which have been poured out and are be- fore our eyes. Nothing more can come of it for our good or for our joy. It has not been, probably, for any -of us exactly what we expected and wished for. To some it brought many sorrows, many failures, many dis- appointments. Its good things were not as good as we "Pected they would be, and many unexpected evils came tumbling out along with the good. And if it has Iseen so with our circumstances, it has been so no less with our performances. As the past lies before us with its tale of failures, omissions, shortcomings; its triumphs 45 self-will over duty; its defeats of good purposes by .70r-masterful affections ; its wasted opportunities; its lost Seasons; its humiliating compliances; its blank pag.es with no record of good done, and its foul pages with their record of evil—how can we look upon it but with a sense of dissatisfaction and shame.—lhe Bishop of Bath and Wells in "The Quiver" for January. WHO ARE TO BLAME FOR SINS OF TRADE.—IL 19 easy to denounce as unprincipled the whole system of "cheap Bales," from the inventor and maker of the adulteration down to its vendor. But it may be asked whether the blame is to be laid entirely at their doors? Are. the manufacturers and merchants alone responsible for evils which are eating awe canker into the commerce of the couatry? Is the salesman who, with plausible tongue, palms off the counterfeit—sheltering himself under what is termed "the habit of trade "—to be alone chargeable with the immoralities which that habit has imposed? Must the tissue of customary frauds, daily perpetuated in factory anti warehouse, be imputed solely to those immediately engaged in them ? Assuredly not. If you were to question these persons they would tell you that it is the public demand whin has forced competition to such a degree, that it is impossible to conduct business in any other way without incurring ruin; that were they to act differently they would lose tiaeir market ; that the public insists on having goods at a certain price, and as the genuine article cannot be so supplied, they are com- pelled to give what may best imitate it. . . . If the merchant is guilty of practical falsehood, assuredly the runners after "bargains" are his accomplices. It ought tiserefore to be a matter as binding as truth with Christian people to insist on honest transactions, and to pay honest prices, and to do their best to put down the villany of lying advertisements, and the knavery of adulteration.—Denald Macleod in "Good Words." The Duke of Devonshire has replied to the deputation of his county Cork tenants, who waited on him at Chats- worth a few days ago to request an abatement hrtheir rents on account of the general depression, His Grace states that he sees no reason why the abatement should be given. • From nearly all the great wheat-growing countries the report is' that the acreage of wheat sown during the past autumn was less than usual. The Ontario Agricultural Returns state that in the western counties of that pro- vince there is a perceptible decrease, farmers being dis- posed to raise more stock and less grain. FROM CaNans.-With the exception of the live cattle trade, in no branch of the Canadian export trade has there been such a wonderful development as in the cheese trade. In 1858 the Canadians exported cheese to the value of £3OO sterling only. In 1883 this amount had increased to £1,300,000. The total exports during the season front Montreal alone amounted to 1,126,002 boxes. THE THREE F's FOR SCOTLAND.-The Scottish Farmers' Allianceehas passed the Rubicon. At the general meet- ing held at Perth it was decided to adopt the report of the deputation which recently visited Ireland, except in relation to arrears of rent That is to say, the Affiance has committed itself to the demand for the three F's, pure and simple, to be administered by Land Courts. It was also agreed to demand the further reform of the Game Laws, free trade M land, representative county government, and a bill to break current leases. The programme of the Alliance has been altered so as to be in conformity with the enlarged scope of objects.-The directors of the Scottish Chamber of Agriculture have issued an address in which a reduction of rents is strongly recommended ; but it is fully Understood that the Chamber Will not follow the Scottish Alliance in its new proposals, so that the proposed amalgamation is not likely to take place. Pigs of large breed, £10; ditto of SnAll breed, £ll.' COStrizomnsei Skx.-The savans have been trying for years to solve the problem of controlling sex in animals. About every other year some philosopher exclaims, Eureka, I have found it, but the facts in the case soon, cover him with confusion. We are inclined to the opinion that this power of controlling sex in man or animals is one of the powers specially withheld by the Creator. Possibly that veteran old stock-raiser' Jacob, who knew some cute tricks in the business that -would make a fortune for a modern agricultural editor, knew of it, for in his family there were twelve boys and only one girl, but if 'be did, he did not let the boys into the secret, and fortunately, for if he had girl babies would have been dreadful scarce for a thousand years. We have one farm that has been headquarters for females for five years, and this year the males are almost unanimous. Out of a hundred new comers in the pig yard, three-fourths are male. The provoking thing is just now everybody wants to buy females. And so it goes. The only being on earth that knows how to control sex is the queen bee. She lays drone eggs and female eggs just as she pleases, and keeps a business eye on the weather and honey crop in deciding, butalthough we have often asked her to whisper the secret to us so quietly, that the splillosophers can't ,hear it, , not even Father Clarkson or Orange Judd, not one of our queens will tell us. Provoking, of course, but how can you help it? Thus the secret is locked, up in the beehive-a secret that would' make' the' "lowa Homestead)* the richest paper in America-but the queen won't tell us. -Homestead. • ' WHY FARMERS Hen SOLD WHEAT FREECY.-The Net; York Produce Exchange Reporter says :-It has been per- sistently asserted on both sides of the Atlantic since harvest, by those who oueht to know, and, in many instances, do know better, that the extraordinary large sales of wheat by farmers at the almost unparalleled IoW prices which have prevailed since the harvest was gathered, is satisfactory_evidence of the great abundance of the crops; whereas, it proves nothing of the kind. There are a great many farmers in Great Britain who, from causes very generally well understood, are financi- ally in greatly straitened circumstances. There are many in this country similarly situated, but more particularly in the far West and North-West, where so much new land has in late years been brought under cultivation. There, many of the fanners are more or less In debt for their farms, for the buildings on them, and for agricultural machinery, &c.; and however low prices may be, they are compelled to sell at least a portion of their produce to meet their payments. But if they re- ceive for their wheat only 50 cents' per bushel as against 75 obtained last year-and that is about the difference -it will readily be seen that to get the same amount of money, three bushels have to be sold this year to two last year-an increase of 50 per cent. As the situation in Great Britain is, in its effects at least, not unlike that -in this country, the comparatively heavy deliveries of wheat there since harvest, in proportion to the size of the crop, are similarly accounted for. It will thus be seen that very heavy deliveries in the first four to six months after harvest at extremely low prices is no evi- dence of large yields, but is perfectly consistent with an average crop, since, in fact, it is the very low prices that have enforced the heaviest deliveries; and, 'conversely, the heaviest deliveries have, to a very considerable ex- tent, enforced the very low prices. Burreansn.-At a meeting of the Society of 'Arts, held on the 10th inst., Mr. Anton Jurgens read a paper on " Butterine or Oleomargarine Butter." As Mr. Jurgens is one of the proprietors of the largest manufactories of binterine in the world, his paper was naturally compli- mentary to that commodity. Yet he was graciously pleased to admit that "it is not pretended that butterine does, or. ever can, take the place of the best fresh but- ter." He proceeded to urge, however, that the demand for edible fats in the United Kingdom was so large that the supply of pure butter cannot meet the requirements of consumers. He estimated that about 248,000,000 pounds of butter are produced annually in the king- dom; but allowing a quarter of a pound per head of the population every week, the quantity required would be about 455,000,000 pounds, leaving a deficiency of 207,000,000. This deficiency. he thoueht, could be best met by a supply of butterine. Mr...jurgens Admitted that it was not right to sell butterine as butter, but de- nied that a great industry should be suppressed because there were a few cheats connected with it But Mr. Otto Hehner, speaking as a public analyst, said that very few people sold butterine under its proper name; "it was nearly always sold as butter, and herein lay the great evil." Mr. Hehner is by no means disposed to endorse the flattering remarks made by many authorities in re- lation to this sham -butter. Anyone listening to the paper, he said, would gather the impression that this was practically butter, except for a little butyric acid. He asserted, on the other hand, that it only resembled butter in its consistency; in every other respect it was totally unlike it. Butter, he added, had an absolutely unique composition amongst fats, and there was no other analogous to it. It was very easily saponified, and saponification being one of the processes of diges- tion, it was, therefore, easily digested-far more easily than any other fat, with the exception of cod-liver oil. The building of silos is an expense quite unnecessary; and another step is gained towards very economical and advantageous storage of green crops without danger of injury from the usual excess of humidity and rainfall to which the British climate is I subject; and also to effect of producing a greatly in- creased quantity of fodder in every respect—as it ap- pears to me—acceptable to the stock, and of improved value for feeding purposes. Although the stack was effectually "tucked" and relieved of all looseoutsides, there remained about nine inches thick of rotten grass, as well at top as at sides, but probably not more than would result from storing in a silo, although it has re- mained altogether uncovered with thatch or other pro- tection, excepting from portions of the refuse placed on the top, the hardness of the stack (up to the top) quite defying any penetration of moisture or power to decay. Large quantities of sap or juice escaped from the rick during its construction, which was decidedly sweet-tasted, as of saccharine contents, as well as quite saline, although without any supply of sugar or salt or other improving ingredients. REAR AND Fa-max.—ln an article by Mr. S. Macdonald, read a fortnight ago, the writer goes in for "rearing and fattening." He says:—" An experienced farmer, who has been eminently successful in the rearing and fattening of stock, and to whom I am indebted for much useful information, tells me that he has found it decidedly more profitable to rear and fatten than simply to fatten. The system formerly was to buy in cattle almost fully grown' and fatten them for slaughter. Latterly, he hes taken to the buying of calves and rearing them, and fattening them off when from 24 to 28 months old. And as this latter system has Veen found decidedly more profitable than the former, a few words as to the plan of operations may be useful. My friend goes to the. fairs in Aylesbury dairying districts in August, and buys calves 10 or 12 days old. He pays from £3 to £3 10s. for them, not grudging a few shillings extra when he knows the calves are bred from a good class of cows. They are mostly of a good class of shorthorn crosses, chiefly from mixed bred dairy cows and shorthorn bulls. For two weoks after being taken to their new quarters these calves get new milk—two quarts in the morning and the same quantity in the evening. By degrees a , little skim milk is introduced. The skim milk is scalded '-by being put into tins, which are inserted into vessels filled with hot watcr; The sliinunitic is continued for about I eNil a ef "-- e months, a e prepare hies, . g.ven when the calves are about six weeks old. Sweet fresh hay is placed within their reach as soon as they will eat it. A little bean-meal is found to do well in the early food of the Calves, the bean-meal being sometimes mixed with cut chaff or hay. For a few days at first the calves are tied up to prevent sucking. They are then allowed to run in a loose box, and they get outside a good deal and have plenty of fresh air and exercise. As a rule they are weaned from milk by abput the middle of November, yilien they get bean-meal, crushed oats, and -a little ' pulped_roots, all given in one mixture. They are turned out to grass as early as the weather and the supply of grass will permit. The hand food is continued for about two weeks after the youngsters are put to the grass. This point is specially worthy of attention, and it is often much neglected. I mean the carrying of the stock from one season and system of feeding into another. It is well to avoid sudden changes—better far to make the change gradually, taking care that the animals do not lose condition, or get upset by any sudden change. When visiting my friend the other week I saw in one field 35 yearlings, which had been reared in the way de- scribed. The field had carried one of these yearlings to each acre during the whole season' .and maintained be- sides a small lot of sheep. A few days before my visit the yearlings had been valued by a competent man as worth £l3 a head, and their average age would have been at that time about 13 months."

When he came to settle down to goin' to theft house more than elsewhere, he was better plemed with gettia' out and Brother Juniper an' Ruth (ilayler,blushin' and tremblin', bein' married then and there before my 'em than ever; but whether 'twas Anna or Jenny or Ruth? —that was she p'int poor June was a-wrestling with in- eyes, an' my drivin' home to the Gaylers in my best style. "You can imagine how the village was stirred up when ternally, for weeks an' weeks. That fall his uncle Jared next day part o' the story got out. Only part; for all the Kittery died an' left him the Stone farm; an' brother said I widow's folks kept Anna's share in it still as a mouse, an' so that he'd really ought to pick out a wife and settle down. did June an' me. Everybody was wantia' to know Why in "One night I found it out. He let me understand, very sheepishly, just how he felt. 'You see, brother Ebenezer,' the world them two young folks'd been married in that queer sudden way! Nobody outside of us two families ever found he said, am terribly peeplexed, an' suppose I should find after I was married that I made a mistake.' out. As for Anna, she was just as delighted any woman could be. She'd suspected bow Ruth felt and Jane too, all "'Well, Jane,' says I, 'don't see that you're likely to get far enough on to make a mistake. A man ,who don't' along, an' had hoped that after this joke was all over, brother might think some day seriously o' Ruth. But, of course, know his own mind had better draw lots for a /partner.' I Spoke rather contemptuous, I dare say. she'd no notion of so sudden a wind-up of the thing, in just "Brother Juniper jumped up from his chair by the table the way she wished. As for Ruth—why, she made June the with a sort of angry sparkle in his eye; but ,he gave a short best and lovin'est wife in the world, an' he's been as happy laugh. Not a bad notion, Eben, says he. I sat by the with her as the day is long at the farm." table, occasionally sayin' a word here an' there with re- ference to the three girls; how Anna was so well educated an' Jenny such a first-rate house-keeper, an' Ruth such a pretty, sensible sort of a young ,female,—all [more to tease June a little than anything else. All at once, June jumped up. He had three pieces o' paper in his hand. Blest if be hadn't written on one of them Anna,' on another 'Jane,' an' 'Ruth' 'on the last.' 'There,' says he, shakin' 'em together in my hat,' much obliged to you .for your good advice Brother Ben. I'm goin' to draw for one of those girls. Whichever name I get—she's the one I'm goin' to ask to be Mrs. Juniper Kittery before Sabberday." "I laughed, takin' the hull matter as a foolish joke. Ala right,' says I, hold the hat.' So I did. June shut his eyes and jammed in his fist. Read it oat ! ' says Ito him. Anna 'he answers, rather slowly an' as it not so astonish- in'ly I;appyfied. He tossed away the paper an' said no more. Thinks me, 'June has got some sort of an in'nard preference for one o' them sisters, after all: and he don't know it, but it isn't for Anna.' "I never thought seriously of that caper we two had cut that evenin', until Saturday night, when just as I was closin' up the house, last one to go to bed, in steps Jane. "I've done it, Eben,' says he, with a sing'lar sober face. "'June!' says I' not Anna-d.' "'Yes,' he answers, 'l've Anna-d; not Jeney-d nor Rath-d. Don't you recollect last Monday evenin' ? That settled it. I've abided by that piece o' paper. She said she'd have me. It's done; an' I'm glad.' "Well,' said I, 'I give you joy, June; though I must say your way o' clearin' up your doubts ain't to my taste for common usage. Anna's a fine girl.' "'But that ain't all, brother Eben,' he went on. Anna's got an amazin' queer notion o' gettin' married. 'Teeems she's been a readin' some novels or stories and so forth- an' I guess they've made her fanciful. She thinks' that it'd be grand fun to surprise our folks along with ma and the other two girls, by us two bein' married on the sly, the night be- fore Christmas—an' then comin' home and tellin"em. I don't see any fun in that—not a bit! I think it looks rather foolish. But Anna—l declare I don't know what's got info her !--she will hold to it! The long and short of it is that' You've promised to do it,' says I. " ' Yes,' he answers. 'I suppose it'll make a stir ; but that can't be helped. I've promised. None of her folks nor oars must know anything about our engagement yet. On Christmas Eve I'm to call for Anna with the sleigh. I want you to come along too, Eben. go straight down to Battle Hill, to Parson Latham's an' have the knot tied. Then we'll come back an' let it out to the Widow an' Jenny an' Ruth. After that, the hull crowd of us will pile down here; an' have the pleasure of seen' father an mother and . everybody here open their eyes. That's Anna's Idea. As I said, I don't specially admire it—but, still, I give In to it.' "Thinks me; Master Frank, there's some game here that clever girl's up to! Mebbe—an' mebbe not. But I told Juniper I'd go with him on Christmas night. You two can sit in the back seat and I'll drive,' I said. June laughed. See here, Jane,' I says a moment later just as we went up the stairs, 'I hope that you'll never let Anna know how it was that you picked her out from her sisters.' "June blushed an' stammered something like Cert'nly not—it would have come out this way in any case '—an' went into his room. 'H'm ' I thought, 'l'm not so sure of that. I must give you a good talk, to-morrow.' "When I tried to talk, however, Jane wouldn't hear to me. 'He knew what he was doing '—so he persisted. Anna was the girl who would make him just the wife he wanted; an' the Stone Farm was all ready for them to move in right away.' He had 'rather taken a, fancy, he re- membered, to Ruth at one time, but that hadn't amounted to anything.' I said no more, but I kept up quite a thinkin.' " the night before Christmas of that year was as clear as a bell. There was three feet of snow all over the country. At seven o'clock, June an' I drove to the Gayler's door. Almost before I got the horses still, a figure all tightly wrapped up slipped out the gate. Poor Anna! She seemed terribly nervous as June helped her into the seat by him. " ' Oh, June,' I heard her say, I a'most wish I'd never thought o' this Billy plan.' "June did almost all the talkin', while we spun down the street and out on the Battle Hill turnpike. Anna sat with his arm half round her and seemin' for the first time to realise that she was taking an important step in life. "I hardly looked at 'em after Anna was in her seat by June. The horses was in a complete gale. I had to give them my hull attention. It required whip an' reins an' everything else to make 'em behave. The parsonage at Battle Rill is only two miles and a half from our village. We fairly flew over the road. Then, just before we passed the big gates that lead to Squire Loftus's place, Dollar gave a lunge. That set Prince it-goin'. Before I could help it, they wheeled sharp, overset the sleigh, an' ran themselves up to their shoulders In a snowbank. There they stood. We, meanwhile, were pickin' ourselves up as best we could. "In the name of goodnes !—' I heard Juniper shout in a voice that frightened me half to death, I scrambled up and looked at the other two. It was bright moonlight. There stood brother Juniper. In front of us was the person who'd come with us in the sleigh—Ruth Gayler. "Before either of us could say a word she burst right out a-cryin'. Then followed the queerest, the most mixed-up and ginerally surprisin' explanation of what had took place an' how it had come about, thit ever I expect to hear in all my mortal life. Most of the time Juniper just stood there, pale and bewildered. I put the best part of the bad ques- tions there was to ask, holding the horses' heads. It must have looked a curious picture. "Our hired help and Lucretia Tabb, who'd been dress- makin' at the Gaylers' for a couple o' weeks, off an' on, was great friends. That night when Brother June had drawn that lot,—we'd ought both to have been ashamed of our- selves for such foolishness,—our Amira'd overheard the hall

. . . . . Ebenezer stopped. Young Parson Frank thanked him laughingly for his story, and, after a little discussion of it, departed. Just as he was getting out of earshot, Ebenezer called out," Mr. Frank !' . ___ ...

" Well," replied Latimer, wheeling round. " Oh, nothin'," responded Ebenezer with a. rather embar- rassed expression of countenance—" but—but I thought that you'd like to know that—that Heldy an' me—have de- cided on gettin' married next month. Now get away !—I won't be plagued. That's the reason I haven't: told you be- fore!" Here the axe came down so energetically that the astonished and delighted young man did not dare to clap Ebenezer on the back. He remained pouring out his feli- citations from a safe distance with persistency and mirth, until it occurred to him that Huldy was in the kitchen to also be congratalited —From the Detroit Free Frees Christmas Number.

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

• POULTRY IN 1884.* - The year Eighteen Hundred and Eighty-four will be remarkable as the first year in which poultry have been included in the agricultural returns of Great Britain. Statistics and figures are often sneered at, but they have a very decided influence upon the 'mind. Generalities can be put on one side as the imaginings of those who utter them,. but figures 'may not be so treated. When reliable, they represent hard, stern facts, which cannot be gainsaid, but demand attention from all, The figures issued by the Agricultural Department of the Privy Council are both hard and stern, showing that those who have for years pointed out how farmers have neglected an important part of farm work have been right in their contentions. For this nation to pay foreign countries three and a quarter million pounds sterling in one year for eggs and poultry, and yet only to maintain three fowls to every five acres of cultivated land, when the number might be trebled or quadrupled very easily, is a*startling fact, but one which needed these undetuable figures to prove their truth to many minds. As we so recently dealt fully with this question, it is quite un- necessary that we should say more, except to remind our readers that the increase of productive power can- not be made en bloc, but must be done in detail. If every farmer and cottager will do`his share of the work, then the end will soon be arrived at; and with land at his disposal, food cheap, and time on his hands, there is no reason why, during the next year or two, the .produc- tion of eggs and poultry should not be enormously developed. Surely the thing is worth a trial, and whilst we do not urge poultry keeping as an entire remedy for agricultural depression, we believe it would do some- thing towards the ending of that depression. Small in itself, perhaps, yet in the words of the Scotch phrase, " Every mickle makes a mucide." This year will also be noteworthy from the fact-that the Royal Agricultural Society has resolved to again in- clude poultry in its annual show. For years this step has been advocated, but the failure of some 17 years ago, when fowls formed part of the Bury St. Edmund's Show, has heretofore been a deterrent to " The Royal" Council. At last, however, they have yielded to the strong representations made to them on the subject, and next July we hope to see a really good show at the Moor Park. It is intended to make this show for farmers and breeders, not fanciers, and to that end the varieties re- presented will be restricted to the useful breeds, as dis- tinct from ornamental ones. We are not able as yet to give particulars of the classification, but will go more fully into it when the schedule is issued, which will be early in the new year. We hear that the plan adopted is to be a novel one, namely, that a cock and three hens are to be exhibited in each pen, but, if this is the ease, we fear the arrangement is a mistake. However, on that question we shallhave more to say later on. It is suffi- cient to know' that fowls are to be included in the show. That is a great gain, and we hope the exhibition may be so decided a success that there will be no fear of its again being omitted from the Royal Agricultural So- ciety's schedule. As the prize list will be a liberal one, we hope that farmers, especially Lancashire farmers, will support it by their entries, and breed suitable birds to compete therein. Thus much for the past year. Now a few words about that which is coming. To secure success hatch- ing should take place early, and if the pens are not yet mated together no time should be lost in carrying out the work. Early hatched two-year-old hens are what we like best, either mated with a vigorous cock, or one hatched very early last year. Failing this arrange- ment, early hatched pullets that have been laying for some time should be selected, and have with them a vigorous two-year-old gentleman. Either of these should soon give strongly fertilised eggs, and produce hardy chickens. We need not say that pure bred, well de- veloped birds are the best, and even if they cost a little more in the first place they are the cheapest in the eft], as the progeny are the most satisfactory. Only by hav- ing good stock an good progeny be secured. What that stock is must be left to the individual choice, and to the circumstances of place and demand. But the farmer or cottager, who takes a real interest in his poultry, will soon discover which are the best birds for him, and it shall be our object in this column, as it has been in the past, to give him all the help we can. We shall be glad at any time to answer questions addressed to us on matters oi this kind.

div.head: SEASONABLE HINTS.
div.p: SEASONABLE HINTS.

Mien the breeding pens are already mated, as they will be in many cases, it is important to tee that the cocks have sufficient to eat, for neglect of this simple thing often is the cause of unfertile eggs. Some cocks will not eat until all their hens are satisfied, and if they are not separately provided for, they will not obtain any food at all, a result of which is that the cock gets thin and weak, his natural vigour is lost, and the eggs arc not fertilised. If this is suspected, it is better to feed the cock separately, either before or after the hens, or his gallantry may prove disastrous.

I measured my- self, an' I hope Gabrielll miss me at the final roundup if I hadn't grown six inches in two weeks. I couldn't account for it for some time till at last I tumbled to the fact that thar war holes in my boots, and the infernal soil got in thar, an' done its work."—.Detroit Free Press.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING
R
bandage,

• Young Cauliflower plants, or those sown in August, will need protecting during severe frost. Up to the present some of ours have been entirely exposed to the weather, whilst others have had an old glass light placed over them far the past three weeks, with the view of protecting them from a superabundance of moisture, which may of itself be harmless, but where followed by a severe frost it acts most perniciously on the delicate vegetable tissue. Cauliflowers will amply "repay for the use of A frame, as the produce from plants so sheltered will be ready for use some weeks before the spring ones. Indeed, with the assistance of pm) of these, and attention in other ways, we have cut cauliflowers the first week in June, which is about the time the spring-sown ones are fit for planting. Another method of furnishing protection is to place a deep squire ham- per—or any other shape for the matter of that, but as the beds usually partake of some form of a, square, we give preference to that shape—over which old sacks, or any other protecting fabric, may beeplaced. Over these again, straw, bracken, dry grass, or leaves may be placed, and these slightly covered over to prevent blow- ing away. Boxes may also be inverted over the plan* and covered in a similar manner, though hampers are much the best if the plants are covered for any length of time, inasmuch as they soon assume a blanched appearance, in consequence of the darkness, and espe- cially the total exclusion of air. The sunny side of the hamper can be daily uncovered, if there is any sun, 'if only for an hour. This will slightly warm them, as well as supply them with light, without which no class of plants can long maintain their verdure. There are other contrivances which gardeners have recourse to for protecting these and other plants. For instance, for the protection of small Lettuce, sticks are placed obliquely on both sides of the bed, and intersect at the top, where they are bound together with string, which strengthens them considerably. If placed a yard apart, with a longitudinal rod resting in the armpit formed by them, and secured to them, we have the skeleton of a tent, for which we must leave it to the ingenuity of the cottager to provide'a covering. Light litterer bracken is occa- sionally lightly laid three or four inches thick on the plants. Lettuce are not so tender as Cauliflowers, but for all that they manifest their gratitude for protection from frost by putting on a much better appearance after the frost is gone than those which have been exposed to its crippling influence for any length of time. tram CIIRRAkTS.—Of bush fruit these are usually the first to be pruned, because it is considered that birds do not interfere with the buds. Never before last year have we known them to violate the trust we hitherto placed in them, though they may have done so to a slight ex- tent, but last year they totally stripped some trees when the flower buds were visible in their sheath of embryo leaves. In pruning black currant trees first cut away smile of the thicker branches close to the bottom. By doing this annually the trees are prevented from being too crowded. All weakly shoots of the past season's growth, as well as some of the strong, are moved if at all crowded, so that by the time the buSh is completed none of the young growths appear any closer than six inches to each other, which would be tar to crowded if only that distance all over the tree. All good fruit growers are very particular to have their 'trees of all kinds well thinned out. We have never 'heard of, any one regretting over doing it. THE FRONT GARDEN. Cottagers and .others are puzzled to know what sort of edging is the best for the beds and borders in their small gardens. The edging may be formed of either dead or living articles. The first are no doubt the cheapest in the end, for after once they are properly placed they require no. further atten- tion. Live edgings, which are formed of dwarf box, grass, or thrift, require trimming as well as repairing occasionally. Of these three we prefer thrift, as it gives the least trouble always looks green, and, unlike the box, it does not die 'off. It is moreover, very showy when covered-with its rose-coloured flower heads. Old- fashioned gardens are the places to find this in use. Tan Wmow.—The temperature of the water used for the plants in the window must not be overlooked dur- ing frosty weather. It is a rule with all good plant cul- tivators to have the temperature of the 'water a little higher than that of the apartment the plants are growing in. This is as applicable to the cottage window as to the most costly conservatory. No doubt many at this time of the year disregard this, and draw the water from the pipe, pump, or well and apply it to the plant, as they have been in the habit of doing during the summer, which even then is bad practice, on acc.Dunt of the dis- parity of temperature between it and the *soil the plants are growing in.

GYPT AND TH.E f.OUDAN. PROGRESS OF THE EXPEDITION.—' AN ADVANCE THROUGH THE DESERT. I(nuel, SATUILDAY.—Tbe pinnace of KM S. Monarch has eeturned here from hierawi, having made the trip in nine Moms. The distance is seventy miles. The arrival or the .Pinnace at Merawi much immessed the netivee, and at the request of the Vakeel she steamed some distance beyond the 'yen, in order to prove to the friendly tribes that the eritish were advancing. Koren, SUNDAY.—The let Battalion of the South Stefforcl- Ihire Regiment (38th), 550 strong. started up the river to- • Y. The eight was very impressive and eff ,ctive. The Use are in fine health and ready for anything, inured to the .11,....erk of rowing, and longing only for the more exciting et ftehting. The Black Watch is expected to win Lord ewolseleyni prize of £lOO offered to the battalion which Thelma the distance between Sarrae and Debbeh in the ' Anickest time and with the fewest accidents. KORTI, MONDA.Y.—The following is the position of the •'British advance r—eieneral Earle will collect the lefantry -brigade at Hamdab about the Fourth Cataract, from which '4loiWs he will take measures to punish the Moaassir tribe ~lor the murder of Colonel Stewart. General Earle will then Inleh on to Abu Earned, and open the desert road between ',that place and Korosko, whence stores will be forwarded. she mounted infantry and the Guards' Camel Corps, under command Of Brigadier-General Stewart, will leave here e‘enonorrow with a large convoy of camels, laden with stores e-for Gakdul, a distance of ninety miles. A detachment of 'lhe Guar le• Camel Corps will remain behind in garrison tere to guard the stores. The mounted infantry will bring ack the convoy of camels from Galsdul after they have been •Itnloaded, and then the headquarters, the rest of the Camel Corp, the Artillery, and 19:h Hussars will move forward ina Gakdul and Shendy to Khartoum. A garrison will be eft at Kuril, which will constitute the advanced base. The , :telegraph ire to Merewi has been cut by the rebels. CAIRO, SATURDAY. According to an efficiel telegram "Icien Suakin, letters from Massewah announce that the gar- •!risen at Kassala has made a sortie and driven back the _rebels. Money is much wanted at Kassala for the purchase ; `tlf provisions. CAIRO, SIINDAY.—A telegram was received here from the udir of Dongole, dated the 26th inst., stating that a native Khartoum has arrived at Dongola, having taken a fort- , 'gilt to accomplish the journey. He stopped at Drudar- Mame by order of General Gordon for four days, in order to • f ether information regarding the Mandi'a position, and to urine RIG Dongola. The messenger reports that the Mandi and his followers are suffering severely from famine, and that the dead bodies. of several of their number are to be 'wen unburied in the surrounding country. FRANCE.—RIOTOUS SOCIALIST MEETING. Peers SUNDAY.—A. meeting of Socialists was held to-day in the Salle Levis, at which 3,000 persons were present. The formation of a bureau gave rise to a tumultuous scene, as the Monarchists wished to secure the nomination of their candidate. A hand-to-hand conflict cussed, the seats being used as weapons by the combatants. Three or four persons were injured. The meeting subsequently adopted an order of the day convoking unemployed working men to hold an open-air meeting en January 15th. FRANCE AND CHINA. Pants, TUESDAY.-An official &vetch received this morn- ing announces that the French troops have made a movement in advance from Tuyin Quan, in the course of which they inflicted considerable loss upon the Chinese. The loss on French side was insignificant. PARIS, TUESDAY EVENING.—The journal La Liberte un- derstands that instructions have been sent to the French Commanders in the far East pointing to a more virrous ac- tion in Tongain and Formosa. A telegram has been received in London stating that great irritation has been produced among the Chinese officials at Canton in consequence of the facilities given to French vessels to make Hong Kong: the base of operations to carry on the war, and that the export of provisions to that place will shortly be prohibited. Pants, TEIESDA4 —General Brier e de Lisle telegraphs that the recent engagement at Hong Yen was with pirates, who lost 300 men kill and two cannons, the French lasing no men. Their names were respectively Samuel and Moritz Woltitz. EXTLIQUAKE IN CARINTHIA. VIENNA MONDLY.—A severe sbeck of earthquake was felt yesterday at Jarvis, in Carinthia. The military from Gran were sent for, and restored order.

PORTUGAL.—TIIE PEERS. Lrsnos, SATIIRDAY.—Senhor Fontes Periera de Mello, the Premier, to-day submitted to the Chamber of Deputies the draft of a supplement to the Constitution which will have the effect of modifying certain of the articles. The most important of the projected reforms has reference to the Chamber of Peers, which, it is proposed, shall hebeeforth be composed of 100 life Peers, appointed by the King, and 50 elected by an indirect process. 13th the life and elected peers are to be chosen from the same social classes. The elected portion of the Chatnher may ba dissolved by the King.

THE NICARAGUA TREATY. NEW YORK SUNDAY.—A. despatch from Washington published here states that daring the debate in the secret sitting of the Set.ate upon the 20,h inst. upon the Nicaragua Treaty, one of the speakers emphasised the fact that the tre ‘ty placed the Senate in an embarrassing position. He pointed out that if it failed the White would be understood by Europe as a practical abandonment by the United States of their Isthmian policy, which, it was urged, would be a great humiliation. UNITED STATES.— THE ASSUMPTION OF OFFICE BY THE DEMOCRATS. NEW Yons.,MormAY.—A letter from Governor Cleveland to the National Civil Service Reform League is published to-day, in which the President-elect declares that he regards himself pledged is Civil Service reform, having promised the people to enforce the Act. Efficiency, fitness. and de- votion to public duty are (continues the letter) the condi- tions for continuance in the public service. Although the coming Administration xvoald be Democratic, due regard to the people's interest would not permit faithful party work to be always rewarded by appointments to offica, while tae Democrats might expect all proper consideration. GERMAN ANNEXATIONS. MELBOURNE, WEDNESDAY. -- Mr. Murray Smith, agent- general for Victoria in London, bas been instructed to make a vigorous protest against the recognition of German claims to New ninea, and to declare that if the territory in ques- tion be not claimed back, and the New Hebrides preserved, the feeling of estrangement on the part of the colonists from the mother country will increase. SOUTH AFRICA.— BRITISH ACQUISITION ON THE ZULU COAST. A telegram from Durban states that the point at which the British flag has been hoisted on the coast of Zululand it( Bt. Lucia. Sir Henry Balwer has asked the Hume Gov- eminent to approve of this step. The military preparations for the Bechuanaland expedition are vigorously proceeding along the line of march between Clapetown and Kimberley, and the recruiting of volunteers goes on actively in bath places, there being no lack of eager applicants for employ- ment. The intentions of the B )ers remain inscrutable. THE BECHUANALAND EXPEDITION. CAPETOWN, DEC. MM.—Large and enthusiastic public meetings have been held at Capetown, Kimberley, and Port Elizabeth, at which reeolutiens were passed condemning the Ministerial settlement in Bechuanaland, expressing loyalty to the Queen, and satisfaction at the appointment of Sir Charles Warren. Sir Charles Warren is now arranging the plan of campaign.

_ GLAIEBROOK The annual tea meeting in connection wish the Primitive Methodist Chapel was held on Christ- mas evening. A large number sat down to tea. The public meeting was addressed by Rev. It. Crewdson, superinten- dent of the Leigh circuit, He dwelt on the matters in dis- pute with the late members of the church. Messrs John3on Shuttleworth, Neye, and other friends also addressed the meeting. GLAZEBROOE SALVATION ARMY under the leadership of Messrs Bradbury and Bridge (late Primitive Methodist Church), held two or three meetings on Christmas Day, in their new place of worship. In the evening they had a tea followed by a public meeting which was well attended. It was presided over by Mr. Bridge. Several members of the army addressed the meeting. Much interest was manifested in its gatherings all day. RIXTOM WESLEYAN CRAPEL.—Tho annual tee party has been held in the above chapel, when a goodly number of the friends and scholars sat down to a substantial tea, pre- sided over by Mesdames. Down, Rays, and Tongue. After the tqa a public meeting was held: the chair was occupied by the 'Rev. R. Dilton, superintendent of the circuit. Ex- , cellont addresses were delivered by Messrs Hopewell, Jack- son, Williams, and Whitfield. Mr. Clarke, of Durham, gave two recitations in the Lancashire dialect. Recitations and hymns were rendered by the children and the choir, and a very enjoyable evening was spent. I Itteam.—The usual Sunday school festival in connection I with the Wesleyan Chapel, was hold in the schoolroom on Friday. The school was well filled, and to a good tee ample justice was done. The room was beautifully decorated. The minister of the circuit presided over the public meeting at the close of the tea. After the opening address et the chairman, prizes were distributed to the children whose conduct during the year was of average merit. The choir sang some appropriate pieces at intervals. Two excellent dialogues were given as well as recitations by the children. The interest of the meeting was well sustained to the end.

div.p: The returns of the National Lifeboat Institution for the I past year show that during 1834 621 lives were rescued, 17 vessels were saved from being totally wrecked or were brought safely into harbour, and 159 lives have been saved by means of shore boats, making a total of 780 lives saved through the instrumentality of the Institution. FOUR PERSONS BURNT TO DEATEL—At nine o'clock on Wednesday night the London firemen were called to an out- break of fire which had occurred in a private house in Holles-street, Clare Market. The flames burst out from the i house very fiercely, and caused great excitement n the crowded neighbourhood. Although it was too late to save any lives, for the flames had by that time obtained too strong a hold, an entry was effected immediately the fire was sufficiently subdued to admit of this being done. On the first floor were found the charred remains of a woman, subsequently identified as Mrs. Black; on tin second floor , two bodies burnt to a cinder were discovered; and on the ' third floor a fourth body was found. A later account states that the bodies found: were those of two men and two women. They have been recognised as those of Mr. Alex- ander Clarke, aged 66 ; Mrs. Alice Clarke, aged 58; Mrs. Black, aged GO ; and Mr. Mandeque, aged GO. THE ALLEGED MURDER OF A RUSSIAN SAILOIN—The hearing of the charge against William Rauscher and Ferdi- nand Kollpein, second mate and boatswain respectively of the American ship I. F. Chapman, of having caused the death of a Russian sailor named Jansen whilst at sea, was concluded on Thursday before the Birkenhead Stipendiary Magistrate. The master and mate of the vessel were called, I and deposed that Jansen was an idle and incapable member of the crew, who shipped at San Francisco on the pretence of being an able seaman. Ile never made any compl lint to the captain or mate of having been subjected to the brutalities spoken of by previous witnesses. These wit- nesses did not see him lashed up in the lower rigging, but considered such a method of punishment to be rather severe for a man in weak health. Both prisoners denied having struck or kicked Jansen, whose body after death bore no ' marks of external injury. The magistrate remanded ' them until Monday, in order that he may fully consider ; the contradictory evidence which has been laid before him. HAYDOCH Sr. JAMES'S V. EARLE,TOWN.—The &et teams of these clubs met on the ground of the latter at Wargrave Moss on the afternoon of Chrletmes Day, when there was a large concourse of spectators. The home team were minus their two full backs During the first half the visitors played up hill, and for some time possessed a slight advan- tage. After about 15 minutes' play the St. Jamee'l team scored a goal amid the cheers of their eupaorttre. This was the only point registered before half time, up to which period the play had been on the whole very even On the change of ends the Earlestoniane tried hard te score, but were net with splendid play on the part of their opponents. The latter, however, were gradually forced on the defensive, and 20 minutes from the close the ware was equalised to the intense delight of the Ettlestown spectators. The remainder of the play wee all in favour of the home eleven, who met with hard lines, and failed to secure an additional point. & good and exciting game thus resulted in a draw of one goat each. J. WRALLEy'S TEAM (EARLEsTOWN) V. C. M. LIND- SAY'S Teem (Ltynepooe).-1 very fast and exciting match neis played at Wargrave Moss, Earlestown, on Friday, when a very strong team from Liverpool, under the captaincy of C. M. Lindsay, met a team of the Earlestown club, captained by J. Whalley. Tne latter was the first team of the club, with the exception that Dagnall and Sims were unable to play, and their places were filled by second team men. Througbeut the play was very exciting, but the home team had the advantage, and held the lead to the finish, when they had secured a capital victory by three goals to two. Teams—J Whalley's team: J Harrison, goal; R Green and J Green, backs; J Danbury, R Bowler, and Whalley, hill barks; IV Rich and J Ellison, right wing; J Appleton. centre; W Murray and J Ogden, left wing. C M Lindsay's team: C Jolt& (8 Benedict's), goal ; J Mil- roy (St Peter's) and H Richerds (Everton), backs; A E Welsh (St Petei's), A. McLennon (St Peter's), and 3 Pickup (St Peters), half backs; C M Lindsay (Everton), B Cope. land (St Peters), S Williams (Newton), J F Whittle (Everton), and W Finlay (Everton), forwards. The players and a few friends afterwards sat dovia to tea at the Sunbeam lan, and subsequently spent a very enjoyable evening. EARLESTOWN V. OstvESTRY —The Earlo.stown first team journeyed to Osvrestry on Saturday and met the first team of the 03westry club, the winners and present holders of the Welsh Challenge Cue. The visit of the Earlestown team, as runners-UP for last season's Liverpool and District Chal- lenge Cap, created some interest in the district, and there I was a large concourse of spectators. The home club turned Out its full strength, with the exception of Farmer, who was unable to play; while Whalley (captain) Was unable to ploy with Earlestown. T. e home eleven won the toss, and shortly after half.pest two Dagaall carted the leather for Earlestown. For a considerable time the game was very even and exciting and both goals were in turn endangered. The Earlestoniane, however, possessed a slight advantage, and after about 20 minutes' play Sims scored their first goal. The Oswestrians tried bard to score before half-time, but owing to the good defensive play of their opponents they were unable to do so. On the change of ends both elevens kept up their form remarkably well, and splendid play on the part of both was warmly applauded. Ten minutes had only elapsed when Sims from a free kick in front of the Oswestry goal scored a second goal for Earlestown. Im- mediately afterwards the home forwards made an attack on the visitors' goal, and after an excitlig scrimmage Appleton threw the leather outside the posts. The Oswes- trians, however, alleged that the ball had pre- viously been through the the goal, and to the surprise at the Earlestown team the referee allowed a goal. The point was disputed by the visitors, who after some demur, restarted the game. They began by making another attack on the OswEstry uprights, and after some splendid passing Ellison shot the leather through, and thus added a third goal for Earlestown. The remaining few minutes of play was hotly contested, and amid the hearty cheers of their supporters Oswestry notched a second goal from a free kick close to the Earlestown posts. No other point being registe,ed when time was called Earlestown, after a splen- didly fought game,bad succeeded in defeating the Welsh Cup holders by three goals to two. Teams :—Earlestown : J Appleton, goal; R Green and J Green, backs; It Hawker, J Duxbury, and A Clayton, halt-backs; W Bich and J Ellison, right-wing; A W Dagnall,' centre ; J Sims and J Ogden. left.wing ; umpire, Mr T Bell. Oswestry : Duncan, goal ; J Williams and Powell, backs; S Smith, M Evans, , and E Roberts, half-backs; 3 E Davies and F Brian right- wing; 3 Evans, centre; J Roach and T Davies, ; referee, Mr W H Gough, Oswestry F.C. LIVERPOOL CET TIE: EARLESTOWN WANDERERS V. LIVERPOOL STANLEY.—As stated last week, the decision of the committee of the Liverpool and District Football Aseo- dation that the Earlestown Wanderers v, Stanley tie in the cup competition should be played over again created a very bitter feeling among the supporters of the Wanderers' club. This found an outlet on Saturday. when the Stanley team met with a reception of an extraordinary character. It will be remembered that on the firet meeting of the two clubs the Wanderers won by three goals to two, but the Stanley team protested against the victory on several trifling grounds, and, as stated, the match was Ordered to be re-played. When the Stanley men arrived at Eallestown, on Saturday they found public feeling all against the as- sociation. In the that instance, the Earlestown people were grieved that the tie was declared postponed at one o'clock on the day it was fixed to be contested, through the associa- tion getting Stanley to take the place of Denbighshire in the district match. Then they claimed to have beaten Stanley, and on appeal by the latter the victory was an- nulled by the association, and the game ordered to be played again. The bitterness against the association was consequently very intense. The Stanley team was met at Earlestown by a large crowd of lads and young men, who had their hats garnished with bands of coloured paper bear. the word Fraud " printed in large letters. Each person carried an instrument of some sort, viz., tin pans, cans, and even old buckets, and the possesors of these looked upon it as their duty to make as much noise as posible on them with sticks. The Stanley players made their way through the town amid hooting and groaning, and each a reception the club Dever got before. A fog covered the ground, and the players could scarcely see across, much less from goal to goal at the commencement. Immediately after the start the Wanderers carried the ball up the field, and in less than a minute a shot from the centre scored the only goal of the match, which left the Wanderers the victors by one to nil. Just before half-time the fog lifted, and Stanley began to show some form, occasionally pressing their opponents. Champion playe I a brilliant goalkeeper, and Lowe was also good at back, but Shaw was the best of Stanley, and Wright in goal decidedly a success. The ground was hard. This second victory of the Wanderers created great enthusiasm amongst their supporters, and they were heartily cheered as they left the field. Writing to a Liverpool contemporary on Monday, a correspondent says: "All who had gone to Earlestown were heartily glad to leave it, and the proceed- ings of the day were a blot on the game of football and a disgrace to the club that permitted such rowdyism."

NOTES BY PIE WAY. Oa Saturday, in the second round of the Association Cup competition, the Druids beat Newtown. In the sixth round of the Scottish Association Cup competition, Renton beat Glasgow Rangers; Vale of Leven beat Thernliebank, at Thernliebank ; at Edinburgh the Hibernlans beat Annbank. At Glasgow, the Third Lanark beat Glasgow Northern; Kilmarnock and Lugar Boswell played a drawn game at Kilmarnock; Oar Boys, at Dundee, beat Arbroath; Queen's Park defeated Dumbarton, at Glasgow; Johnetone beat St. Mirrens, at Paisley; the Casuals beat Derby County, at Derby; Leek, who on Saturday will meet Queen's Park in the Association Cap competition, beat Aston Unity; at Bolton the Wanderers beat Walsall Swifts; the Old Fores- ters beat Old Westminsters ; Cambridgeshire beat Notting- hamshire, at Nottingham; Sheffield beat Hendon, at Shef- field ; Great Lever beat Westbromwich Albion ; Halliwell beat Airdrieonians; Deby Midland beat Staveley, at Derby. A movement is on foot, the object of which is the forma- tion of a Rugby Union for West Lancashire and border towns. Indeed, the arrangements are so far advanced that an executive committee has already been formed, and one or two excellent contests are being arranged in the hope that a further impetus will be given to the popu- larising of the sport in West Lancashire and the border towns. The Liverpool Courier, in a summary of the doings of local clubs, says :—" Warrington is another club that has shown a bold front, and with Wigan. Runcorn, and Widnes seems destined to take high rank in the Vi'est Lancashire and Border Towns Union. The St. Helens and the Recrea- tion although perhaps a trifle less fortunate than their neighbours, have little to complain about in the way of for- tune's smiles ; while Aspull telegrams denote a continuance of success. Newton and Sutton have had to struggle under exceptional local difficulties, but with an active spirit at work and aided by a powerful organisation, there is hope of a speedy revival of the Rugby code in these dtstricts." The same plper, in alluding to association clubs, stated that "Earleetown, or the silver-medalista,' as the rtinners•nn of last season prefer to be titled still enjoy a high reputation in the district, •notwithstanding the beating they received at Anfield, at the commencement of the season. That form was altogether wrong, and should the final of the Liverpool cup swain be fought out by Everton and Earlestown there will be a rare struggle for supremacy. Golborne and the Earlestown Wanderers in their best form are no mean oppon- ents." The Liverpool Daily Post, in an article on the pros- pects of the Liverpool cup, states that " Unless the unfore- seen happens the result will be very much an it was last season, when Everton and Earleetown ttied conclusions In the final."

CHHIST CHURCH -CHRISTMAS TREE AND SALE OF WORK ' A Christmas tree and sale of work was oprind in the Croft Schoolroom on Friday afternoon. Ile Jai. Hatton, on behalf of a large number of ratepiyers and. inhabitants of Croft, presented the Rector, the Rev. T. P. Kirkman:A.lW an illuminated address to place upon re- cord their appreciation of the valuable services the rev. gentleman had for the Last ten years gratuitously rendered as Chairman and Clerk to the School Board of the district. He said they thought the manner in which Mr. Kirkman had discharged the arduous duties of the office demanded their warmeet gratitude. (Applause.) They regretted his resijna- tion, and trusted his life might be crowned with prosperity. The address was signed by 157 residents of the district, and had been beat(' ully written by Mr. Calvert, Friars' Green, Warrington. Mr. Hatton read the address, which was as fellows :—'To the Rev. Thomas Pennington Kirkman, M.A., F.R.S. Rev. and Dear Sir,—We, the undersigned ratepayers and inhabitants of Seuthworth-with-Croft, de- sire to place upon record our appreciation of the valuable services you have for the past nine years gratuitously ren- dered as Chairman and Clerk to the School Board of toe above district. We feel that the uniform ability and geniality with which you have discharged the duties of your office demand our warmest gratitude. We regret that circumstances have led to your resignation, and we trust that many years of so active and useful a life may yet be granted you, and that peace and prosperity may attend the remainder of your days. We pray you to accept this address, not for its intrinsic worth, but as a token of the re- spect And the esteem with which we regard you." The Rector said it was a great pleasure to him to receive the address. It had been a great pleasure to him to act as chairman during the nine years, and he should always prize theaddrese he hal been presented with that afternoon. (Ap- plause.) The rev, gentleman then introduced Mr. L B. Weile, of Northwich, who opened the bazaar. Mr. Wells read a letter from the Rev. Canon Whitley, M.A., rector of Wargrave, the rural dean' stating that he was unable to be present, bat enclosing a donation of two guineas and wishing the undertaking evegy £llOOOB9. Con- tinuing, Mr. Wells said he had no doubt they all keew that the proceeds of the sae ware to be devoted to necessary re- pairs and alterations The church was given to them fifty years ago, and had, since that time, cost them very little. He was sure that their hearts were all right, for the address which had been nresented to his fatker-in-law shoved that the hearts of the people of Croft were of the right kind. (Applause.) In conclusion, he mentioned that the church- wardens had received £5 each from the following land- owners of the district :—Sir Richard 'Cross, M.P., Mr. Philips, M.P., Mr. Withington, and Mr. Himmers. (Ap- plause.) The sale was then proceeded with, amongst those present being the Rev. T. P. Kirkman Mrs Kirkman, the 11.3,7. W. H. and Mrs. Williams (Pedgate), Dr. Blackie, Mr. W. Kirkman (Manchester), Mr. L. B. and Mrs. Welle,,Mr. and Mrs. Sou- thern, Mr. and Mrs. R. Owen (senr.), Mr. and Mrs. R. Oven (junr.), Mrs. Roberts (Hollins Green), Mrs. Seftoo, Mrs. Greenough, k 2. The stalls, which were well stocked with useful and fancy node, were presided, over AB follows :—Choir stall, Miss Ball and the female Members of the choir ; Mrs. Kirkman's stall, Mrs. Kirkman, Miss Kirkman, Miss Gawthorp, Miss Robinson • Mrs. Owen's stall, Mrs. Owen, Mrs. B mrdman, Miss Southern, and Miss Birchall ; refreshment stall, the Misses Bate (three), Miss Butch- The sale of work was re-opened on Saturday afternoon, and, as on the previous day, there was a large attendance, Very few articles were left at the close of the sale at 9 p.m., and these it is proposed to dispose of at a sale to be held at some future time. The Croft Drum and Fife Band played selections of music at intervals, in a creditable manner, under the conductorship of Mr. Ball, the bandmaster. Shortly after nine o'clock, the sale being closed, the Rector ascended the platform and said the bazaar had been one of the most successful undertakings of any kind that had ever taken place. The total receipts are £O5 Sc, besides previous , donations of cash.
