div.p: OVER THE SUNSHINE OF EXISTENCE HiNGS A BUCK CLOUD.

With Gas uncertainty of life is minted the dark mystery of death! While, on the one hand, we catch the welcome sound of a new breath of life that tells of an addition to our species, on the other we shudder as we hear the rushing wings of the Destroying Angel! The mighty voice of the Great Influence which rules the Universe has pronounce', our fate; the dread flat has gone furth, and every mortal man is doomed to die! But, though we cannot prevent, can we postpone death? The question Is momentous, even if it concern the prolongation of life but by a single hour, inasmuch as every instinct prompts us to fight the boldest battle we can for this glorious boon of ex- istence. The promptings of instinct are but the spontaneous voices of nature, and it Is our duty to obey. But there still remains the question, can death be postponed by a single hour? Yes; for the wend works in obedience to certain laws; and a study of these proves that those who have the judgment and the will to buckle on the shield, which nature places ready to I their grasp, may ward orf the insidious attacks of the haaplac- able enemy of life, until, in a rips old age, the vital faculties gradually decay, and the Angel a Peace glides softly Into our I presence, leading us, at it were. in a gentle slumber to the regions bey ,nd the shadow of the tomb. The Fell Destroyer makes his first approaches In many forms. but none are more favoured by him than that of a deadly toe now veying upon the very vitals of Modern Society. What is this foe Tnere are few among us who have not been or are now to some extent its victims. Would the reader know if be. Um, is under the ban of this frightful scourge? Let him ask himself whether he experiences any of the following symp- toms :

There are pains about the cheat and sides, and sometimes in the bark. The mouth has a bad taste, esrecially in the morn- ing ; and there are feelings of dulness and drowsinees. The appetite is poor, a 14 )rt of sticky slime collects about the teeth, there is a feeling as of a heavy lo id on the stomach, and some- times a faint, all-gone sensation at the pis of the stomach, which food does not satisfy. The eyes are sunken, the hands and feet become cold and feel clammy. After a while a cough sets in, at first dry, but attended in the course of a few months with expectoration of a greenish colour. The sufferer feels constantly tired, and sleep seems to afford him no rest. Ner- vousness, irritability, and evil forebodings follow. When rising suddenly, there is a giddiness, a sort of whirling sensation in the head, The bowe s become costive; the skin is cry and hot at times; the blood becomes thick and stagnant ; the whites of the eyes are tinged with yellow ; the urine is scanty and high coloured, depositing a sediment after standing. There is frequently a spitting up cf the fo.d—at times with a sour taste and at others with a sweetish taste. This is often attended with palpitation of the heart or impaired vision, with spots before the eyes, accompanied by great prostration and weak- ness. All,cf these symptoms are in turn present. It is thought that nearly one-third of our populat'on has this disease in some of its varied forms. Medical men have mistaken the nature of the malady. Its true name is Dyspepsia or Indigestion ; for which a cortain remedy is to be Lund in Mother Seizel's Cura- tive Syrup—a medicine which has won in both hemlspheres a confidence founded only on its great virtues. SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A GENTLEMAN.—A. geMleman, named T. C. Clartnont. of Sandhurst, aged about 30, who had been staying in the White Hart Hotel, Windsor, for several days, committed suicide on Thursday mornlng. It appears that upon the proprietor asking him to settle his account he referred him to his uncle, Major E. Clarmont. The latter came and saw the deceased, staying with him until about two this morning. Deceased subsequently went I to the stable at the back ef the house and shot himself I through the head. FREEING CHESTER BRIDOP.S.—On New Year's Day the Dee bridges at Chester were formally declared open and free from tolls which have been charged for many rars past. The claims of the bridgeowners have been satisfied by the payment ef £33,000, towards which sum the Duke of West- minster contributed £lO,OOO and the Corporation £15,000. The Duke and Duchess, with the Bishop, Mayor, and many other prominent citizens of Chester, took part in the cere- monies, which included a procession through the city and a luncheon at the Town Hall. A Manchester gentleman has received the following, which may be considered in the light of an offi- cial communication from the Greonwicla observatory. It is - dated Christmas Eve :—'The change which will be made here on January 1 is not the adoption of 24 hours instead of 12. for we have counted hours from 0 to 24 every day for many years past, as is customary with all astronomers, and a public clock outside the observatory is so divided : but on Januarys' we shall change the beginning of the day from noon (at which time astronomical clocks have been acess- ,Sll-7aaynaby; is a question for p Di? corned to show Oh. o,n. °secs.) to midnight, thus btinging it into accordance with the civil day, R,w far the public adopting the 24 hours' aelndasalliovninOgntailps h a them to decide." wills va temme Mil. A LEG BROXEN.—James Smith, a carter, in the employ of Messrs Greenall, Whitley, and Co, brewers, was proceeding to his home in Park-road on Monday night, when he fell to the ground and broke his leg. P.C. Rat- cliffe happened to be at band and " splintered " the broken leg, after which the injured man was removed home. SHOCKING NEW YEAR FATAISTY.—AbOIIt one o'clock on Thursday morning an extraordinary burning fatality occurred at St. Helens Junction. Reuben Fowles, an engine driver in the employ of the London and North- Western Railway Company, who resides in Taylor-street, had, with his family and a few friends, been watching in the New Year. They were retiring to rest a little before one o'clock, and Mrs. Fowles, carrying a lamp in one hand and her daughter, thirteen months' old, in the other arm, had reached the turning at the top of the ' stairs, when she stumbled forward. The glass of the lamp broke by contact with the wall, the oil became ignited, and the flames caught the nightdress of the child and also the wearing apparel of the mother. She shouted loudly for help, and when the filmes were extinguished it was found that she was badly burned on the hand, right arm, and face. The chili was burned all over its head and face, hands, and arms, and parts of the shoulders and breast; and an elder son, who had gone to his mother's assistance, was also badly burned on the hands. Dr. Casey, whose surgery is near, was promptly in attendance, but notwithstanding his utmost skill the child only lived a few hours,

SATURDAY. JANUARY 3, 1885.

THE Egyptian question may be lost sight of for a time; but it is like a bad shilling—it keeps turning up. Just now interest in. it is reviving as much from political as from military considerations. The Government at home have their hands full; for, not only are they called on to watch narrowly every step taken on the Nile with a view to the rescue of General GORDON; they are required to check- mate every move that Prince BismARCK may make with the object of rendering " confus- sion worse confounded." It is no secret that the German CHANCELLOR has taken a dislike to Mr. GLADsToNE and his Government. He has fish of his own to fry, and he has got it into his head that the British PREMIER keeps the frying pan too much in his own hands. He is the "man of blood and iron," and alto- gether unscrupulous in his ways. Mr. GLAD- STONE looks upon mankind as his own flesh and blood; he is strong but gentle, and scru- pulous to the last degree. Prince BISMARCK ,cannot understand why the British Govern- ment having bombarded the forts ofAlexandria, routed ARAB!, and taken charge of the admini- stration of Egypt, do not annex the country as a British possession; he has himself al- ways acted on the principle of " the spoils to the victors," and has at heart a contempt for a policy which is governed by regard for a plighted word. It is to be feared that there are many Conservatives and some few Liberals who look at things from the Brs- mARCICIAN point of view, and herein lurks, and has lurked for some time past, the dan- ger to Mr. GLADSTONE's Government. We are pledged as a nation to leaye Egypt to the Egyptians as soon as the country has settled down, and a strong Government has been established ; but events are sometimes stronger than men, and there are politicians of easy virtue who have already persuaded themselves that the time has come for assum- ing a distinct Protectorate over the land of the PHAROAHs. Mr. GLADSTONE, we need hardly say, is not amongst this class, and we would rather see him defeated and driven from power than purchase safety by listening to the base voices of Jingoes and bondholders, whose Consciences may be slackened or tightened by a pull at their purse-strings. What if BISMARCK do frown and intrigue to bring about a change of Government ? Is that not rather a reason for clinging closer to Mr. GLADsToNE? It is surely the duty of the PRIME MtNISTER of this country to act in the interests of England rather than those of Germany. France and Austria are being re- presented as servants standing one on each side,of PRINCE BISMARCK. Let us be thank- ful that England does not occupy so humi- liating a position. The German CHANCELLOR is powerful; but he is not all powerful. . He cannot indeed frighten the German Parlia- ment into doing everything he wishes it to do; but he is artful and clever, and there isteed to beware of him. If England were to annex Egypt, it would serve him in varicus ways. He is anxious to keep France from thinking of Sedan, and of a .war of revenge. Next to England, France, amongst the European Powers, has the greatest interest in the for-

hat tunes of Egypt; and it is needless to say t,se annexation of that country would cAaio-us, France as of old to look upon " Perfilie Albion" as her deadly enemy. A WIDNES GAOL BIRD.—The Widnes magistrates on Monday sentenced Mary Wright, a married woman, to.a month's imprisonment for being drunk and disorderly. This was her seventh appearance during 1884. THE SUPERINTENDENCY OF THE WIDNES WLSLEYLLII Cincurr.—The Rev. Robert Pardon, of Cleckheaton, has accepted the unanimous invitation of the Widnes quarterly meeting to become the superintendent of the circuit at the next conference. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCORN.—At the Navigation Inn, ,Canal-street, Runcorn, on Monday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway held an inquest touching the death of Clarissa Annie Shallcrass, daughter of Thomas Shallcross, of 10, Mason-street. The deceased, who was ten months old, was taken sadden's, ill on Saturday, and died in a few minutes. It was supposed that as the child was teething .convulsions had caused death, and a verdict to that effect was returned. ICE ACCIDENT AT DIITON.—OU Sunday morning A young man named James Kenyon, a porter at the London and Nosth-Western Railway Station, Ditton, had a narrow, escape from drowning whilst on the ice at Halebank. Keayon was skating on a pond known as the "Cock Fit" when the ice gave way beneath him. His brother threw him a coat, which he clutched until a rope was fastened round his waist and he was drawn safely to the side. WIDNES C.E.T.B.—A meeting in connection with this society wee held in the National Schoolroom on New Year's Eve, the Rev. C. Rumfett in the chair. There was a good attendance Addresses were delivered by the Chairman, the Rev. A. P. 11. Wilson, Messrs. F. Cave, J. Fishy, T. Richards, R. N. Wharton. Refreshments were provided by Mrs. Fairclough. At the close of the proceedings the members adjourned to the Parish Church, where a watch- night service was held. The Rev. J. RumZitt preached an appropriate serscon. MILTON-ROAD CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, WIDNES.— On New Year's Eve a miscellaneous entertainment took place at Milton-road Conaregational Chapel. The first por- tion was devoted to the partaking of suitable refreshments that had been provided, and the second portion was an en- joyable musical entertainment. Songs were given by Miss Travis and Mr. Johnson, while Mr. E. T. Warne gave a re- citation. Mr. W. Mayne read a paper on " Old maids." 'the proceedings were presided over by the Rev. R. G. Hughes. Subsequently a watch-night service was held. WIDNES AND THE SHIP CANAL —A meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Widnes Local Board was held on Tuesday afternoon, in order to discuss the probable effect of the Manchester Ship Canal scheme upon IVidnes. and the beat means of protecting the interests of the town. Messrs T. S. Timmins and 11. W. Deacon attended as a deputation from the Traders' Association, and a long con- ference took place. Eventually Messrs Gossage, Carey, Handley, and Midwood, who have formerly dealt with the subject, were requested to draw up clauses which would meet the commercial, sanitary, and other necessities of the town. i..IIOCKING DROWNING FATALITY AT WIDNES.—Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Mersey Hotel, Widnes, on Thursday, touching the death of Samuel Marshall, 18 years of age, son of John Marshall, of Pen- keth. On the 4th December the deceased and his brother were assisting their father to navigate the flat Lelia up the river. A heavy gale was blowing at the time, and when the vessel was under Runcorn Bridge the main boom and gaff broke. The falling timber struck the deceased on the head and knocked him overboard. As he could not swim, he sank, and was drowned under the eyes of his father and brother. The body was not recovered until Tuesday, when Robert Button, of 30, Cholnsondeley-greet, Widnes, found it lying on the sands near Halehead. A verdict of el Ace- dental death " was recorded. ALLEGED THEFr FROM A GIRL AT BUNCORIC—At Ran- earn Police Couat, on Thursday, James McTurk, a middle- aged mau, riga charged with stealing ed.—lt appeared that on Sunday afternaOn _Sarah Hoxworth, a ktl.gavS Margaret Webster. another ghl, 01 tO taka Cate af. As the girl went up Greenway-road she was stopped by the prisoner, who put his hand in her pocket. She afterwards missed the money. At the tine? :,weral members of the Runcorn Foot- ball Club arrived on t'm scene, and, hearing the girl's com- plaint "up-ended " the prisoner, and a 61 and several cop. pets dropped from his pocket. The girl identified tire As there Was no corroborative evidenCe the Bench dismissed ' the prisoner.—The prisoner was also charged with conduct- ing himself in an indecent manner shortly after the occur- rence narrated above, and he was fined 20s. and costs.—P.C. Wallace apprehended the prisoner. CHRISTMAS TREE AT WIDNES.—At the Widnea National Schools, on Tuesday evening, a Christmas t:ee took place, and there was a large attendance ef young folk. The tree a occupied a prominent position in It Centre of the room, and pending from its branches wa..; a street variety of useful and ornamental articles, while Surrounding the base were large pieces of 1. frosted Coal," which greatly enhanced the ap- pearance of the tree. There were also two stalls containing !many useful articles. Mrs. Kilcrosa and Miss Kilcross be- ing in charge, The success of the gathering was largely due to the assistance of Mrs. Williams, Mrs. Rumfitt, Mrs. Kilcross, Mrs. Cane, Mrs. Crawford, Mrs. James White, and Miss Wrench. The tree was erected and decorated by Mr. Liaison and Mr. Crawford. The proceedings were opened by the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vicar, in a short but appropriate address.

ROSIBERT FROM A Rl:meow; FLAT.—James Smith, a boatman, was brought before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. James Handley at Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, charged with feloniously stealing Ds ed, the money of Geo. Williams, On the previous day Williams and his wife and

the prisoner went to the Bridgewater Arms, Top Locks, where they had some drink together. In the cabin of the narrow boat of which her huecand was the captain, Mrs. Williams had left in the copboard in a small box the sum of 98 6d. The prisoner, under the pretence of fetching some corn for the horse, went to Williams' boat. He sent the girl, who was on board, for the corn, and it is supposed that in her absence he took the money, for when she returned it was gone. Subsequently the prisoner was apprehended by P.C. Kelly, and at the police station he told Mrs. Williams that if she would net have him locked up he would give her the money back.—The prisoner was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment. FAIINWORTN OGITRCH OF ENGLAND MIIPERINCE SO- CIETY —A demonstration in connection with this society took place on Christmas Day. In the afternoon the mem. hers met at the mhool-room, and accompanied lry the Widnes Soap Works lattss band, proceeded through the village and I Appleton, stoppages being made at the reside-aces 6f Mrs. Hibbert, Mr.Trock, Mrs. Deacon, Mr. Brtnner, and Mr. Carey. Subsequently they returned to St. 'Luke's Church, where divine service was held. The prayers were read by the Rev. 6.'Bond, vicar, the lessons by the Rev. J. Holden, and the sermon was preached by the !RV/. G. A. Leßert. Tea was then provided in the school-rcom, and the after-. noon's ,prbeeedings were concluded by an entertainment, I ever which lir. H. Wade Deacon presided. lhe chairman delivered an appropriate address. 503g1,9 were contributed by the Mimes Bond, Miss Haddock, Miss M. Fogg, one Messrs. Black, F. C. Davies, A. G. Davies, and F. An address on temperence was ,da- livered by Mr. L. 0. Stubbs, of Liverpool. CASE PLAYING AT WIDNES.—WZRDEROUS ATTACK or; A PoLlo—Laefore Mr. H. WlDNate DRUNEARDS.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr A R Gladstone and Mr H Gaskell, jun., the following persons were dealt with for drunken- ness :—Martin Mitchell, fined 20s and costs; Thomas Clawes' :Is 6d and costs; Thomas Greenwood, is 6d; and Patrick Purcell, Joseph Shea, Michael Byrne, Catherine Wicking, and John Benson, were each finecafive shillings and costs. A DANGEROUS PRACTICE AT WIDNES.—For years the Widnes magistrates have unsuccessf ally attempted to stamp out the dangerous practice of sleeping in the chemical works at Widnes, but on Monday they passed a sentence upon an offender, which will doubtless have a deterrent effect. Michael Henry, deecribed as an idle worthless fel- low, was prayed to have slept in Hutchinson's chemical works on Sunday night. He had been convicted of a similar offence on seven precious occasions, and he was sen- tenced to two months' hard labour. A VIOLENT THIEF AT WADNES.—Before Mr. R. Gasket!, jun., and Mr. J. Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Thoinas O'Toole. labourer, of King-street, was charged with stealing a tin of corned beef, weighing 141b5., value Es, from the shop of Thomas Smith, grocer, Widnes-road, Widnes. Lbout half-past ten on Saturday night the prisoner was loitering about the shop door, and he was seen to snatch a tan of corned beef and tun away. Mr. Smith gave .chase and overtook the prisoner, who placed the tin upon the , ground and struck Mr. Smith a violent blow. At this point P.C.'s Evan and Lamb arrived on the scene, and appre- hended the prisoner. The prisoner was sentenced to two months' hard labour. WIDNES SCIIOOI. BOARD AT WORS.—At Widnes Patty Sessions, on Wednesday, Mr. G. H. Denby, clerk to the School Board, prosecuted the following persons for neglect.. jog to send their children regularly to school :—Henry Burgess, William Smith, John Mercer, Patrick Hyland., / Matthew Smith, Thomas Respan, James Cunliffe (two , cases), Henry McGee, Richard Traynor, John Murphy, Daniel Sculley, Michael Devere.ux, William 'Thompson, William Rotherham, Michael Molloy, William Morley, Thomas Dunne, Robert Yates, James Casson, Christopher Cockerhain. CHESHIRE AND TIIE SEATS BlLL.—There is a large attendance of representatives of both parties and of local de'eaates at an inquiry op, ned at Chester Castle, on Friday m•fling, by Major Hector Tulloch. The Conservat:ves are dissatisfied with the Commissioners' plan for carving up the ' , county into eight divisions, and have prepared a separate scheme of their own. The Liberals, on the other hand, are present to support the original draft scheme. Representa- tives are present from Macclesfield to alter the name of Congleton division to that of Macclesfield. Runcorn is ask- ing for a separate division. The salt interest is represeired by a deputation to have a member assigned to Northwich and Winsford, which are in the heart of the salt district ; and Tarporley wishes to stand sponsor for the Eddisbnry district, which is purely agricultural. REMARKABLE PIGEON STORY.— An incident worth re- cording has occurred at Winwick. Mr. Copple, of the Her- mitage Inn, on Sunday week missed one of a flock of favourite pigeons in his possession, and nothing more was ' seen of it until the Wednesday, when the missing bird was found under extraordinary circumstances. Noticing a heap of soot falling into the kitchen grate, and hearing a strange sound a few feet above the blaze of the fire, an in- vestigation was made, when the poor bird was discovered on a protruding brick exposed to the full heat of the fire and as black ste a crow. On being taken down, and a pot of water and some grain had been placed before it, the bird, I which must have been blown or had fallen down the chim- I nay, drank and pecked most voraciously, and it is now as ' well as ever. The wonder is how it could have survived its three days' incarceration tinder PO aMtraft!clinary circum- stances. LORD SALISBURY AND WIZ WESLEYANS AT gATFIELb. I —At last, it is said, Lord Salisbury has made a concession to the Wesleyans at Hatfield, by offering them a site for a chapel—not in the town near his own magnificent gates, and within sound of the Established Church bells, but away some three-quarters of a mile, on the bprders of the next parish, at a plots lltd Newtown. This is very much like asking for bread and getting a stone. The humble folk who frequent the little stable where worship has been conducted , through many weary years will seareely &trete give tip even! that indifferent accommodation for roomier premises away in the country almost a Sabbath day's jenrney. It does uot yet appear that the Wesleyans of Hatfield have accep- ted the offer; and it may be that they will not. Lord Salisbury has hitherto declined to let Methodists come nigh his gates On any land of his, and he declines still, is con- sistency cannot be ialpeached ; whatever may be eaid of his Christian charity and fraterrity.—The Liberator. A DistrONEST SON AT RIINCORN.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, William Henry Hardley was charged with stealing 56Ibe. of rope, the property of Messrs. Jas. Taylor and Co.—Edward Hardie's said the prisoner was his son. He (witaess) was the captain of the flat George, be- longing to Taylor and Co., which on Saturday last was lying in the Old Qlay Dock. About eleven o'clock on the morning of that day he found the prisoner coming from the forecastle of the flat with the rope (produced), which was worth ss. The prisoner had no right on the flat.—P.C. Wallace deposed to apprehending the prisoner.—Hardley informed the Bench that his son had given him a great deal of trouble. For several months he bad not worked at all, and had left his wife and children to thernselves.—Saperin- tendent Leah stated that the prisoner was an idle, dissolute fellow.—The Prisoner argued that because he had not car- ried the ropes away from the flat he had not stolen therm— The Bench, however, sentenced him to throe mouths' hard labour. THE PREMIER'S -75TH BIRTHDAY.— Mr. -Gladstone on Monday completed his 75th year, haying been born on the 29th December, ISII9. As is usual on such on occasion a large number of conaratulatory telegrams were received, and amongst the senders of these were the Prince and Princess of Wales. The Warrington 'Liberal Associa- tion sent a telegram as follows ;—'4 Warrington, December 29th, 1884. From 11. Roberts, Liberal Association, War- rington. To 'the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, Her Majesty's Prime Minister, Hawarolen Castle, near Chester. The Liberals of Warrington send you their heartiest con-, gratolations, and wish you very many happy returns of the day." An address was presented to the right bon. gentleman from the Manchester Liberal Association, in which warm tribute was bate to his long public services, and placing on record an expression of high admiration of the skill and-patience with which he tad guided the nation throughoot the late grave 'crisis. About 200 gifts of various kinds were received. Among other congratulatory telegrams was one from a meetingof Manchester merchants,. held on Monday at the Merchants' flotealtfarket-street, and sent to Mr. Gladstone by Mr. Eli Sowerbutts. Clarke, President of the Southport Liberal Cinks—" The members of the -Soathport Liberal Club offer their congratulations on your77sth birthday, and' wish yea many happy returns?' WALTON CHURCH, &c.—The chief feature of the Christ- mas number of The British ..4rc7.itect is "An Autumn SketchingE-xcursion by Mr. T. R. Davison." The village of Great Bud worth is sketched with u loving hand, the views beiog very numerous as well as highly artistic. There are some pretty sketches, too, of the church built by Sir Gilbert Greenall at Walton, including a general view, a corner of ' the reredos, the vestry door, the porch, the chancel, and the reading desk. The accompanying letterpress gives an I architectural description of the church similar in terms to . that which we placed before our readers when the structure was completed. Tun " G.Ik.CIDIAN " ALMANAC "—The imp- that troubles the souls of printers seems to have been specially mis- chievous in the office of our contemporary. Whilst some have been mixing liquors, the "P. Dl' ha a been mixing type—possibly he may have been engaged in both occupa- tions. The Spart:ng Chronicle of Thursday thus refers to the result :—" One of our Warrington contemporaries gives away to its readers what it is pleased to call an ' almanac,' though 'all-maniac' might have been a happy designation for the very eccentric work. I haven't had time to study all the way through its many perplexing ,peculiarites, but I observe from itofirst three columns that ' Plough Mon- day' occurs on a Tuesday. that ' hluove Sunday 'happens On the same day of the week, whilst 'Ash Wednesday ' is stranded on a Friday, and that a 'fall moon' is promised for the '33t10 ' of !Carob. These items suffice to show that 188.5 is likely to prove a very extraordinary sort of year down Warrington way—but that is, of course, nothing more than what one might have expected, considering the . perplexing character ef the new time measurements which , the year brings into operation, and the strength of the gin ' sold at the Warrington pubs. during this festive season." MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL —At a meeting of the Pro. Ivisional Committee, held in the Board-room on Monday afternoon, Mr. Daniel Adamson, the chairman, presiding, the estimates of the cost of the works proposed N be car. tied out under the Bill introduced to Parliament for next sassion were submitted and finally approved. The details will appear in due course after they are printed and deposited in the manner required by the standing orders of Parliament: The Chairman brought up the following resolu- tion, which at his suggestion had been passed by the direc- tore of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce at their meeting on Tuesday :—" That it having come to the know- ledge of the Board that alterations are contemplated by the Bridgewater Navigation Company in the rivers Mersey and Irwell it is resolved. This chamber is of opinion that no Improvements will be satisfactory to the commercial and manufacturing interests of thia-dietrict, which do not pro- vide under Parliamentary guarantee for a substantial re- duction in the present railway, canal, and dock charges, be- tween Manchester and Liverpool."

It appears that when the religious census was taken in 1851 the number of chapels credited to this body was :'.9,,244, with 1,002= sittings. Recently, with a view to secure accurate and authoritative informa- tion, the Committee of the Congregational Union applied to every known chuech or mission station for a &aura of the number of their sittings. div.head: TERRIBLE DEATH OF AN OLD WOMAN AT • RUNCORN. A DANGEROUS ROAD.
div.p: TERRIBLE DEATH OF AN OLD WOMAN AT • RUNCORN. A DANGEROUS ROAD.

Yesterday afternoon Mr. T. 3: Ridgway, coroner, held an inquiry at the Suncorn Police Court, into the cause of death of Jane Rooney, a widow, aged 61 years. The evi- dence showed that Mrs Rooney lived with her eon at 76, West-street, Oldham, and that Mary Sullivan, of Mersey. street, Runcorn, was her sister. On 'Tuesday the deceased was expected to arrive at her sister'a house, but about a ' quarter past five Mrs Alice Kuight, of the Ferry Hut, heard moans outside her dwelling. She went in the direction of the sound and found an old woman lying at the bottom of Ithe wall in Castle Reck-road. The woman was insensible and Mrs Knight had her removed into her honse, and re- vived her with a cup of tea. She then ascertained who she was, and cent for Mrs Su livan. D.ceased was afterwards I removed, and Dr. McDougall called in. Considering the II shock the poor woman Lai sustained the doctor did not think it judicious to make a thorough examination at that i i time, but be ascertained that her right shoulder was dis- located ad the right collar bone fractured badly. She I Informed the duct ir that she had fallen over a ' wall, and the injuries were such as might have been caused by such a mishap. There was no suspicion of I foul pl iy. The probable explanation was that the de- ceased turned by Mr. Tonk's shop in Church-street to go the short way to Mersey-street, but taking the higher in- stead of the lower road, and not finding out leer mistake waked off the wall:es though she were on a level road. She would have a fall of about 12 feet—Mrs. Knight informed the corqner that there wits no proper fence to tee wall. There had been four persons injured at the same spot. In ft answer to the foremin of the jury (Mr. S. Yarwood) she field there had been two iron hurdles on the wall where the ' deceased must have (Pea, but they hal been recently taken away. It W 39 a very dark night, and there was not a lamp lighted at the place at the time.—The son of the deceased stated that his mother was very active, and had there been a protection to the wall she would not have fallen off.—Daring a short conversation Dr. Mac- pougali looms! the 99r1T4 Olt the r9a4 Iv" 117:7=; had not yet been adopted by the Board of Commissioners.—The Coroner, in summing up, said whether the road was private or not it ought to be so protected, even for the persons who resided in the houses in that neighbourhood, that an accident should be quite im- possible. From what little be knew of the district, he could say, and he thought the jury would agree with him, that if a fence was not erected the place where this woman had been killed was very dangerous indeed for a stranger.— Mr. Yarwood: Very dangerous indeed.—The Coroner con- firmed that if the Commissioners had not power to compel the erection at a fence, be hoped that the owners of the pro- perty in the neighbourhood when they heard of this fatal accident would take what steps were really necessary to have not a temporary, but a really substantial and perma- nent fence erected for their own sakes the sake of their children, and of everybody else. It ought to be impossible for anything of the description of this accident to happen.— Mr. Yarwood observed that the coroner's remarks had ren- dered it unnecessary for the jury to make any reference to the dangerous condition of the road, but it was to be hoped the property owners would remedy the existing state of affairs.—A verdict of accidental death was recorded. THE REV. J. D. THOMAS ON WYCLIF.

On Sunday evening at Bethesda Congregational Chapel, Runcorn, the Rev. J. D. Thomas, pastor, delivered a special sermon on "The life and labours of Wycliffe in their rela- tion to the religions liberties of England." lsir. Thomas said the proverb that "a prophet it not without honour Rave in hie own country Wined lobe fulfilled in the case of Jahn Wyctif. Although an Englishman of Englishmen, and one of the nobleet defenders Of British liberties, yet the celebration of the quincentenary of his death had evoked a degree of enthasiabm so email that it could only be ac- counted for by the prevailing ignorance with regard te the obligations they owed him for the first English Bible, and for the prepagetion of principles which had long since placed this country in the vanguard of the nations. He would not attempt to take away from the honour which were so richly deserved by Martin Luther; but Luther, even at his death, was far behind Wvelif in many respects, although their views in respect to the doctrine of justifica- tion by faith were almost, if not completely identical, yet with regard to such questions as the sacraments, church polity, and the relations of Church and State the views of the English Reformer were mere nearty akin to those which they conalved were contained in tke New Testament, and which were strenuously upheld by most Nonconformists in the present day. In twelling upon the re- lation of Wyelif's life to elle social and religious • liberties of England, the rev, preacher drew a Contrast of the condition of England at the begin- ning of the fourteenth centrs y rod that of the present time. Reviewing it nationally he pointed out that after John mude peace with the Pope the country passed into a state of vassalage, and for the honour was malcted in an anntt,t tribute cif £1.2"410 sterling. While the English people 'were being taxed for the support of distant expedi- tions, a sum et money ,exceeding the king's revenues was being sent annually'to the French Pope and his creatures at Avignon, and thercettrald be no doubt that the money thus ,filtbed envoi 'England was afterwards employed in the hir- ing of troops to do 'battle with English Boldiers. He then briefly sketched the'iniquities of the feudal system, and re- %larked that if it were possible to present a complete sniCture of social life in England at the period it would show 'that the whole-state of society was bad. Any description of the condition of England in the fourteenth century • which did not take into account the numerous friars that overran the country like an army of locusts and canker- 'worms would be very imperfect. These brethren were -chiefly of two orders, viz., the Franciscans and Dominicans, which had been founded early in the present century. 'Under their seeming gentleness of disposition there lurked • ,a frenzy and hatred which fitted them to become the blood- hounds of the Church and the °dicers ef the Inquisition in succeeding ages. It was necessary to remember that with all the evils in the land Wycliffe had been face to face from 'his boyhood. That they bad long made an unfavourable impression upon his mind was evident from the strength of 'hiseonvictions when he came to speak of them ; bat it was not until he was 42 years ef age that he appeared on the scene, and then so suddenly that he had been likened to the prophet in the wilderness. This appearance was in the charac- ter of a political parson and not of a religious reformer, although his politics were grounded in his religious faith. Hay- ing-shortly alluded to Wyclif's labours, the preacher said his remedy for the oppression which the poor suffered was net in revolts but in the spread of knowledge, especially the knowledge of the Word of God. He contended earnestly against all who said, "It is heresy to speak of Holy Scrip- ture-in English, and that the priest alone is the lawful inter- preter of God's word." In addition to the temporalities of the Church and the social condition of the people, the government and sacraments and doctrines of the Church occupied his attention, and on these matters he found himself no less opposed to the dignita les of Rome than on the former. In his teachings he struck at the very foundation of the Papal system, and also at the shackles by which the minds of men were enslaved. It was little won- der that Popes pronounced their anathemas upon him, and that lesser dignitaries of the Church sought to put him to silence. Bat for more than twenty-two years, while he sowed the seeds of truth broadcast, a gracious Providence shlelded hint from all harm, till, released from the mortal tabernacle, his soul mounted into glory to dwell in the light of the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne.
The deathis announced of 13r. Given, Professor of Orien- tal Languages at Magee College, Londonderry. He was choked at dinner.

ATTACKS OIsT TEAM- CA2 CONDUCTORS MAGISTERIAL WARNING —Another case of assault on a tram-car conductor was heard at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before Messrs. W. Blinlehorn and A. Sinclair, John Barns, a resi- dent of Sutton, was summoned for assaulting John Stubbs, the .conductor of a tram car running between St. Helens and 1 Peasley Cross, on the 24th ult.--The complainant stated that on Christmas Eve the defendant was riding on the car. ad when he was asked for bis fare be alleged that he had paid it. fie afterwards began swearing, and made an attack on him, knocking him down and striking him several times in the face. He also took the sash bag and threw it at him (complainant.)—The defendant stated that as it was Christmas Eve be had had a little drink. He had not bqd any drink for two years, and after meeting a few friends he took some drink. He did not know what he was doing.— The Chairman said the Bench would not lightly pass over those attacks on the guards of tram-oars. The defendant's drunkenness was no excuse in the matter. He would be fined 203 and costs, or in default of payment oue month's imprisonment.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The expedition for the relief of General Gordon cheer- fully spent its Christmas at Korti, and by New Year's Eve were already well advanced on what is the last stage of the journey to Khartoum. By to-day, if all goas well, General Stewart, wall his eleven hundred men, will bivouac at the. Gakdal wells, as nearly as possible half way across the desert roste between Korti and Shendy. Once at Shendy the rest is easy. Gordon, it will be remembered, at a time when he was understood to be sorely beleagured, usad antly to occupy his spare time by steaming down the river to Shendy and firing a few shots at the MabLii's men. The river is lower now than then. But the men who have rowed the hard passes of the river from DonguLa will not be dis- mayed at anything they may find in this more favored stretch. Besides it is by no means improbable that by that time the main body of the infantry, going the long river route round by Abon Hamid and Berber, will had that the etmelry have already accomplished tha appointed task.. Between Shendy and Khartoum is a desert rkle of a bun- dred miles. This, at the rate the little fyce has pushed OD across the desert from Korti, would be covered in less than four days. Whether Lord Woledev will ritk the rush with his supports slowly coming up by the river remains to be seen. If the journey across the desert to Sbendy shows that the tribes have thrown up the sponge, the forward movement will certainly be continued, and within a fo:t. night Gordon may be delivered. -

• . Nothing has been heard of the perpetrators of the outrage on London Bridge, nor id it likely that anything will be fonnd out. The police absolutely have no clue. Their be- lief is that the deed was accomplished by foreigners, who came over from the United States commissioned for this particular work, and who returned immediately it was cver,, leaving no trace behind. Fortunately there has been no re- petition of tbe attempt upon other public buildings. This is much to the regret of the news boys, who, however, meet the conditiornazf affairs with imperturbable spirit. Driv:ng homewards through the Strand at eleven o'clock last night, the great crowd that people's this thoroughtaie at this hour was set upon by a tlying column of newsboys who cried in all discordant tones "Blowing up of ‘Vindsw Castle, special ten o'clock edition. Windsor Castle blJwed up." Shouting this, with piles of newspapers over thJir shoulders, and single copies extended to the eager purch tEer, the boys went dying through the crowd, jumping up ou the steps of cabs and carriages, creating a scene of some excitement. Witksuch tremendous news to barter nothing less than Gd. would satisfy the first demand, though they, as a final re- source, would not disdain 2d. The papers sold by hundreds, and a neat harvest must have been reaped.

It seems marvellous with policemen everywhwe that this kind of thing is permitted to go forward in a main thorough- fare of Landon. It is not a matter of oocasional occur- rence. I remember three semi ens age driving to the House of Commons through the Strand with the guilty knowledge that, on what seemed a very quiet night, I bad stolen a couple of hours to be present at a first night, I had a con- viction that something would happen, Sometbine• always does happen if I leave the House for an hour. The same flying column of boys was out, and the air was filled with cries of "Arrest of Parnell." I hurried on to the House in the expectation of finding it in a state of high excitement, and hand Mr. Parnell on his feet addressing the Speaker in mildest mood. I suppose the police think that the initia- tive lies with the public. It would have been open to any. sae who had paid sixpence for a penny paper on the assur- ance that it contained a certain piece of news, to have the vendor brought up for obtaining money by false pretences. One difficulty in the way world be the necessity of first catching your vendor after be has pocketed his F lap ence. And again, no one is inclined, going home at eleven o'clock, to get out of a cab, chase a small boy it.ronAh a dense crowd, and spend the midnight hoar in tal.ing prtparatory steps for vindicating justice.

I The long companionship of the Princess Beatrice and the I Queen is about to be broken, and the last of her children will leave her mile. Princess Beatrice is not not so widely I ka•own in the country as some of her sisters are. The Princess Louise, for example, is a very familiar figure, but the Princess Beatrice has been kept closely at her mother's side, companion of her travels abroad and her walks at home. This gentle, faithful character is cue which par- ticularly recommends itself to the English people, and Princess Beatrice is not the least loved of the Royal Family. Possibly for this reason the coming marriage is not looked upoa with anything like enthusiasm. There is, to tell the truth, an uncomfortable idea that here is another obscure and impecunious German princeling effecting for himself an establishment at the cost of a wealthy nation. There was a time when a marriage with the Priace Imperial was spoken of, and there seems to hi some truth in the story of the Princess's affection for the handsome, gentle, gallant boy. Such a union would have been highly popular. With respect to that actually projected, whilst warmest good wishes will go with the Princess Beatrice in her new sphere of life, I cannot honestly say that, ad far as I have heard opinion expressed, the marriage is likely to be popular.

The Privy Council at which, h 1 accordance with State regulati in, the announcement of the betrothal was made wa eieeeding small. As a matter of fact it was simply Composed of the necessary quorum. When, drawing nigh to 50 years ago, tho Queen announced her own betrothal to Prince Albert the Privy Council was a very different affair.. both in respoct of numbers and pummel. Croker was present and made a note in his diary. At the present time it is interesting to recall Lis glimpse of a priveleo.d inte- rior upon a historic occasion. Stye Mr. ()raker, "When we ; had assembled to the number of, I think, seventy or eighty ; (two to one Conservative), and as many had taken their I seats as could, at a long table, Her Majesty was banded in by the Lord Chamberlain, and bowing to us all reund, sat down, saying, ',Your Lordships' (we are all Lords at I the Council Board), wal be seated.' She then unfolded a paper and read her declaration, which you will, before this I can reach you, have seen in all the newspapers. I cannot describe to you with what a mixture of sel f-pcasession and femenine delicacy she read the paper. Her voice, which is naturally beautiful, was clear and untroubled ; and her eye was bright and calm, neither bold nor downcast, but firm and soft. There was a blush on her cheek which made her look both handsomer and more interesting; and certainly she rlid look as interesting and as bAndsom e as any young lady- I ever saw. I happened to stand behind the Dk t lington's chair and caught her eye twice as she directed it- towards him, which I fancy she did with a good natured ina terest. After the Lord President had asked her permission to publish her declaration, she bowed conser,t, handed him the paper, rose, bowed all round, and retired, led as belore, by the Lord Chamberlain te the outer-room, where the at-- tendants, who were not of the Conncil,had waited..

This is impressed upon the memory by reason ot the fact that, whenever the subject comes on in the House of Commons, independent Naval authorities protest against . this incessant coddling of the yachts.
