RAFFLES AT BAZA- . Sir,—Your cerrespondent " Fair to All" has chosen a very misappropriate non: de plume. Such a one as "More than fair to Borne and less thin fair to others" vkuld have more suitably closed his epistle. He admits that lotteries are illegal, but he seems to claim exemption from the opera- tion of the law for some, while quito willing to band other over to the tender mercies of Puritanical magistrates. On , what ground he makes this claim is not very clear— whether on the ground ot the unfairness of the law, or on that of the motives of the law breakers. If he contends that the law which makes lotteries illegal is not a good or well- cons'clered law, there are plenty who think that people can- not be made virtuous by Act of Parliament, and that laws ought not to be made to save fools from their folly, who will agree with him. But that a law is not good is no reason why it should be made worse by not being applied impartially. He asks you to define the distinction between a draw for a Liverpool lottery ticket and a draw for a Bel- gian lottery ticket. The simple answer is that there is no distinction to draw. Then he asks, "If the law of England would commit the speculator in an English lottery ticket to the degrada'ion of imprisonment, why should the same law permit thousands of foreign lottery tickets to be circulated through this country continually?" The answer to this is that the law of England does this for the same reason that it punishes a delinquent bank manager or forger who is in England, while it does not punish the delin- quent bank manager or forger who is in Spain, or any where else beyond the jurisdiction of extra- dition treaties, that is to say, because the foreign circulators of tickets cannot be got at. If I am not mistaken, when the Birmingham authorities first began to move in this matter it was suggested that the issuers of these foreign tickets should be punished, but the difficulties in the way of getting at them were so great that the idea had to be given up. Then as to the motives, your correspondent says the bare idea of his being called a rogue and vagabond be- cause he went to a Wesleyan bazaar, got up for the purpme of raising money for new schools, and there patronised the I lucky bag, makes him laugh. Now, I should like to know if your correspondent is not compounded of the same fish and blood as other men are. It he is, it is, legally, just as easy to set him down a rogue and vagabond as anybody else. He Might laugh, but he would in ties eye of the law be a rogue and vagabond all the same. Then, again, one feels curious to know how far he is will- ing to allow his doctrine of motives to carry him. He. might have varied his illustration and said De you mean to say that, if I put my hand into somebody else's pocket and took out five shillings and handed them over to help to erect Wesleyan schools, 3ou would call me a pickpocket ?" I leave the Mayor in his judicial capacity to answer this query. Let us consider the application of this doctrine of , motives a little further. At the moment I write there stands condemned to death a German Socieliet. Reinedorf, for having attempted to take away the lives of his Emperor and other high dignitaries. There was nothing mercenary or ignoble about this man's motives. His objett was to re- deem the masses of his fellow-countrymen from their misery and secial degradation. Yet will your correspondent main- tain that in this instance because of the motive the crime ought to be condoned? The truth is that no motive which prompts people to break the law can safely be recognised as a justification of the offence, and if the chief magistrate of a town says that it can, then all I will say is that we ought to be well pleased that each court in which justices' justice is administered is provided with a competent legal adviser. But I cannot help thinking your correspondent has taken the Mayor rather too seriously on this point, and 1 fancy that all he need do to have his ideas somewhat abruptly eectified is to appeal from the Mayor at a bazaar to the Mayor on the bench. As a magistrate, I am sure his wor- ship lays aside those ingenious spphistries of which be is such a master, and shows FAVOUR TO NONE.

TEETOTALISM AT EARLESTOWN. Sir,—l notice in your isene of last week a letter under the above beading, and signed " Moderator." Will you kindly allow me a little space to refer to this subject. Let me say fiat that I was glad to notice your correspon- dent has not adopted the phrase "disgusted ;" and I hope we shall not see it again. Personally, I have learned to be a little charitable towards those who differ from me in opinion, more especially if I can believe their opinions are honestly and conscieratiously held ; and I sincerely hope that whatever may be said or written on this subject, for or against it, may he free from vulgar personalities or even bitter sar- casm ; if that is indulged in no good will be accomplished. We want argument, and reason, and fact ; not sneering, or rancour, or vulgar abuse. Contempt is all such epistles deserve. And now with reepect to the question at issue, I wish to say that, in my opinion, any increase to the stock of his. torical knowledge possessed by your that correspondent, by a personal application to a "certain rev, gentleman," would not have been satisfactory unless such knowledge had been made public. The statement itself—that it is an "historical tact that Christ was not a teetotaller "—cams from the same "certain rev. gentleman" himself—from the pulpit to the public, with no attempt at proof, or any reference whatever as to where such "historical fact" may be traced ; and the remark having now been backed up by "Moderator" the teetotal section have a very reasonable claim upon the "op- position " to pablicly substantiate the etatemests made. We want the" fact" so energetically put forth clearly showa. There is an old saying that facts are stubborn things, but mere assertions or opinions are not facts, and don't as a rule. satisfy phlegmatic Britons of this day and generation. The reasoning of "Moderator" is not at all clear. He says—" If Christ was a abstainer, where was the sting of the people's iemark, that he was a wine-bibber ? " I would ask, where would the sting be if Christ was not an ab- stainer? Hypocrites can generally stand very great pres- sure be.fore they feel the sting. But, I suppose " Moderator " would say, that Christ was not an abstainer, because the people said he was a wine-bibber, so the reading of his letter appears to indicate; if so, then Christ was also a glutton, for the same people said so, and it must have been equally true. They also said that John the Bap- tist was possessed of a devil, or evil spirit, but do we Chris- tian people to-day believe that was true? Do we not know of a certain evil habit of "slandering ? " Throughout the] Gospels the Scribes and Pharisees were always noted for , anything but honesty and integrity, and they prove very indifferent witnesses. Second, "Moderator "says, during the life of our Sa- viour, the Greeks and Romans ever great drunkards, and the Jews, in this sin as in many others, were no doubt much I like their neighbours. This is no proof that the Jews were a drunken people at all. I hold an opposite opinion, and should take the comparative silence of our Saviour on this question as a very strong inference that such teaching was not specially needed. Are there any historical facts "of our Saviour referring to and condemning the drunkenness of either Jews or Gentiles ? If so, let us have them. " His- torical facts" ought to have something stronger to sup- port them than inferences. I should feel obliged for a little more enlightenment from our friend "Moderator " or anyone else. Will you allow me to say in conclusion, that, in my opinion, whether we believe Christ to have been an ab- stainer 1852 years ago or not, it will not alter the histo- rical and scientific facts " that alcoholic drinks to-day are poisoning the bodies and destroying the souls of thonsands of our fellow-creatures ;" that drunkenness is the curse of Britain, physically, mentally, morally, and spiritually ; that the late Prince Leopold spoke of drink as the only terrible enemy that England has to fear. It is an " hietorical fact" to-day, that " the struggle of the chinch, the library, and the school against the beerhouse and the gin palace is but one development of the war between heaven and hell." So said Mr. Charles Buxton, in words that have rung from one end of the country to the other hundreds and thousands of times. It is a sad, but terrible and indisputable "historical fact," on the authority of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, M.P. that the great evils flowing upon us threugh this traffic in alcoholic liquors exceed in magnitude the combined re- sults of the three great historical scourges of war, pesti- lence, and famine. This is what temperance reformers are more concerned about to-day than the teetotalism of the New Testament—the great battle-ground of Christian and non-Christian " Moderators." True teetotallers are afraid of no battle-ground; the cause is only strengthened, like tiue Christianity, by opposition. These last few lines are, I admit, outside the question at issue, but. I think, will do no harm to go forth, and may do good.—Yours very respectfully, TEE-TEE. 30th December, 1884.
THE ANTI-VACCINATORS AND THE WARRINGTON

GUARDIANS. Sir,—Since Mr. Button, the clerk to the Warrington Guardians, is come home and enjoying Christmas with his family friends, the Warrington Guardians, I purpose with your permission to redeem my promise, and in the interest of "Old Lang Syne " shake his legal paw. Mr. Sutton now poses as the champion of anti-vaccina- tion law, and insinuates of his opponents the keeping back of some letter from the Local Government Board that would conciliate his championship. Briefly, the matter stands thus :—the anti-vaccinators were summoned and re-sum- mooed; at the instance of Mr. Cooper, the vaccination officer, a man specially appointed as required by 34 and 35 Viet., chap. 98, sec. 5, to prosecute defaulters under the Vac- cination Acts. At the hearing of these summonses, Mr. Button, who is not a solicitor, claimed the right by author- ity of his Guardians to act as advocate, and in this claim he now asserts himself as champion. How far this is true your readers may form their own opinions. Be request, the Home Secretary promised and made in- quiries ; Mr. Sutton's employers', the Local Government Board, demanded of their servant the reasons for hit thus act- ing, atd eventually the following letter was received from the Lona (London) Government Board in reply to the one ad- dressed. to the Home Office : (c OPT Local Government Board. Whitehall, S.W., 25th September, 1835.

Sir,—Adverting to the letter which the fo-cat Government Board addressed to 3 ou on the 2nd Instant, I am directed to in- form you that they have made inquiry upon the subject of the communication which you addressed on the 11th ultimo to the Secretary of State, and we are informed by the Clerk to the Guardians of the Warrington Union that the prosecutions re- ferred to in your letter were instituted by the Vaccination Officer by the directi n of the Guardians, and that. In obedience to their resolution, the Clerk appeared with the Vaccination Officer in support of the informations. 1 am, Sir, Your Obedient Servant. WALTER J. SEEDALL, Assistant Secritary. ,To Mr. Alexander Forster,

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 3, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JANUARY 3, 1885.

Whether this letter credits Mr. Sutton as champion, your readers having an option, a local option, can themselves de- cide. Mr. Sutton, it is admitted, is not a solicitor, and can therefore make no claim to the Solicitors' Act as available in this instance. Indeed, he bases his claim (when at home) on the 7th and Bth Viet, which simply enables the Guar- dians to appoint any officer to institute and conduct prose- ciations on their behalf. So far so good; I;iut the same Guardians are obliged by a later Act to appoint not any but one (the vaccination) officer only to take proceedings in vaccination cases, and since this is (by 27 years) a later I Act, does it not displace the former Act ? Again, the orders of the Local Government Board, which I Mr. Sutton admits are concurrent with the statutes them- selves, state distinctly that the Guardians shall give in- structions to their vaccination officer to take proceedings in all cases (vaecinational), and without these instructions no magistrate can legitimately convict. But in this instance Mr. Sutton claims not to proeecute but to advocate. The vaccination officer himself, with instructions signed and , sealed from his Guardians is present, and in his name the whole prosecutions are determined. By the 'Vaccination Act, 1867, section 33, the statute known as " Jervis' Act" (except section 2) in made to apply to all proceedings under that (Vaccination) Act. Hence by section 12 of Jervis' Act any complainant or prosecutor is at liberty to have his case argued, advocated, and witnesses examined and cross- examined by counsel or att rney on his behalf; but Mr. Sutton iu neither counsel, nor attorney, except in the esti- mation of his Warrington Guardiars. The letter referred to by Mr. Sutton from the Local Go- vernment Board is an equivocation, intended to shelve the real question. The anti-vaccina'ors contention is that Mr. Sutton not being a solicitor, neither he nor his Guardians I can have any right in the police court to prosecute in vac. ' cination cases, except in and by their properly appointed vaccinatton officer. By Mr. Sutton's advocacy in the late cases an illegality was practised; and an injustice done to each defendant, and the present instance serves as another illustration to the double dealing of the Local Government Board, when vaccination or any one of its officers are to be saved from reproach. The Local Government Board was fully informed that Mr. Sutton was not a solicitor, and no complaint was mode respecting the proceedings on the part of the vaccination officer. Hence their reply (while it leaves the question still open) is a shuffling on.—Yours, ALEXANDER FORSTER, 19, Regent-street, Earlestown. December 27th, 1884.
1885. Sir,—Before you publish this letter the year 1884 will hive become a thing of the pist. To many it his been a year fraught with trouble, and few, very few, can look over

- - its history with satisf action. We wish etch other " A. Happy New Year," but this conveys no impression to the mind diet we intend for the future to make " Life worth living." No, with the year 1885 will commence anew the struggle for existence, and again will the weakest have to make way for the strongest. A week or two ego I ventured to say that " the rich were growing richer.' I said this without for a moment think- ing that the poor were growing purer. It would be an un- fair way of putting it. During the past twenty years thirty men have died, leaving fortunes amounting in the aggregate to over forty millions of money. And yet it is I quite true that we in Warrington, at Christmas time, can hear of one in our midst being found starved to death. This is a stern fact, Mr. Editor, and one that will have to be grappled with shorty. Men live amongst us possessed of immense wealth, give thousands of pounds for the conversion of the Japanese, and vet at their death forget our own institutions. A bell is given to the Pariah Church in memory of the rich man, but the poor worker is asked to allow a portion of his wages to be 0 stopped in ' to support the Infirmary. How long will working-men put up with this sort of thing? Cannot they see that all this wealth comes out of their la- bour? Fortunts to the amount of £3,200;000 were left by the two Crawshays, of Cyfartha. Great iron kings were these men, turning a fair portion of Wales into a black country. Where is the benefit to the people ? One more iron district to help on the great question of horns competition, and spread out still wider the area of useless labour. In a sketch of travels recently issued, the writer asserts that in none of the countries to which we are kind enough to send missionaries, are the poor in such an abject condi- tion as we see them in the back Blume of our own large towns. What a statement to make about the richest coun- try in the world. Where a keen, competing, trading com- munity exists, there you must look for all the algae of marked and bitter class antagonism. Inordinate wealth brings despotism, luxuriousness, and a callousness of feel- ing that entirely blunts the sense of justice, and men ask, withoet a sense of the wrongness, "Can I not do as I like with my own?" To receive a plain " No" for an answer is, no doubt, startling; yet it must be so. During the past three years this answer has been given inure than once. The coming year is pregnant with the fortunes of the resi- dents in these islands to an extent that is little dreamt of. I can fancy that before very long, many a man will be told, to at once render an account of his stewardship; failing this, "bag and baggage" will be whispered to him. A very few years since I ventured to urge the nationalisation of the land. This called forth such a denunciation that I was half persuaded I had gone wrong; and yet to-day, one who was always the friend of the people,-John Bright-states : I If land is not worth rent, it should be, and will be, rent free." In a very short time this will come to mean "The land for the people." If I might venture, without being charged "with abusing working-men," I should say turn your undivided attention to politics. The men whe have amassed the huge fortunes, to which I have referred, have more things than their individual perseverance to thank for this Big incomes are netted by men who scarcely leave their arm chair. The banking, brokering, and other doings in the money market are subjects that would engage a Par- liament representing the people, but will never be touched by men who exist on its frauds—l ahnuld say legalised, frauds. Take up your Times and read the Vienna corre- spondent's letter of December 19,h, and note carefully the reference made to the bank frauds in that city by a bank manager. " Herr Jauner was always considered an upright man, and enjoyed unlimited confidence. He was very i religious, went to church every morning before going to his °Mee •, the exact deficit is 2,059,0001" To how many does this mean ruin? Swindling of this kind always has ; an injurious effect on trade, because traders all over the world are so connected in their business relations with each other that a link snapped affects the whole chain. Going further afield, and looking more at the position of • the workers, in Russia things are deplorable. The Emperor, a prisoner, is little better off than the meanest in the gang bound for Siberia; nor does he deserve to be. With a European connection and almost a European education, he still knows no better way of governing his people than by threats of exile. Respecting Russian trade, I enclose a cut- ting from a trade paper. • Please print it. Surely from it such working-men as have taken a fancy to the Fair Trade fallacy will learn a lesson :—" Industrially, Russia," a corres- pondent of the Times says, "has experienced great disillu- sions. The Protectionist and almost prohibitory system which the Moscow manufacturers strove for, and at length obtained, with the view of shutting out Silesian competition, has turned against them. The Silesian manufacturers, fading it impossible to struggle against the prohibitory duties on the frontier, have crossed over and established themselves in Russian Poland, especially at Lodz, which has now become a kind of Manchester, with hundreds of factories, built by Germans, with German artisans, German processes, and German management ; and the products of these factories reach the Moscow market at prices 5 or 10 per cent, lower than those bf Moscow goods. Moreover, the Russian cod- quests in Central Asia had induced manufacturers, by the prospect of a considerable market, to increase production to such an extent that, in orsier to diminish their stocks and avoid ruin, they are forced to work only three days a week, from 8 to four o'clock, whereas they used to work for seven days and during all the 24 hours. When the manufacturers tried to dispose of their goods in Central Asia, they found it impossible to face English competition. They are now ex- posed to English competition in Central Asia, and to the comp tition all over the Empire of Germans settled in Rus- sian Poland. The result is that these German manufac- turers have been petitioning for a farther increase in Cul- tome duties, wbereaa the Moscow manufacturers have been petitioning against such a step—some even going so far as to ask for a Customs line between Russian Poland and Russia proper. There is thus not the slightest improvement in Russia, as regards internal security, religious toleration, finance, or industry since the European press became silent." The land question in Russia carries the same importance as at horns with us. Nominally free, the peasants in reality are Serb ; consequently we see such education as the Russians have forces her thinking population into the ranks of the Nihilists. Ills bard to have to acknowledge the ne- cessity for secret societies, but the slightest acquaintance with human nature will force us to confess that confined feelings, like confined steam, must have an outlet. Woe to him that sits on the safety valve ! Most of us must have felt a certain amount of uneasiness during the passing of the eventful year 1884. Science has placed within the reach of all such a powerful weapon that nations now stand in dread of the dynamitard. Spreading from Russia into Germany, we read of poor compositors travelling over half the world seeking work, introducing te the Emperor William's notice scientific machinery, thatenot only shortened a Rus- sian Emperor's career, but in our own metropolis threatens to make England a world's talk. Do we ever ask ourselves the meaning of all this? Do we wish 1885 to bear the same kind of dead sea fruit that 1884 has given to us? If not we must certainly be up and doinv. lam sadly afraid that while we are spending blool and treasure in putting other lands to rights, we are neglecting our own. Itishmen have proved the existence of innamerable grievances. Men, the descendants of a land-grabbing:nobility, have been made to disgorge some of their plunder, and not a doubt remains, that Irishmen have pointed out to Englishmen the only way to settle the land question. Let them now clear oat Duolin Castle. Platform agitation will do it; there needs no other moms. and the first rouge in the ladder that leads up to comfort will have been passed. Let me press earnestly upon Irishmen the great need that exists for their taking steps to stop the war of dynamite that is being introduced into England. The only object gained by this inhuman mode of agitation will be to help our rulers to rivet afresh the fetters which it has taken so long to loosen. Irishmen and Englishmen must commence the New Year as politicians, determined to work for one object, the greates comfort to the largest number of people possible. With the Redistribution Bill will come great possibilities; labour will get nearer to the point where respectful attention will be given to her demands. Just now the working-man is subject to numerics influences, and when members of his own class are placed in representative positione, and ac- tually experience what it is to guide the State, he may

naturally hope to know the influence that works for his good. - Questions of importance will come nearer home to the new constithences. They will be able to see why questions such as those I have rocently put to Fair Traders are not answered; that with Americans amongst us owning land, and driving our own countrymen off, so that they may have the pleas- ures of a deer forest, lies one of the oecrets of bad trade; that with a state-supported Church, taking from the people £40,C00,000 to support a class of people that gives no return, lies another of the secrets of bad trade. 1884 has elven us a Franchise Bill. 1885 will complete the work, and as soon after that as may be possible we shall have a general election—with the chief cathedral cities al- most disfranchised; and, a Corrupt Practices Act passed, we may hope for a little fair play And if the next Parliament does not contain more men pledged to the cause of labour it will much surprise z CLIFFOAD DIX. December 28, 1884.

SOIREE AT ST. FIELE‘S ON MR. GLA.DSTONE'S DIRT aDAY. The Liberals of St. Helens commemorated the 75th anni- versary of the birthday of the Right Ron. W. E. Gladstone, M.P., by holding a soiree in the Assembly-room of the Town Hall on Monday evening. The gathering was a most successful one numerically, and the proceedings were of a hearty and enjoyable character. In honour of the occasion, the room had been very attractively decerated. Mr. Richard Pilkington, of Rainford Hall, kindly granted the use of his choice plants and flowers, and these were arranged in front of the platform and along the tea tables, which occupied all the available space on tbe ground-floor. The crimson dra- pery behind the president's table had a very pleasing effect, and the banner of the association, bearing the words " St. Helens Liberal Association," tended to still further im- prove the appearance of the room. About 450 persons sat down to tea, the tables, numbering 20, being presided over by the following ladies :=airs. Richard Pilkington, Mrs. W. W. Pilkington, Mrs. 'r. Cook (Mayoress), Mrs. W. Gamble, Miss Gamble, Miss Sinclair, Mrs. Twyford, Mrs. R. Belsher, Mrs. J. Boydell, Mrs. E. Bramwell, Miss Broek, Miss B. Duff e, Mrs. J. G. Dunn, Mrs. W. Fletcher, Mrs. J. Forster, F Mrs. W. H. Foster, Mrs. C. Gallie, Mrs. W. Gentles, Mrs. W. Harris, Mrs W. Harrison, Mrs. Haswell (Port Said), Mrs. J. Hewitt, Mrs. Jamison, Mrs Dutton, Mrs. J. Jones, Mrs. H. R. Lecey, Mrs. J. B. Leach, Mrs. H. Martin, Miss McNicoll, Mrs. D. Mc Kechnie, Mrs. J. Pennington, Mrs. C. J. Richards, Mrs. T. Roberts Mrs. F. W. Tinker, Mrs. W. Tyrer, Mrs. W Twist, Mrs. J. Walker, Mrs. R. J. Ward, Mrs. J. M. Wilson. The following gentlemen acted as the manag- ing committee :—Messrs H. Martin, J. Boyden, J. B. Leach, J. Forster, and A. Muir. At the subsequent proceedings Councillor Richard Pil- kington, J.P. (President of the Council of the St Helens Liberal Association) occupied the chair, in the absence of Lieut-Col. Gamble (President of the Association). The Chairman on making his appearance upon the platform, accompanied by the following gentlemen, was received with loud applause —His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Thomas Cook), Alder- man Johnson, Dr. McNicoll, Councillors John Forster, W. W. Pilkington, R. G. Brook, W. H. Foster R. Belsher, Revs J. Shipharn (Wesleyan), G. Smith (Wesleyan), R. J. Ward (Congregational), Drs Twyford and Jamison, Messrs W. Gamble. A. Sinclair, J.P., H. Martin, J. Boydell, John Pen- nington, R. C. Richards (Manchester), H. R. Lacey, J. Middhurst, W. Harris, R. A. Clark, W. Harrison, T. Roberts, J. B. Leach, James Burchall, and F. W. Tinker. The proceedings were commenced with a pianoforte solo by Mr. J. Edmundson, after which Mr. J. G. Morris excel- lently sang 'The Pilot.of the State." The audience heartily joined in the chorus, and an encore was demanded. Mr. Morris repeated a portion of the song. The Chairman next addressed the meeting. He said he regretted very much that owing to the absence of Colonel Gamble it devolved upon him to Wee the chair. He would much rather have seen their president in that position, but ill-health prevented it. But he (Mr. Pilkington) thought they must all feel glad that the Liberal party of St. Helens had been able on the 29th December to have a soirée such as that. (Applause.) He congratulated the Liberal party on that occasion, because he thought that was an occasion, so far as a soiree was concerned, that they had not had for many years. (Applause.) It was not time now for Liberals to march with banners flying and weapons ready to take the field either at Eerlestown Common or elsewhere. It was not a time for martial music, but rather a time for celebra- tion, or, he might say, feasting and rejoicing over a victory which they had won. (Applause.) When a victory had been won, troops laid down their arms, and took, it might be said, of the spoil. That eras their position that evening. They had fought well, and won well, and were able to look upon their enemies, not as enemies, but, he hoped, as friends. (Cheers.) The result of the hard struggle in which they had been engaged was a result of which they might well be proud. The bill which enfranchised every householder in the three kingdoms was passed—(cheers)—passed through the efforts of the Liberal party and through the efferte of the Conser- vative party, the latter in moving out of the way (Laugh- ter.) The efforts of the Liberal party were in one direction and the efforts of the Conservative party were in the same direction as soon as they turned round. (Renewed laugh- ter.) They (the Liberal party) might congratulate them- selves that the • Conservatives had got out ef the way, and the Conservatives might congratulate them- selves, for if they had not got out of the way a little struggle would have ensued, and he (Mr. Pilkington) would leave it for those present to say who would have had the best of it. (Laughter.) The Conservatives, however, claimed it as a victory, but if that was a victory the more they had of that sort the merrier for the Liberals. ( Ap- planes ) Remarking that that was a fitting opportunity to look over the past 50 years and consider the great and isplendid triumphs of the Liberal party, and the progress of this country, net only materially, but in freedom, liberty, and heppiness, the speaker proceeded to review the measures which had been passed by Liberal Governments during that period, and the services of Earl Grey, Sir Robert Peel, Earl Russell, Lord Palmerston, and John, Bright, were referred to. But there was another name more dear to them than any other, and it was one which completed the list of those six great men whose names shone out in those fifty years— the name of their great and splendid leader, Mr. Gladstone. (Loud applause, during which "Three cheers for Gladstone" were called for, and heartily given.) Those 50 years and the splendid work of the men be had named would be amongst the grandest and noblest pages of English history, and it was good that they should remem- ber it. There was a retson why the 29th December should never be forgotten, and that was because it was the birth- day of Mr. Gladstone. That day he reached his 75th year, and in his time he had done some of the greatest work that it was possible for an Englishman to do, not only in Par- liament, but outside, in the way of educating public opinion, and he (the chairman) was sure it gave them all the great- est delight and pleasure to wish him joy and happiness, awl express that satisfaction for the services he had rendered to his country to which he was so richly entitled. (Applause.) He (Mr. Pilkington) would conclude by stating that be had sent from that gathering the following telegram to Mr. Gladstone :—" The Liberal Association assembled in the Town Hall at a soiree held in honour of your birthday, wish you many happy returns of the day and every possible hap- piness." (Loud applause.) The St. Helens Vocal Union, under the condnctorship of Mr. J. T. Elliott, then gave a glee. Alderman Johnson stid they were assembled for the pur- pose of celebrating the anniversary of Mr. Gladstone's birthday, and they did it because they believed he was a great man. (Applause.) He wished he could transport those p-esent to Hawarden Castle, that they might per- sonally tell Mr. Gladstone in their own way of the joy they felt that he was still so hale and hearty, and that they were living in hopes he would be preserved for many years to rule the destinies of this great nation. They had not met to celebrate Mr. Gladstone's anniversary on account of his being seventy-five years of age,. or on account of his being Prime Minister, but because they believed Mr. Glad- store by his efforts, and industry, and perseverance, and courage bad conferred upon the people great blessings, for which they honoured him. (Loud applause.) Mr. Glad- stone had done moon for Ireland, and he hoped the day was not far distant who the people of Ireland would recognise Mr. Gladstone as one of the best friends they ever had. (Hear, hear, and applause.) "Seventy-five and Hard as Steel" was then sang by Councillor R. Belsher, who was enthusiastically applauded. The Chairman next called upon Dr. McNicoll, who had been announced to deliver a "Eulogy upon Mr. Glad- stone?' Dr. McNicoll was warmly received. He did not think it right that they should extctly indulge in any great spirit of boasting or jubilation after the laid party warfare, because they were now all in the same path of liberty and reform. But if they did not exhibit any spirit of boasting, they might at least congratulate themselves as a party on the position they now held in the country. They had not far to seek why Liberals occupied the proud position they did. In the first place they ILA a good cause—good in its principles and practices and goad in whatever way they looked at it—a cause of progress and growth as against the cause of etagnation and standstillness. (Applause.) It was, too, the cause of the people, and it was a winning cause. A very strong and large factor in their success had been the fact of their having been led by one of the greatest and most distinguished statesmen of this or any other time. He had been a general who had marshalled them in the way they ehould go to fight their battles, and by his political strategy caused them to win again and again, and they only hoped that be would for many years survive until he had carried out that great programme and .chenae which he had brooded over in his inmost soul, and when he should pass away he would leave a name and legacy that England would not soon for- get. He had all the qu ditiee of the greatest statesman. He had the philosophic mind and imaginative nature of Edmund Burke ; he hod the eloquence of Lord Chatham, and what was better he bad the moral courage of a Peel ; and he had crowned his long labours with two magnificent 1 measures of. reform. (Applause.) They knew what the verdict of this generation and of posterity would be— that Mr. Gladetone's mind overshadowed and overtopped every mind of this generation; and in conclusion he could only echo the wish and the prayer that he might long survive in full strength to add fresh lustre to the Victorian age ; that he might continue to lead them on in the path of renown and reform, and that when his career was finished all Eng- land would be able to say, ' Take him all in all, we ne'er shall see his like again." (Loud applause.) After Mr. T. W. Mahood, of Liverpool, had sung "When Britain really ruled the waves," Major W. W. Pilkington, ..1.1'., gave an address. He said he thought Mr. Gladstone might be congratulated upon the

settlement of the great question of the franchise, as it seemed to have been the act of his life which showed the most consummate generalship. They could congratulate themselves that it had been settled without any upsetting of the constitution, and if ever the day came for a change in the House of Peers he hoped it would be done not in pas- sion, and not in anger, bat quietly and with the consent of the whole nation. They had now their Franchise Bill and there was no doubt before long they would have a good Re- distribution Bill, so that he hoped they would afterwards have good, sensible, and quiet legislation. Speaking of "women's rights "he said he thought the women had some- thing a great deal better to do than 'messing about" —(loud laughter)—like politicians. There was something greatly wrong about the education of the girls and young women. Instead of teaching them how to cook a mutton chop or beefsteak, they began telling them all about the colour of the black man, where he came from, and such like. If they would only teach them how to dress a baby, and how to cook, it would be a great deal better for them. (Ap- plause.) He congratulated them upon everything that had been accomplished in the past, and was only sorry that Mr. Gladstone was 75. He could not have many years longer to serve them, but it was a grand thing for a man to have done what he had done. (Renewed applause). Another glee was sung by the St. Helens Vocal Union, and Mr. T. W. Mahood sang "The Speaker's Eye," and "The Old Brigade." Addresses were also given by Mr. R. C. Richards (Man- chester) and Mr. A. Sinclair, J.P., both of whom joined in congratulations to Mr. Gladstone on attaining his 75th birthday, and hoped he might be long spared in health and strength to promote those great measures of reform which he had striven to pass during the last 50 years. On the motion of his worship the Mayor (Alderman T. I Cook), seconded by Mr. H. R. Lacey, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the ladies who presided at the tea tables, and to those who had taken part in the entertainment.—A similar compliment was paid to the Chairman on the pro- position of Mr. W. Gamble, seconded by, Mr. M. Martin, and the Chairman in responding thanked the Committee for the exertions they had put forth to secure the success of the gathering. The meeting then concluded.

div.head: SPARROWS' MEETING.
div.p: THE SPARROWS' MEETING.

[The Secretary of the Wirral Farmers' Club states that representatives of the farmers have been appointed in each township in Wirral t 3 pay for the destruction of sparrows, of which some thousands have been killed during the year. The Wirral Club have further resolved to pay for the destruction of sparrows from the let of Jaousry, 1883, till the end of March next.— Tide Daily Papers.l Sparrows, sparrows, perky sparrows, Good at feeding, or at fighting, Darting hither, darting thither, Crying—" Muting, reat mass meeting; To he held this Christmas evening, In the barn of Farmer Wurzel. Question: Life or Death to sparrows. Sparrows! meet in mighty numbers ! " Qulckly answering to the summons, Met they, and the barn was crowded; Crowded every beam and rafter, Breaking in upon the spiders, Who were glad to cower in corners; Something gained that life was left them; For your demagogic sparrows—] Hot-foot in redress of grievance— Little care for rights of others. Twitter-Bob was voted chairman; He was plump, and sleek, and oily, And could stir up insurrection Without ever entering in it. Well be turned the pros. and cons. o'er, Hinted at a revolution, And was loud in protestation 'Gainst the slaughter of the sparrows; Slaughter in a Christian country; Slaughter on the eve of Christmas— Preaching peace on earth to people, While the hands are red with slaughter! Oh, the chitter, Oh, the chatter, - Oh, the tumult in the rafters When tit:a stirring speech was ended. There were cries of "Shoot the lanallords! " "Shoot the farmers!" "Shoot the shooters! " "Get some dynamite and clockwork, .Ay, and blow them all to pieces ! " Such the tumult in the rafters; It was as the House of Commons When, the nation in a crisis, Everyone would be a speaker. Who can say what would have happened? Wings were in a lively flatter, Feathers in the air were scattered, When an Owl, that from a loophole Had been watching the proceedings, Suddenly began tuwitooing. With a voice that pierced the discord; Followed by a pause of silence. "Sparrows," said he, " Sparrows, listen, Listen to the voice of warning, Listen to the voice of wisdom— Voice of Graybeard of the Sages. Say what would ye with the creatures Who go forth and seek to kill you ? Would you turn upon and rend them? Would their misery make you happy? Look abroad on hapless mortals, Hapless all the wide-world over, See them, ever keen for slaughter, How they prey upon each ether. Shall they spare you then, ye Sparrows, When their kith ald kin they spare not? Grievances? Of course we all have; But your lot, why, it is happy— Glorious if you only think so ; Man, the marplot, is in torture When compared with your existence. Have you not the merry sunshine? Have you not the playful breezes Coming to you unpolluted— Fresh as from the fields Elysian? And your crops, ah, there you have it; They are always full—l know you. Think you now of Farmer Wurtzel, Poor, and nigh upon starvation— Scarcely one good crop in seven. You can eat and drink contented; The supply will never fail you. You can take wing, hither, thither, None to question, none to stay you. Life to von is full of leisure, Full of fun, and love, and mating. Shot at last! you answer; well. thee, What of that? A little powder, Flash and smoke, and—all is over. Turn ye now to beings human, To the creatures you would punish. See them striving, toiling, moiling, In their pent-up, smoky cities ; See them grinding in the workshops To the grinding of machinery; See their mazy heads a-whirling To the whirling of the spindles ; See them broiling at the forges, All but in the fiery furnace ; See them underground a-pooling, Lost to free air and the sunshine; See them haggard, standing idle E'en when willing to be working; See them wretched, wildly drinking Of the drink that burns and maddens; See the prison and the workhouse, Monuments of crime and misery ; See the little children naked, Starving in the slums and alleys, Souls and bodies steeped in poison; Happy they when Death has touched them! Talk of slaughter 0, ye Sparrows? Seamen make their hellish engines— Grinning Satan's precious playthings; . See them rush upon each other, Breaking heads in, letting life out. Slaying thousands, tens of thousands, Rolsbing mothers of their darlings, Robbing dear wives of their husbands, Robbing children of their fathers! Go your ways, ye foolish Sparrows, For the world is past your mending ; Eat and drink and make you merry, For to-morrow ye may perish." "Make us merry! Make us merry !" Rang a thousand chirpy voices! "Make us merry, while yen tell us Tales of misery and slaughter! Out upon thee, mocking Graybeard; Die thyself as others perish !"

Then arose a mighty tumult; Clash and clang, and up I started, Knowing that I had been dreaming, Knowing joyous batls were ringing, Ringing in the gladsome promise Of the good time coming, owning, Ever promised, ever coming. Warrington, Jan. Ist, 1835.

The Claimant is said to have been warned by the Home Office to use more guarded language at meetings, or his ticket will be recalled. THREE BOYS DROWNED WHILST BELTING. —Three boys, namely, Joseph Wood, Joseph Walker, and John James White, were drowned while skating at Hunwick, near Bishop Auckland, yesterday. A man named Gains endeavoured to rescue °nevi the lads, but was too late. The bodies have been recovered. A JEWELLER'S STIOP ON FIRE. —About half-past two o'clock on the afternoon of New Year's Day a fire was discovered in the lock-up shop of Mr. Thomas Chesterton, jeweller and optician, Liverpool-road, St. Helens. The door was broken open by Mr. David Kenny, who lives near, and the fire brigade was sent for. Buckets of water were poured upon the burning material, and the flames were soon ex- tinguished. Mr. Chesterton left the shop at one o'clock to go to his dinner, and apparently everything was then all right. He estimates the damage at £2OO. which is covered by insurance. Overheating of the stove is supposed to have been the cause. MEDICINES, ELASTIC STOCKINGS, CIXEMICA.LS, DEMOS, by parcels post, under llb,, M. Say Bros., Stockport,-40t.

div.p: WIGAN.
SERIOUS RAILWAY COLLISION NEAL

An alarming accident occurred on Monday, at Crow Nest Junction, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, between 20 and 30 passengers receiving injuries. The junction is situated between Hindley and Westhoughton Stations, and connects the Chorley and Horwich branch with the main line from Liverpool to Manchester. A coal train, after being made up for Entwistle, was shunted on to a loop line in order to allow the.l-40 p.m. express from Liverpool to the Yorkshire district to pass. The facing points at this spot were, as it was auppesed, released, and the signal lowered for the passenger train to proceed. The train arrived at Crow Nest Junction about 2-20, and was running at the rate, it is said, of 30 miles an hour, when it dashed into the loop line, on which was standin, the En- twistle coal train, with an ordinary pilot engine in front. The driver of the passenger train, William Wallwork, of Great Lever, and his stoker, James Hayter, manfully st. ck Ito their posts, the former at once reversing his engine, and the latter applying the break. The train was not, however, provided with the vacuum break, and into the stationary mineral train it smashed with terrific force. The tender of the bank engine was foremost, and in this the passenger train literally embedded itself, lifting the engine completely off the metals. Fortunately, the driver and fireman of this engine and the breaksalan jumped off when they saw the approaching collision. The guard's van of the coal train was completely wrecked, and several waggons split up. Tee passenger engine was, of collie, much damaged, but it kept on the line, and the first two carriages suffered most damage the ends being driven in. It was in these two that most damage, passengers who were injured were riding. Mr. Whitehead, coal inspector of the locomotive department of the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company, was in the train, and word was at once sent for medical assistance, which very quickly arrived. The following is as complete a list as could be obtained of the injured : Elizabeth Jack-on, Heaton Norris ; injury to head. Thomas Greenwood, Sandbed, near tiebden Bridge; alv,ck and wound above the nose. William Ocv•per, The Mosses, Bury; cut on :eft hand. John Riley, Liverpool ; shock. Mrs, Pilliog, Woodhall-street, Bury ; Mrs. Cheatham, Cleveland-road, Manchester; shock. Joseph Peace, Moses Gate, Bolton; injured nose and bruise on right side of face W. J. May, Nicholsan-road, Heeley, Sheffield; contudon of right leg. Robert Dodd, River-street, Liverpool; chock, Mr. Wlltehead. Bolton, coal insp-ctor for the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway Company; serious wound on forehead, Richard Hamer, B•lton ; wound on forehead. Mrs. nalaall ; injury to seine. Mary Dawber, Farnworth ; cuts on the head. Ada Dawber (daughter of ab3ve), aged 13; broken leg. Miss Crofts, Dalton Vicarage; bruised knee. Mrs. Gore, Spring-view, Lower Ince; contused eye, bruises about the head, and severe shaking. Squire Dunkerley, Southport; Injuries to the head. H. Emmett, Clayton; slight general injuries. Thomas Bramwell. Little Lever, B dton ; ditto. ThomatLeyfield, Aczringto,a, guard of the passenger tam serious cuts to the head, Miss Amelia Martlew, Millgaie, Wigan; shaken. Miss Sarah Martlew, same address; concussion. W. Wallvvork, driver of the passenger train, 13,adford-strect, Great Lever; severe injuries to hips. B. Wenzell, Belmont-terrace, Bit-don; concussion and sup- posed internal injuries. Mr. James Akeroyd Preston; shock and bruised leg. He rode in the same carriage as Mrs Dawber and her daughter, and at once continued his journey home v.:cr Manchester. Captain Brewer, inspector of factories, was riding in a first-class compartment in the train, but he escaped. Ile states that the train was going at a good speed when it swerved right on to the loop line. He called Out that something was wrong, and immediately he was thrown against the other side of the carries, which was fortunately cushioned. His fellow-traveller, Mr. Low, of Bolton, was II not quite so lucky, but he received only slight cuts on the head. Asked as to what he thoueht was the cause of the accident, he replied that, undoubtedly, the points must have been open. An examination of the spot was afterwards made by the officials, when it was found that the points had been open. The pointsman, after having shunted the coal train, had put over his lever all right, but owing to one of the "cotters" on the connecting rod having become us- stripped, it had failed to move the points, and these re- mained as placed for the coal train. Toe signal was also down for the passenger train, no blame therefore attaching to the driver or the poiutsman.
EARLESTOWN

NEW YEAR'S HOLIDAYS.—The Viaduct Waggon works, the Vulcan iron foundry, and other smaller works in the vicinity of Earlestown stppe4 on Wednesday night until next Monday, but the extensive works of Messrs. Geo. McCorquodale and Company, printers, Newton, were only stopped for New Year's Day. Jtrvarnmn Tam:mans' TY.a. Ilitnicrixo. —The membera ,of the Juvenile Temple, in connect= with the Good Templar Lodge, were regaled with their annual treat on Friday evening in the lodge-room, Bridge-street, under the superintendence of Brother E. Newman. The tea and edibles served to them were heartily enjoyed, after which they spent a very pleasant evening. Songs, recitations, &c, were given and several games were played. _

CONCERT AT CARRINGTON.—Tne annual concert for the benefit of the schools has been held in the schoolroom, which was tastefully decorated for the occasion. Several glees were sung by the choir in a manner which reflects great credit upon the careful tuition of Mr. Brereton, the choirmaster. The room was filled with a large and appreci- ative audience, who testified their saiefaction by loud ard frequent applause. The sum of £8 33 was taken at the doors.

GOOD TEnDLLEY.—The weekly session of the mem- bers of the Hope of Eerlestown Lodge of Good Tempters was held in the ledge room. Bridge-street, on Nlond sy even- ing, when Brother George E. Warburton, 1'.W.0 r., presided in the absence of Brother John Taylor, W.C.T. After Vie arrangements for holding the annual tea party had been com- pleted a social meeting was held. Several hymns and melo- dies were sung by members, the evening being pleasantly spent. HIGH LEGE( TEMPERANCE Socrwre.—The fiftieth annual gathering of the Temperance Society of High Legh and dis- trict was held at Northwood Ferns on Christue is Day, and was largely attended. After singing and prover, the chair was taken by Mr. George Okell, of Leigh, who said he had been fighting the battles of temperance for upwards of fifty years, and he was glad that at hie advanced age he was able to attend their annual gathering, Mr. Thoinas Okell, Mr. John Naylor, and Mr. James Hewitt addressed the meeting. Sons, recitations, die., followed. FATALLY SCALDED WITH TEA.-OR Tuesday afternoon Mr.W. T. Husband, deputy coroner, held an inqacst at the Wargrave Inn, Wargrave, touching the death of James Naylor, two years of age, son of Robert Nayle, a boiler- maker, residing at 3, Liverpool-row, Vulcan. From the evi- dence given it appeared that on the 17th December the child Was getting its tea with an aunt named Phoebe. Ander- ton. He was seated in a chair at one side of the table and wished to be placed at the opposite sP.e. His aunt was lift- ing him over the table when the child's frock caught the spout of the tea.pot, which was filled with hot tea. The pot was pulled over and the hot liquid flew upon the child who was so badly scalded about the beck and chest that its skin peeled off with its clothes. Elizabeth Critchley, a neigh- bour, was called in and the wounds were temporarily dressed until Dr. Foulston (assistant to Dr. Handyside), who had been sent for, put in an appearance. He subsequently at- tended the child up to its death, which occurred on Friday night. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," igen L.R V. PRIER Mmerreici.—The annual prize meeting in connection with the F Company of the 19th LILY. (Liverpool Press Guards) took place on New Year's Day. The present strength of the company is 95 men, and Captain J. L. Wood, who is in command, has manifested a keen interest in its welfare, and had striven hard to bring it to its present high state of efficiency. The shooting took place at the Highfield Moss range, and on the whole was very good. The weather was fair, but a cold, stiff breeze prevented high scores being made. There were 65 com- petitors, and, all securing the requisite number of points, no one was prizeless, though the priz.s were of different value. Sergeant Moister won the first prize. By the kind- ness of Captain Wood the men weie supplied with refreshments at the range, and at the con- clusion of the shooting the committee formally handed the prizes over to the winners. The prizee had been kindly presented by the tradespeople of Earlestown and Newton, and the company expressed their indebtedness. The members of the company and a few friends afterwards adjourned to the Leah Arms Hotel, near Newton Bridge station, where they partook of their annual dinner, which was of a sumptuous character. Among the gentlemen present were Mr. Henry Houghton (who presided), Mr. W. D. Burdie, Mr. Kirby, Mr. Mellor, Mr. G. Wright, Mr. W. Maudsley, and others. The proceedings were of a pleasant character.

div.head: NEW YEAR FESTIVITIES.
div.p: NEW YEAR FESTIVITIES.

New Year's 13. a; was celebrated at Earlestown and Newton with the heartiness of former ye irs. There were several attractions for the public, but the bitterly cold weather tended to mar the enjoyment of pleasure seekers. There was a slight downfall of rah. on New Year's Eve, but it did not last long, and it fortunately held off on the following day. At many of the places of worship special watchnight services were held, and these were well attended. In the early hours of the morning several bands of carol singers were met with, and occasionally the strains of a brass band could be heard. Most of the shops were closed for the day. In the afteinoon the coursing at Haydock Park attracted a goodly portion of the sport-loving fraternity, while several football matches in the neighbourhood were an attraction to others. The more soberly disposed individuals spent the afternoon and even- ing at one or other of the numerous tea parties, while the public houses lid a good business at night.. Reports of the festivities are appended :--- GOOD TEMPLARS.—The annual tea party was held in the Lodge Room, Bridge-street, on New Year's Eve. About 60 members and friends sat down to an excellent tea, -after which an entertainment was held. Bro. Sheldon, of Wells, Somerset, presided, and gave an encouraging address. Bro. John Taylor sang "Vote it out" in a very spirited manner. Bro. E. Newman gave a temperance reading, Which was followed by a part song "Wake the Song," by Sisters M. E. Clarke, E. and J. Clarke, and Brothers 'George and John Clarke. "A long time ago" was then re,zited by Sister Barnard: and Bro. A. Allison sang "Wait till you get it." Bro. James Barnard gave a good reading, a.r4 was followed by Bro. George Clarke, who sang with eff ,ct "Which way is your musket a-pintin' to-day ?" Bro.. George E. Warbur- ton made a great impression in recitinf„; "The three Christ-

man Eve's." A song was given by Sister Allison, " Thir Postman's knock ;" and Sister J. E. Warburton gave an ar propriate reading "On guard." A melody was next gh'en by Sister and Brother Clarke, "Touch not the cup Bro. John Clarke recited "The muffin man and Bro. A. Allison saw,." " dowil an original song (written by himself). Newton Lake" which caused much amusement. On being re" c Men he sang "Sign the temperance pledge." Bro. Job% Warburton sang with much feeling " The brMal wine cap if alad was followed by Bro. John Taylor, vrlisang "Bit 0.. ribbon blue." A Lancashire reading was given by Bro. CT. ' Clarke, entitled, " the boggart o'th stump ;" Bro.
