div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

BA.PPIST SALE OF WORK AT WIDNES. On Thursday afternoon a sale of work was held in the "Baptist Chapel, Widnes, the opening ceremony being per. 'formed in the preeence of a fair audience by the Rev. It. 'Yeatman, the pastor. The object of the sale was to add to - the funds for the erection of a new chapel, an aim which has animated the members of the congregation for several , years past, and to accomplish which they have been as- sidionsly working. especially since the advent of Mr. It Yeetman, who has infused new energy into the denomination. I 'Daring the past sixteen months 18 new members have been I added to the roll, and since June three have been baptised, and the chapel is progressing in a highly encouraging way. The present structure is situated in Nelson-street, a locality, which at ohe time, it was thought would be the centre of the town, and the principal thoroughfare, but unfortunately I the desired development did not take place, and the build- eing is left stranded as it were in an obscure and unprepos- liming street. within the radius of which is alarge chemical warks. As the result of subscriptions and a previous baz- aar, the trustees have the sum of £l3l tils 7d in hand as the -EraolPos of the building fund, and with steady perseverance it is hoped that a sufficient amount eto commence operations will be raised. On Thursday the chapel was neatly decorated, and several tall, bearing goods of many shapes and hues, and for many purposes, were arrayed along the wall. The ladies in charge were—the Misses F. Passey, A. Wood, E. Seddon, E. Wright, E. Cooke A. Bailey, and Davies. Presents towards the bazaar, which had been organised by the young ladies of the congregation, from Mesdames J. Davies, Streets, Bailey, Lomax, Holden, Clifton, Baker, E. Edwards; Misses Young, F. Edwards, C. Cook; Messrs. Streets and Ware- ham. In declaring the bazaar op.n, the Rev. R. Yeatman wished all present a happy new year, and said it seemed to him that they had commenced the year in a very satisfac- tory manner, and in a manner likely to cause them all a considerab,e amount of happiness. They saw before them the result of the hard and earnest labour on the part of the young ladies of the congregation. Ile was very grateful to them for the amount of energy they had manifested in collecting those numerous and beautiful goods. They knew they wanted to build a new chapel, and he need not say anything about the neces- sity which existed for it. Everything at present seemed to be against them in the position in which they were placed, and they could not male that amount of progrese that they should like. They bad many difficulties to encounter, they were but a few people and they did not get that help from outsiders which was , generally found to be the CASO with weak bodies. He com- p,iLe• ' t,d thpir friend Mr. Baker for his very seasonable and encouraging gift of £5 towards the bazaar. The amount they had raised, as a church, did not seem much, but they must bear in mind that the sum had been subscribed in ad- ditioe to discharging all their liabilities, and also that the weekly offerings during the year had, instead of falling off, increased. Ha felt that if they went on in the came way, and could maintain confidence in themselves and the Supreme Ruler, they would ultimately reap the success they were working for. (Applause.) He then declared the bazaar open, and the sale commenced.

RUNCORN ,COUNTY COURT. TIIESDAT.—Before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes. ACTION AGAINST THU SLTEEINTENDENT OF POLICE. David Widders brought an action against Jesse Leah, superintendent of police of Runcorn division, the terms of the clam being as follows :—"For that you did wrongfully convert to your own t. 13 and deprive the plaintiff of the use and pe-eoseion of two Bank of England notes, of the value of each,the property of the plaintiff."—Mr. T. Shepherd Little, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. Burton), appeared for the plaintiff; and Mr. Cartwright, Of Chester, for the defendant. A jury, of which Mr. W. I Blythe was foreman, bad been empannellecl to hear the case. I The learned counsel in his opening statement narrated the facts of the case, and remarked that there was nothing sus- picious in a Tatman having several bank notes in his pos- session and if the jury believed that the plaintiff had no reasonable cause te suspect that Hoxworth had got them dishonestly, then they would return a verdict for the plain- tiff. The plaintiff said he resided at 12, Derby-place, Edge. lane, Liverpool. He was a joiner by trade, and at the time Of changing the. notes he kept the Nelson Inn, Rutland. street, Runcorn, On Tuesday, the_ 7th October, Thomas Hoxworth, his brother-in-law, came to his place. lox. worth was captain of a fiat. Ka asked for a glass of ginger beer and paid for it in copper. He then said he had been over to Widnes and drawn his freight of £2O, and that he had three £5 notes he wanted changing. He (plaintiff) re- plied that he cou'cl change him two of the notes. He did so;and. gave him ten sovereigns. At this time be was aware Of the death of a relative of Hoxworth, Which took place On the let October, and that Hoxworth had £l7 club money to draw. On the 9th October he heard that Hoxworth had been taken into custody, and he immediately went to the manager at Parr's Binh. The manager handed him a police notice. On the same day Superintendent Leah went to his house and asked him if he had changed any bank notes He replied that he had. The superintendent asked to be allowed to look at them, and plaintiff replied " certainly." He pulled out a pocket book and compared the notes with something in that book. The superintendent then handed the notes over to Sergeant Walley and told him to take care of them. He (plaintiff) informed the superintendent of the circumstances under which he had changed the notes. On S tearday, the 11th, he went to the superinten- dent and demanded the notes, but he refused to return them. He had kept the Nelson Inn for seven years, and &Olen had frequently come to his house and be had changed them bank notes occasionally. He had never changed notes for Bosworth before. Cross-examined by Mr. Cartwright He did not think it strange that Hoxworth had three £5 notes to change. He had never seen the police notice offering £lO reward for the recovery of the bank notes. At the Quarter Sessions he applied to the chairman fr the tree notes. The chairman replied that he had no jurisdiction. Henry Johnson, foreman in the employ of Messrs. Mar. wood and Co., s'iip brokers, and residing in New Egerton- , street, Runcorn, said he knew Hoxworth by sight. He was -Captain of a flat. From his (witness's) knowledge of the shipping trade the captain of the flat generally received the freight, but so-netimes the owners drew their own freights. Twenty retail would be a good freight.—By Mr. Cart- wright: Ile did not know whether Bosworth was authorised a to receive heights. Frederick Bibby, sail maker and ship store dealer, Widnes, said he lived in Runcorn, and he knew Hoxworth was captain of the flat Widnes. He gave similar evidence to k last witness. Forrester Bate, flat owner, Runcorn, corroborated, and added that Hoxworth received the freights for the flat of which he was captain.—Cross-examined by Mr. Cart- wright: Some owners drew their own freights. He (wit- -ness) drew his. Mr. S. Taylor drew part of hie, and the Navigation Company also drew their freights. In fact in ituntern the majority of owners drew their own freights; but in Liverp-01, where Hoxworth was engaged, the captain of the at received the freight. Sarah Widders, wife of plaintiff, confirmed her husbend's etatement. Sane Dodd, servant to the plaintiff, deposed to seeing the plaintiff change the notes. The court was then adjourned for luncheon. On resum- ing, Mr. Cartwright commenced his address for the de- fence. lie stated that Superintendent Leah possessed him- self of the notes for the purposs of a prosecution, and after conviction had been obtained against the felons, he had to take upon himself to decide to whom he should hand the notes. In the exercise of his judgment upon the facts of the case, be handed the notes over to Mr. Jones, the original owner, who had been robbed of them. His defence was upon the title of the original owner, and ha asked to have Mr. Richard John Jones, draper and grocer, Lianfairfec- hen, mede a co-defendant to the action. A short argument took place with His Honour, and the learned counsel pointed Out that when the plaintiff applied to Superintendent Leah for the restitution of the notes, there had no conviction taken place. The Superintendent bad at that time no de- fence. —His Honour said no doubt the Superintendent acted wrongly—imprudently, but of course be could quite under- Stand that the Superintendent being concerned in the pro- secution there was good reason why he should retain the notes, becAuse they were material to the conviction—Mr. Little : Jis Night have interpleaded at that time—His Honour: I think hardly at that time, because you see the prosecution was pending. His Honour added that it was a question whether the Superintendent would be justified in giving up tlaa notes when demanded by the plaintiff. His Honour then permitted Mr. Jones to be made a co-defend- ant on Superintendent Leah paying the plaintiff's costs of the day. Mr. Cartwright then entered into 3 long legal argument to show that the plaintiff ought to have applied for the re- stitution of the notes at the court where conviction was ob- tained, and that he having failed to do so he had now no remedy. and that His Honour bad no jorisdiction.—Tlis Honour said a rule of statute did not take away a common law remedy unless there were certain words to show that. He took a note of Mr. Cartwright's objection.—The Learned Counsel replied, and then His 110110ar ruled against Mr. Ca-tarright —Mr. Cartwright afterwardS addressed the jury at considerable length. He said this was a 'very important case to tho public generally, and he was sure the jury would agree with him that where any property had been stolen, it was a very serious thing on the part of the owner of the property th it no looseness or facilities should be given by people for disposing of that property to the prejudice of the owners of it. Persons who took notes ought to use due Cau- tion, and deal in a tradesmanlike manner with such pro- perty. This unfortunate woman, Mrs. Jones. WAS going from Llantairfechan to Manchester to mike prrchases of goods. She had got £8.5 about her, and the whole of that money was eithor abstracted from .h.er basket, or, haying fallen upon the carriage floor, was pinked np. If there were tb f4cilities to get rid of such oroperte there te; uld not he as much stolen aft there wae, hut it was a well-known f, c' that persons purehaled goods in an indiseriminattyway, and , changed not- eas is this particular case.- Be cenernented strongly upon ttie Lot that the plaintiff and Hoxworth were relateil, that bills offering a reward for the recovery of the "notes were posted through the town before the plaintiff changed the notes, and that there was £4O of the stolen money still unrecevered. He pointed out that Hoxworth a short time previously had pawned a pair of boots for 4e 64, Lot the Olaint,ff had given him credit on one occasion for a pint of ler e and asked whether under these circumstances a suspicion must not have crossed the plaintiff's mind that the notes he was changing were not honestly obtained.

Superintendent Leah was then called, and described' the apprehension of Honworth and Bushell and his wife, and I their conviction. Subsequently he west to the plaintiff's I house, and weed to see the notes which be had changed for lioxworth. The plaintiff handed him the notes, and after the trial Jonesdemanded them, and he (the superintendent) gave them to him. Previous to the conviction, and also I afterwards, the plaintiff bad applied for the money,--Croes- examined by Mr Little: The notes were not identified by Jones, who did not know the numbers. There were seven persons who either changed Lloxworth £5 notes or gave him goods in exchange. Some were changed at public- houses, one at the bank, and be purchased a gold guard at a shop in the town with another. Mr John Coxhill, of the Masonic Hotel, changed a note. Isaac Bryan, police constable at Runcorn, proved finding pawntickets in Hexworth's house. He knew Hoxworth. Mrs Jones then gave evidence of the robbery. She stated that £49 of the £B9 stolen had not been recovered. The bills published did not say the money was stolen. The learned counsel having addressed the jury on behalf of the plaintiff, his Honour summed up. If the jury were net satisfied that these two notes formed any part of the robbery, and they were satisfied the plaintiff gave fall value for them, then the plaint;ff was entitled to recover ' without anything further. He was bound to tell the jury that the very fact of the plaintiff having given full value was a most cogent fact in his favour,.and it threw it upon the defendant to impeach his goad faith with some very cogent evidence in reply to that fact. Had they done so? The plaintiff bad a stronger position.in the fact that he gave change for the note in taco of everybody in the house, and in broad day light. The jury after a short retirement returned into court, and the foreman said they found for the plaintiff; darnaws £lO His Honour then thanked the jury for their attendamce and attention, and entered judgment against the defendants, costs against Jones, exoept for the day, which Superinten- dent Leah had to pay. The case occupied upwards of six hours in hearing, and several other important cases had consequently to be ad- journed. . _

WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse yesterday morning. There were present Messrs. Derbyshire (chairman), Grange, Gibson , Wil I iam Houghton, Cooper, Jeans, Swinton; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), W. Owen ',surveyor), G. Rawlings (inspec- tor), and D. Sephton (medical officer). THE SHIP CANAL—The CLERK said be had received notice from the Manchester Ship Canal people as for as they affected this district, and also a copy of the bill which Mr. Owen would probably report upon it. These were merely formal notices. It was agreed that the matter should be left over till the next meeting.—The SURVEYOR also re- ported that he had received plans of the Manchester Ship Canal and a copy of the bill, and had walked over the course of the proposed canal and made notes of the brooks and sewers interfered with. There were several matters he had now under consideration with the clerk in connection with the bill, and he hoped te bring forward a complete report at their next meeting. THE CANAL BOATS.—The CLERK stated that by the Canal Boats Act. 1884, the duty of enforcing the law and regulatien with respect to canal boats was imposed upon every Sanitary Authority within whose district any canal or part of a canal was situated. He (the clerk) thought this would be one of those things which would give the Autherity much trouble.—lt was agreed on the motion of Mr. COOPER, seconded by the CHAIRMAN, that the inspector be empowered to inspect canal boats when he thought neces- sary on behalf of the Authority. THE CLERKSHIP.—With regard to the clerk's euvestion Ithat the assistant clerk should be appointed clerk to the Authority, Mr. COOPER said he had great pleasure in mov- ing that Mr. S. Sutton be appointed clerk to the Authority, , especially as it was understood that it would make no difference in the attendance of his father.—Mr. ORANGE I seconded, and Mr. DARBYSIIIRE supported this proposal, which was carried, SEWAGE Rnmover. —The only tender or the retnotal of sewage was one from Mr .1 Newton, the present contractor, and it was agreed that the matter should be left over, and that arrangements for the removal of the sewage on the pre- sent system should be made in the meantime. IHE 1-LACE OF MEETING.—The CLERK suggested that the Authority and Assessment Committee should meet at his offices in Bewsey-street, which were more centrally situated.—Several members thought this would be a suit- able change, and ultimately it WA3 agreed to examine the proposed new meeting place. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.--.The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that daring December there had been 27 births and 21 deaths in the Authority's district. The death•rate was equal to 20 per 1,000, against 14.2 in the corresponding month of last year. The district was fairly healthy, the principal Cause of mortality being from lung disease, and due to the sadden cold weather. This was all the business,

div.head: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this committee was held at the Workhouse, yesterday. The members present were Messrs. J. Rylands (chairman), Derbyshire, and Appleton ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), W. Owen (valuer), and J. L. Tunstall (assistant overseer). VALUER'S R EPORT. —The Verona reported that since the last meeting the Clerk and he bad obtained some informa- tion respecting the assessment of collieries in other Unions, but had not been able to consider the matter sufficiently together to bring forward a report upod the question. This they hoped to do at the next meeting. He valued the new theatre in Scotland-road at—gross £9O, rateable £76 103. The asseestnent of Holy Trinity Schools, Museum-street, he was asked to fix at the rate of other nomiaal assessments, and he had concluded to suggest—gross £l5, rateable £l3. COTTAGE ASSESSMENTS.—The CLERK read the following letter, sent to him by Mr. J. L. Tunstal I, assistant overseer, viz. :—"When asking the Assessment Committee on Friday next for a new valuation list for Warrington you will per- haps be so good as to mention the desirability of revising the cottage assessments. The considerations mentioned by Mr. Owen in his " Overseers' Manual," and of which we have hitherto taken no notice in fixing assessments of that class, are as follows :—Frequent changes of occupation; loss of rent which those changes involve, and trouble attending the collection of rent. With regard to the latter item, you are no doubt aware that the usual charge is five per cent. 011 the amount of rent collected. On the other hand, however, the rents of properties let on annual tenancies are sometimes collected by agents, and in those cases the charge is generally 21; per cent. I don't know how far the committee would feel inclined to re-consider the percentages deducted from the gross estimated rental for repairs, eze. At present 15 per cent is allowed in respect of all house and shop pro- party. Now, it must be evident that the amount actually necessary for such purposes will greitly vary according to the class of property, In the case of cottage property the repairs must of necessity be much heavier than in the case of houses such as those in Wilson-Patten-street. Again, a faxed percentage will operate very much in favour of the properties situate near the centre of the town, as the value of the land is included in the assessment, and in such pro- perties probably exceeds the value of the buildings. You will perhaps consider these matters before the meeting, and do what you think necessary. I should like to have the matter settled en Friday so that the new list may be pre- pared in time for the next rate.—After some conversation with respect to this letter it was agreed that a reduction of 5 per cent should be made in consideration of the fluctua- tions of the occupation of cottage property and the ex- penses of collection of rent, and that a further reductbn of 5 per cent as between the gross and rateable value. This was all the business of public interest before the Corn mittee.

MASONIC MEETING AT ST. }Turxxs.—The brethren of the Lodge of Loyalty, No. 897, held their annual installa- tion meeting ow Tuesday, at the Lodge-room, Hall•street. There was a very good attendance of members, and several distinguished visitors were present, including Bro. NV. Good- acre, Prov. G. secretary ; Bro. R. Martin, Prey. G. trea- surer; Bro. A. Young, P.P.G., S.D.; Bro. J. T. Callow, P.P.G. treasurer; Bra. O. Broadbri4,e, P.P.G.D.O , Sfc. The lodge was opened at half-past two by the W. M, Bro. D. M. F. Gaskin, and ether officers. The routine business having been disposed of, the lodge was closed and the brethren adjourned to the Royal Raven Hotel, where a ban- quet was served by Bro. Bennett. The newly appointed w.m., Bro Smith, presided at the subsequent proceedings. ODDFELLOWSHIP IN THE PHESCOT DISTEICT.—HALF- YEARLY MEETING OF DELEGATES.— The half-yearly Meet- ing of the delegates of the various lodges comprising the Prescot District of the Order of Oddfellows, Manchester Unity, was held on Tuesday, at the Brick Wall Inn, Tar- bock, Mr. Robert Wright, the provincial grand master of the district, presiding. The balance sheet, which was made up to December 29th, showed that in connection with the sick and funeral fund account £l3l 4s had been received in contributions from the several lodges during the half-year, which, with the balance of £499 lie 6cl brought forward from the June report, and £9 7s 2d interest, made a total of £6402s 81. The expenditure amounted to £74, leaving a balance of £566 24 Bd, being a gain of £66 lie 21—At the conclusion of the business, which lasted over four hours, the deleotes sat down to a substantial repast, to which full jus- tice was done. DROWNED WHILST SIM-MG.—Joseph Hamlet, 17 years of age. residing with his parents in Clyde-rreet, St. Helens, and employed as a glass " gatherer " at the bottle works of Messrs. Nuttall, was drowned while skating on a reservoir near Fccieston church. It is stated that the deceased bad gone across twice, and was asked by the others to desist, but he said be would go across " once more." He started with that object, but had not got far when the ice broke and deceased was immersed in the water. An alarm was raised, Let Ufa WAS extinct when the body was recovered a short ,rie afterwards. An inquest on the body of the deceased was held before Mr. S. Brighouse, at the Saddle Hotel, 11res liald• street, St. Helens, on Wednesday forenoon. It was stated by the father of the deceased that his eon was of a venture- some disposition. Other witnesses said that the deceased bsd got 30 yards from the side when the ice broke, and be was immersed in 13 feet of: water. The ice WAS an inch thick. After the jury had retured a verdict of " Accidental death," the coroner remarked that it was a pity that so many valuable lives shoald be lost for want of a little care.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 3 1885
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY 3 1885
of

THE NEW YEAR AT WARRINGTON- As far as weathen- is concerned, the- commencement ere \ 1885 was auspicious. The last day of the year now gone WAS bright and fine, and the day fotlowing even more so,' The celebrations attending the departure of the old and the advent of the new, year were of the usual character, mot \ being marked by any particular feature, though, if may- \ thing, the streets were less belay than in former years. Watch-night services were held in connection with many of the places of worship. On Wadneeday and on Thursday s various annual celebrations wars observed. Detailed accounts of these are appended. The town on Thursday bad a semi-holiday appearance, many of the principal place of business. being closed fee the greater part of the day, and lane numbers took, opportunity of the :3oliday to indulge in the favourite winter exercise on. fa wen ponds in the neighbourhood. A considerable number paid a visit tc. Lymm, where the lame was excellent. The places of amusement in Warrington, were well patronised, The ' publicans, too, transacted a. good business, bet notwah- standing this there were TIO indications of increased drunk-1 ennessa the streets being ezeceptionally quiet. The custom I of "letting-in" the new year was extensivelyeaserved, and ' the strains of music were to be beard until an early hour on Thursday morning. The New year was also welcomed heartily at Orford Barracks, where a dance toora place. The aged poor of the town were as usual remembered, and had the satisfaction of commencing the year with a meal which , they will remember with pleasure. Altogether,locally speak- ing, the year 1885 hue had a happy beginning, and it is to be hoped that the, auspicious auguries, accompanying its birth will be fully verified. BOLD-STREET SUNDAY SCHOOL. The annual tea meeting in connection with this Wesleyan Sunday School was held in the new school on Thursday, when a large number sat down to, tea. Subsequently a well-attended public meeting was held, at which the Rev. J. MeTurk oceepled the chair. After singing and prayer an address was given by the chairman, who said that they could not but be reminded on such an occasion how rapidly life passed and of the earnestness and responsibilities of life. Nears gone by were now as memories, but they bad left their blessings, and at the beginning of a new year they must try to conserve the blessings of the past and take a step forward in the future. They had reason to be encouraged, for they were met in a new room, with new appurtmances, and there were those amongst them who for many years had been anticipating that attainment. But they must remember that they had also responsibilities increased and must adhere faithfully to the good work, lie believed all engaged in the work meant to do their utmost to make the school more sucoessful than ever before. It was now 100 years old, and he hoped it would prosper and bear fruit in the future even more than it had done in the past. With the facilities they now had their work should be of a higher order, but they did not in- tend that the mission work carried or. in connection with the church should languish.—Mr. Henshall then read the annual report, which, after detailing the work of the past year relative to the building of the school, stated that the total of expenditure as well as could be ascertained was £3,413. Towards this £2,600 had up to the present been received; £7O mere was promised, leaving a balance to be obtained of £743. The total number on the books was 221 males and 169 temales-390 in all. The average attendance was about 100 in the mornings and 250 in the afternoons.— Mr. Isaac, in the course of a short address, referred to the great change in the Sunday school system since the time of Robert Raikes, and hoped that it would progress still more favourably. He then quoted statistics relating to Sunday schools in the Liverpool district, which placed Warrington circuit in the front rank for arrange. men,s, membership, sad attendance, and the various appurtenances connected with a successful Sunday school. —Mr Richardson said their meeting in that school was the climax of the hopes of 30 years or mare, and he hoped that soon the room would be filled with good teachers and a large number of seholars,—Mr Nicholson spoke on Sunday school wank in relation to church organisation, and the Rey, G. Cutting urged his hearers to do their utmost to I bring the little ones into the Master's fold.--ma. - 17... 'IN .e sow" • A • oandersoo, of Leafs, formerly of Warrington' in the OWN of an exhaustive speech, observed that their numerical strength as a Wesleyan church very largely lay with the ; Sunday schools.—During the evening songs and anthems were sung, and selections on the harp were give:. by Miss Toft and Mr Ford.—At the conclusion, a vote ef thanks was accorded the choir and the ladies who presided at tea, on the motion of the Rev J H Jones. WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CEIURCII. At this church the watch-night service commenced at eleven o'clock, and was continued till a few minutes after mid-night. There was a large attendance. Suitable hymns were sang and prayers offered up, and a short sermon was preached by the Rev. J. Yonge. The rev, gentleman took as his text part of the 29th v., 7th c. let Corinthians, "This I say, brethren, the time is short." That sentence, he said, was given with great accuracy and certainly with greater impressiveness in the revised version of the New Testa- ment, '-This I say, brethren, the time is shot tened." They would see that the sentence had an obvious appropriateness to the circumstances and season in which they met there. They were met there that night as they might say on the outpost and border land of another period of this existence; they were there together in the last half homer of the year. They were met, he supposed, because there seemed to them a peculiarly impressive interest in making the passing of that boundary. They were met together as a testimony of the sense they had of the value and the importance of their years, and he thought that their meeting should have the effect not simply of giving a passing feeling of interest to the season itself, but of creating a deeper impression in all of them of the intense and unspeakable seriousness of life. They were face to face with the fact that their lives were shortened by a year since they last assembled together in this place at that season of the year, and their lives were just shortened by that number of years which they indivi- dually had passed. The race was shortened for them, and they had less time that night than they had bad in which to achieve the great and magnificent purposes for which God created every one of them. He did not suppose that most men realised the greatness of the life which Geri had given them in this world. People were disposed to think that humanity here in this life at its best and noblest and grandest was but feeblest infancy com- pared with what it should hereafter become. But let them think for a moment of the greatness of human life as seen in the results which it worked. Take an example. They all were met that night to worship in freedom and in the en- joyment of advanced knowledge and civilization in that Wycliffe Ch3rch, because 500 years ago John Wycliffe lived and laboured, sowing widely through his career the seeds of liberty of conscience providing an open English bible for his countrymen. and sending forth far and wide his simple preachers to preach the blessed gospel of free salve- I tion by faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Five hundred years ago that day John Wycliffe died, and his work—the work ; of that great human life was still living. How that simple illustration showed to them the greatness of a short humen life. Wycliffe realised the greatness of life and did the most he could for the welfare of his own soul and for the 1 1 , welfare of his fellow countrymen, and for the glory and honour of his God. Mr. Yonge then made an earnest ap- peal to his hearers to make the best of the ememainiag por- tion of their lives, and warned them against the evils of 1 procrastination.—The discourse concluded shortly before twelve o'clock, and the intervening few moments were spent .in silent prayer. after which a hymn was sung and the service ended. TREAT TO THE AGED POOR. At noon on New Year's Day over 280 men of sixty years of age and upwards sat down to a substantial dinner at the Public Hall, Warrington, and in the evening even a larger number of aged women were provided with tea in the same building. The treats are annual ones, provided for by subscriptions, and are under the management of a number of gentlemen, viz. :—Messrs. T. Jones, T. Morris, T. Sutton, S. Jones, C. Skinner, P. Crimes, W. J. Horton, Legge, W. Dooley, J. Smethurst, W. Woods, Peter Corcoran, and J. E. Wright. Amongst those present at the mid-day meal were the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and the Mayoress; the Revs. S. Wilkinson, E. C. E. Carleton, C. C. Harrison, W. Mules, and J. Howell Jones; Messrs. D. W. Finney, J. Hes- keth, H. Toft, A. Browne, J. Domville, J. Ellison, R. W. Francomb, J. Pierpoint, G. Riley, Hutchinson; G. Pilling, ev. Porter; Mesdames goekett, Wilkinson, Venn, Garner, Carleton, Townsend, J. Pierpoint, Percival, Fraser; and Misses Wilkinson, Allton, L. Horton, Legge, and numarous others. The hall was decorated with banners and mottoes, and to add increased cheerfulness to the occasion Mr. W. Woods played selections on the organ daring the progrees of the meal. Shortly after twelve o'clock the long tables were laid with smoking viands which were eyed with interest by rows of hungry men. viands, having been said by the 11,,v. S. Wilkinson, the signal to "fall to" was given, and an animated scene ensued. Numbers of voluntary waiters were requisitioned into the service, ladies and gentlerneu vieing with each other to pay the greatest attention to their guests. The dinner, which was as good a one as could be desired, was heartily enjoyed, and subsequently packets of tobacco were distributed, each guest being also provided with a pipe. To further supplement the treat Mr. J. Pierpoint announced that Mr. Harmston had consented to give to all the guests free admission to the Circus in Sankey-street on Saturday afternoon, to b 3 procured by tickets with which they were supplied. The announcement was received with cheers and loud bmirrahs. Order having been restored, the health of the Queen was honoured most loyally, and the men than settled down to a steady conterdplative smoke— contemplation no doubt being mingled with antici- pations of circus riders and rollicking clowns. Notwithetandina, when the Mayor rose to deliver a short address be received undivided attention and was cheered. He wished them a happy New Year, and expressed the hope that during the next twelve months they would have pros- perity—that the hungry might be fed, and that every man In that roam might never feel the want of a good dinner without being satisfied. That annual dinner had commenced with small beginnings and assumed its present large pro- portions, and he was sure that those 'who had contributed towards it felt even greater pleasure than those who had enjoyed it. The beginning of a new year was a serious thing. It was like opening an account in which would be inscribed daring the year perhaps both their good and their bad deeds. He hoped they would all keep a clean sheet to the end of the year, and that they should transcribe nothing on it that would in the slightest degree disgrace the town of WIT rington. They must constantly watch themselves, for they could not resist the fact that:all had failings and weaknesses, which it behoved them to guard against. The

ay. S. Wilkinson also wished the guests the compliments ef the season. It was said that there was nothing like a :good commencemeat, lend as far as weather WE9 concerned ;the commencement of 1384 had been almost perfect. And l when they met together as then, and saw so many happy !faces around, he thought they might look 'vein it as an l augury of a Happy New Year. Many changes might take place. Many might be what the world called successful, but he was confident that if all did their hest the coming year would be a happy one. Be also urgedeapon them the necessity of attending to relikions duties. The company shortly afterwards diepersed. In the evening the women had a very enjoyable treat and afterwards- a public enter- tainment was held and passed off successfally. Mr. W. S. Wools officiatedes organist and Mr G Riley.a,s accompanist. The following progra.nme had been drewnalp for the occa- sion, viz :—Organ recital, Mr. W. S. Woods; pianoforte solo, Miss A. Wormersley; duet, Messrs Dell and Cavanagh; song, Miss L. Horton ; comic song, Mr. Petty ; song, Mr. Dell; comic sang, Dr. G. L. Coombs; song, Mr. Cavanagh ; comic sketch, Mr. R. Scerisbrick ; comic song, Mr. Petty ; song, Miss. L.. Horton ; comic smog, Dr. G. L. Coombs; song, Mr. Reddish; comic song, Mr. Monogue. RAILWAY SERTANTS' DlNNER.—The.ecoploy6s connected with Lateh:crd station held their "annual Christmas dinner" in, the waiting-room, on Christmas Eve. The dinner, whieh was a very satisfactory one, was supplied by Mr. Thomas Ireland. The usual 7.ote of thanks was ac- corded to the donors' and a very enjoyable meting was brought to a close at 11-30. CHRISM CISURCLI, LATCHFORD.—Service was held at this. place of worship on Wednesday evening, commencing at 1130. The vicar, the Rev. B. 3. Prescott, conducted thai service,. assisted by the Rev. J.. M. Prescott. The vicar de- livered, an address appropriate to the season from Dent. viii, ve 2.--" Thou shalt remember all the way which the Lord thy God led thee." The prayers consisted of the General Confession, the Absolution, and the Lord's Prayer. Psalm xxii, and hymns 24.3,_ 244 (sung kneeling), and 165, lanaient and modern, constituted the musical portion a the ' seevice, which concluded shortly after 12 o'clock. New YEAR. AT Leetet —The advent of the new year was welcomed very quietly at Lymm, bat Thursday was by many of the inhabitants observed as a holiday. 'File mere being covered by a splendid sheet of ice, attracted many skaters. The pastime has been kept up during the week with unabated ardour, and yesterday there was a large number of people on the ice. No accidents of a serious nature hove been reported. On Wednesday evening a ball was held at the Church Hotel, when between 30 and 40 attended, and dancing was indulged in to the strains of Mr Stirrup's band. A supper was partaken of during the night. A successful ball was held at the house of Mr Lake, the Fleece Hotel. WESLEYAN CHAPEL, SANKEY BRIDGES.—A watch-night service was held at this chapel and was well attended, being a considerable increase on former occasions. Several ap- propriate addresses were given by the following gentlemen; Mr. Snodely, on "Ties Journey of Life": Mr. Schofield, on "The Advantage of Personal Religion"; Mr. Brough, on "Taking account of our Stewardship "; Mr. Light, on "The Higher Purpose of Life ". and Mr. Summersgill, on St. Paul's three desires--" In Christ, For Christ, and With Christ." At the hour of twelve the usual hymn commenc- ing" Come let us anew, our journey pursue " was heartily sung, and as the congregation dispersed hearty greetings were indulged in and good wishes expressed for "A happy New Year." PENKETIL—The usual tea meeting and watch-night sea. vices were held at the Wesleyan Day School on Wedaesday night. Tea was on the tables at 7 p.m., when recitations, songs, and portions of scriptures were given by the follow- ing persons:—Mrs. 'Jenks, Misses Moses, Fanny Garnett, Lilly Garnett, and Messrs. Johnston Atherton, C. E. Parker, lima Greenholsh, H. [Ridden, A. Winn, Leonard Jenks. A duet was nicely sung by two girls, " Father pray with me to-night," Marian Ashton and Emma Hobson. Miss Fanny Garnett presided at the harmonium, and Mr. Garnett was chairman. Thera was a good attendance. At 10 p.m. the watch-night service commenced, when an excellent sermon was preached by the Rev. .J. Howell Jones, Warrington, from St. Luke, 13th chap., commencing at the 6th verso, There was a good congregation. Refreshments WM env- nlied during the bateryal of the meetiess. . I. Patna DieTninterioei AT Tai .. OlkHousE.—Veeterday' the annual distribution of toys, Ltc., to the children of the Workhouse schools took place at the Workhouse in the pre- sence of a number of ladies and gentlemen. The Guardians present were Mr. Brown (chairman of the House Commit- tee). Mr. Jeans, and Mr. Bonnell. The toys were presented to the children, at the request of Mr. Brown, by Mr. Mackey, the Workhouse master. The presents, seventy-one in num- ber, were hung upon a Christmas tree, and consisted of a great variety of such articles as are suitable for young chit- di en. After the presentation, votes of thanks were given to Mr. Brown and Mr. Mackey, and the latter in responding, thanked the public of Warrington for their subscriptione which enabled them to get those presents. He was sure that fall the givers had been present to see the pleasure which the gifts gave to the little ones, they would not think their money had been ill-bestowed. (Hear, hear.) Three cheers given by the children for the Guardians brought the inter- esting proceedings to a close. Wecueee COCKIIEDGE MISSION, BRICK•STREET. A watch-night service was held at this place on Wednesday evening last at 10-45, when there was a good congregation. Suitable hymns were sung with spirit and earnestness. "A few more years shall roll ' was sung as a solo by Miss S. Derbyshire, the chorus of which was heartily joined in by the congregation. Short prayers were offered by two or i three of the workers of the Mission, after which the Rev. I W. R. Parry gave a short addre.s, reviewing the past year, and made special reference to the death of Mr. Jonathan Wild, and urged his hearers to more faithful service in the new year. It was then a few minutes to twelve o'clock, and the interval was spent in silent prayer, after which Mr. Parry wished all present a happy new year. The very ap- propriate "Come let us anew our journey pursue " hyma IWAS then sun.; with spirit. The Benediction having been pronounced, Mr.- S. Travis struck up " Praise God, from whom all blessings flow," on the harmonium, which brought to a close a very pleasing meeting a little after twelve o'clock. Hearty greetings were given by the congregation at the close.

MARKEIS. _ MANCHESTER HAY AND STRAW, FRIDAY.—Hay, bd to 64d; clover, 6d to 7;c1; wheat straw, 4d to 4fd ; oat straw, 4d to 41d per stone of 141 b. LONDON PRODUCE, FRIDAY _sugar market extremely quiet; beetroot quoted 10s 34 sellers January. Coffee nominally with- out change. Tea: No public sales will be held to-day. Rice flat and neglected. Cotton market unaltered. Jute remains inactive. Tallow, Y. 0.. 41s 8d on the spot. Raps oil, 28s 3J; linseed, 208 to 20s 6d. Turpentine, 24s 6d. Petroleum, 6fl to 'lid according to quality WAKEFIELD CORN, FRIDAY.—A decrease in the stocks of wheat at ports and dearer advices from abroad, strengthen the trade, and considerable business has been done since the last market at advancing prloes. English wheat firm and fully 2s par quarter dearer; foreign is to 2s advance. Barley held firmly at the full prices of this day fortnight. Maize about la per quarter lower. Beans rather easier. Oats, 6d per quar- ter dearer. MANCHESTER TRADE. FRIDAY.—There has not been an active maker, but things upon the whole are very firm, and in soma quarters the tone is sunewhat hopeful that there will be more doing in a few days. Cops are firm at the full rates of Tues- day. and a small trade is being done. Bundles are quiet. bat merchants have business in hand at low rates, and sellers are not without hope of getting them up a point. In cloth there Is not a deal goue through, but there continues ta be offers for shirtings at very poor prices. In some sorts of,home-trade goods a moderate trade is reported, but, taken altogether, the day leaves very much to be desired. L/vERPOOL PROVISIONS, Patnax.—Beef in fair request at the quotations. WARRINGTON. SUDDEN DI&TH OF AN INFANT.—Mar( Artn..liolbrook,

four years of age, daughter of a glass-Iclower residing at Orford, died very suddenly last week. She was put to bed by her mether, who, going upstairs shortly afterwards, found her in convulsions, from which she died almost im- mediately. An inquest was not deemed necessary._ . .
• THE giFENSES OF A FIRE.— At the Borough Court, on • Monday, the firm of William Longehaw and Sons were sum- moned at the instance of the Corporation, to show cause why

an order should not be made upon them to pay the sum of £7 108, expenses incurred by the Corpecation in extinguish- ing a fire at the premises of the firm at Sankey Bridges, on the 21st of May last. The Bench made an order for the

payment of the money. ALL %urns' Cm:roar, Tumwerz..—A sacred cantata,.l entitled "The Nativity." was sung by the choir of the above-named church on Sunday afternoon last at the con- clusion of the service. A large congregation assembledo, and as each member of it was supplied with a book of the words,. they were enabled to take an intelligent interest in the performance. The rendering, cf the music by the v,il- lage-choir was most creditable. All must have worked hard to produce so satisfactory a result. Tau SUDDEN DEA.ICE ON CMDISTMAS hao not been thought necessary to bold an inquest relative ta the death of Iklary Ellen Smith (464 the wife of a toolmaker, Lythgoes-laoe, which occurred suddenly on the evo.ning of Christmas Day. She was last seen alive at about eleven o'clock, ;when she was under the influence of drink. She remarked to her son that she was going to bed, and he left her to go,to a neighbour's house. On his returm she was dead. Daring thelay she had made a hearty Christmas dinner. ; A Vmtw'r ITAFR.—.At the Borough Court„ an Monday, Elizabeth Ellison, married woman, was charged with dam.

aging windows to the-amount of 5-s, and was fet the offence fined '2O; and costs, or a month in prison. She was also charged with assaulting her husband, Samuel Ellison, on the 23rd ult. The husband stated that defendant struck him on the face, threatened him with a kailb,-and seized some mugs to throw at him. They had been married seven years, and she had many times assaulted him. She was fined 108 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment for the assault. I MASTER AND APPRENTICE. At Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, Charles Ralphson, a young man, was summoned by Charles Edward Cooke, toolmaker, Ashton, for neglect of work.—Defendant was formerly an inmate in the Warrington Workhouee, and four years ago he was ap- prenticed to the complainant. He worked until the 16th April last, when he went away, taking will him his clothes, and he was not heard of again until a short time ago when he was discovered at Prescot. Both parties were agreeable to have the indentures cancelled,and the case was adj. iurned until. the Warrington Guardians were communicat:d with and the wishes of the parties explained to them. StrommeG DEATH FROM Buners.—On Sunday a boy of eight years, son of a woman named Knight, who resides at Hollins Green, near Warrington, died in great agony from Vie effects of severe burns received on the 17th of Novem- ber last. Oa the evening of that day the deceased and a brother, ten years of age, were playing near the fire dressed only in their nightdresses. The deceased, whilst reaching a stick from the mantel-piece, set lire to his nightshirt, and was badly burned on the chest, the right side, arm, and shoulder. He was seen by Dr. Joseph on several occasions between the time of the occurrence and his death.—An In- quest was held on Tuesday respecting the death, when the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." FROZEN TO DEATH.—On Tuesday afternoon Mr. T. Hus- band, deputy coroner, held an inquest at the Three Pigeons Ina relative to the death of a labourer named George Dutton, 35 years of age, of no fixed residence, who w.- found dead on Saturday morning in a ototlyarli. to Mr. Massey, Tanners lane. The di0"....-overy was made by a man employed there named P_:iehard Higham. The deceased was last seen alln at eleven o'clock on Friday kt-e Three Pigeons, and a man named night, when he i.eft Hollingworth ar'.'irised him to procure lodgings for the night,A Woman named Johnson, who saw the deceased's I t+orler, Said that she found a hole in his head into which she • could insert her finger ; and Inspector Berry afterwards found a piece ef coal, sharp-pointed, on which was some blood, No suspicions of foul play were, however, enter- tained, and the jury rettuned a verdict of "Accidental death." at j: stated that the deceased had very seldom spent a night in bed. MORE FAMILY DassayroX.--aAt the Ffarr.,2sgton Borough Court, on Tuesday, John Ford, carter, wh3 hag live 4 be neighbourhood of Langford, but who had been arrested at Liverpool the previous day, was charged with having de. Betted his three children. It was stated that one of the children had been in the Workhouse for six months, and the other two between two and three months, at a cost to the ratepayers of about £ll. The prisoner, it seems, has been living apart from his wife, the children having been left with the latter. They were found in a destitute and almost naked condition by Mr. Shearer, relieving officer, who caused them to be removed to the Workhouse. It was stated that they had been sold by the mother to some gypsie.e. but found their way back home. In the course of the hearing Mr. Shearer said that the vigorous action the magistrates had recently taken in Warrington with respect to deserions of wives and families had had the salutary effect of diminishing the number of such cases. The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was sentenced to gaol for a month's hard labour. JUVENILE TEMPLARS AT LATCHFORD.— A public tea meeting was held last evening week in connection with the Juvenile Templars in the Temperance Hall, Latchford. There was a large gathering. Mr. Marchant of Grappen- h ill, took the chair, and said it was in the year 1850 that he first became a pledged abstainer. Total abstinence was a great blessing, and preserved from a great deal of misery. The entertainment consisted of recitations by' the Misses B. Smith, J. Cliffe, A. Starkey, Bertha Cliffs, E. Muskett, A. MuskAtt, M. Wright, Florence Cliffs, and A. Fletcher John Ne ston also gave two " Lauchashire sketches" in his usual humorous manner. Songs were given by Messrs. E. Ditchfield, S. Newton, L. Hough, A. Ellison, and B. Cliffs. The Templars' Drum and Fife Band made their first public appearance, and gave two selections during the evening, repeating " Home, sweet home" on the departure of the audience. The District Chief Templar of Juvenile Templars (Mr. Dale, of Macclesfield) gave an ad- dress on the "Nature of water versus spirits." A vote of thanks was accorded to him for his interesting address. A dialogue was given by Misses S. A. Barber and IL Green. Brother Luke Ellison, the superintendent, read a report, showing that the society was in a good position. WARRINGTON HARRIERS —On Saturday this club had an interestine run with the Sefton Harriers, Liverpool, thirteen members'of the Warrington Harriers and ten of the Sefton Harriers taking part in the sport of the afternoon. The hares, J Waterworth and W Gleave (Warrington). and J Roberts (Sefton) were despatched from the club-room at three o'clock. and the pack, W J Dumbell (Warrington) and A F Rieke (Sefton), acting as pacemakers, and J Massey (Warrington) and S Reece (Sefton) as whips followed ten minutes afterwards. The trail lay along Wilderspool-road to the Stone-delph, and then turned to the right and went alongside the Waterworks, thence per road to Moore, and down Bellhouse-lane, across the canal-bridge, along the bank to Tom Paine'sebridge, and to St. James's Church, where the word was given to race home. The result was that J Massey. Warrinzton Harriers, came in first, at 4-20 p.m.; W Whitfield, Warrington Harriers, second ; A F Packe, Sefton Harriers, third ; S Reece, Set ton Harriers, fourth ; T Gleave, Warrington Harriers, fifth; J Green, Warrington Harriers, sixth ; W Francis, Sefton Harriers, seventh P • J Fannirv,Serton Harriers, eighth ; ' Bowden Sefton fiar- tiers, ninth; and R Daft. Sefton Harriers, tenth. Distance about 81- miles. After the run 33 sat down to the tea and sciai.

___ _ ORAPPENHALL PARISH CHURCH ANNUAL TEA PARTY.— On Tuesday evening the annual tea party is connection with the Parish Church was held in the large room, Grap- penhall. Tea was provided at six o'clock, and a large num- ber of persons resident in the neighbourhood attended. A. capital repast was served, to which ample justice was dens by those assembled. After tea the tables were cleared, and an entertainment was given, in which the choir of the church, assisted by several 'death], took part. Mr. Harry Antonie, of Manchester, assisted in the programme, and a most enjoyable evening was spent. Before the commence- ment of the prograronv, the rector, the Rev. Canon Greenall, suitably addressed the assembled audience. With respect to the church, several improvements had taken place during the year. The new reredos had been erected and paid for, and they had been presented with a handsome ewer for the font. They had also two new and handsome windows added to the church. They owed £l5O, and towards this he had received promises of help, one promise being for £25 on condition that the whole sum could be raised in six months. He trusted the money would be raised in the time stipula- ted. (Applause.) The programme was then proceeded with, and consisted of choruses, which were rendered by the choir in a very satisfactory manner. The whole of the proceedings were of a most pleasant description, the various items in the programme giving general satisfaction. THE Faosr : FATAL ICE ACCIDENT AND NARROW EscArEs.—Since the sharp frost that set in IN : week several narrow escapes and one fatality have beea reported 'in the neighbourhood of Warrington. On Sunday a man /who was skating on a frozen pond near Latchford ventured on thin ice. He fell and the ice gave way, but by keeping his arms on the unbroken ice he fortunately managed to scramble out with no more serious injury than a very in- convenient wetting on a bitterly cold day. Another man skating in the same neighbourhood had a similar escape, being Immerse 4 up to the neck before he could extricate , himself from his perilous dilemma. On Saturday Mr. T. ' J. Ridgway, coroner, inquired into the circumstances of the death of a young man named John Henry Hayee, who was drowned whilst skating on a pond at Whitley, near War- rington, on the morning of Christmas Day. Peter Hayes, provision dealer, Higher Whitley, deposed that the deceased was his son, who was twenty years of age, and was a builder's labourer. On Christmas morning the deceased left home at about 930 in the morning, and hi body was brought home the same morning. Thomas Walker, labourer, of Higher Whitley, said that he accompanied the deceased to the Barn Meadows Pit to ;irate. Both put on their skates and went on the iae. Witness observed to deceased that it wan not safe, but he notwit's.tar...ing went on. When about the middle of the pit d, ceeee-d fi il down, breaking the ice, and crest into the water. Witness shouted to him to hold up. and ran himself for a rope. A Mr. Hatch returxed with him with a rope, and tbe deceased had then his Itead and arms visible. They threw the rope to him, but he did not catch hold of it, and seemed unconscious. Mr, Hatch west into the pit as far as possible, bat deceasee, took nol inotice, and was drowned. The body was shortly afterwards recovered. The jury returned a verdict to t;pa effect that the deceased was accidentally drowned.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL Courer.—At the Occisional Court, held at the office of Mr. Buck'on, on Monday, a mar. ried couple named Joseph and Mary Higgins were charged with stealing foar sheets and other articles, the property of Sarah Cane, of Winwick.road. Ann Higgins, mother of the first.named prisoner, was charged with receiving the articles. The parties were neighbours in March last, when the robbery was cpmmitted, and directly afterwards they absconded. They did not again appear in the neighbour. hood until recently, when they were apprehended by P,C, Whitthagharn.—Prisoner was remodiC
LATEST NEWS.

The Allegemine Zeitung states that the Czir will be crowned Emperor of Central Aaia in 1886. Mr. Forster, who a few days ago had an operation per- formed on one of his feet, is now said to be making good
progress towards recovery. At Lincoln, on Friday, Rev. Lewis Kerby, curate at Branston' was fined £2O for an aggravated assault on a little girl, the. daughter .of a parishioner._ .

The Marquis of Hartington and Sir Charles Dilke have accepted invitations to be present at the National Liberal Club banquet to Lord Ripon on the 25th February. ; The workmen employed at the railway wok s of- the INorth-Eastern Railway Company, at Gateshead-on-Tyne, kstruck on Friday to the number of 2,000 against longer 'hours. _ _

_ On Friday morning, a retriever dog belonging to the captain of the Grimsby smack, Restless Wave. jumped into 1 Grimsby fish dock and rescued a man named Evans, who ' had fallen in, and was in danger of drowning .
—The Central News learhs that the Gore-mount hare re- c4ved telegrams from Lord Wolseley and Sir Evelyn Baring
confirming the receipt of General' Gordon's letter of the 14th December. The letter is undoubtedly genuice.

In Glasgow, on Friday, Susan M`ElYall and Mary Neiles t were remitted to the.sheriff charged with having pushed or thrown a man named James Hanley out of a two-storey window in High-street, Glasgow. Ile never recovered con- sciousness, and died late on Thursday night. SHIPPING DISASTERS.—A Lloyds' telegram from Balti- more, on Friday, says that the Norwegian barque Lens, from Brazil for Philadelphia, has been totally lost at Hog Island, Virginia. Part of the crew were saved. A Lloyds' Sanfrancisco telegram says that the Lill, German barque, was totally lost at Point Gorda, December 26. The first officer and four of the crew were drowned. FATAL A.STBAY IN IRELAND —On Tnursday night, at Mount -Florence, near Athlone, two men named Stu,rav quarrelled with three brothers. From words they came to blows, and in the course of a desperate fight which ensued, both Murrays were so seriously stabbed with knives that one of them died on Friday morning, and the other is in an almost hopeless condition. The three Lennons have been arrested. FATAL DYNAMITE EXPLOSION. —At Carrickferguss, on Friday evening, whilst a young man named John Hodisin- son was heating some dynamite cartridges for blasting pur- poses, the cartridges exploded with fearful force, almost wrecking the house, and inflicting such terrible injuries upon the man that he died soon afterwards. Deceased's left hand was blown clean off, and has not yet been re- covered. EXTRIORDINARY IMPOSTURE—How the charitable are imposed upon was illustrated at Sheffield, on Friday, when a man named Richard Armstrong was charged with begs ging. He was attired in woman's clothing, had a baby in his arms, and was accompanied by a man tosesented to be the husband out of work. The bab7 was hired.. its mother being an unfortunate, Armst'song was committed fora month. THE ALLEGED CONSPMAOT 'TO MURDER AN INFANT.—At the Lambeth Police Qourt-, on Friday, William Jones, Thos, Long, and George W''';aer were again charged with con- spiracy to murder i-/'"e illegitimate child of Jones. Madeline Gay, a married 'Amman, said her husband had been absent from Englan" . - two years, during which time she became in- timate srit'a Jones. In April she informed him that she was going its have a child by him. He wrote saying that he harl- some stuff to remove her trouble. Her husband returned and disenvered her condition. OVERTURNED.—SbortIy before nine o'clock on Friday morning, an omnibus, plying between Barnsbury and Newington, London, was turning into Liverpool-road, when the wheels caught the kerbstone and the vehicle over- turned. The outside passengers were thrown off the omni- bus, and, as the horses struggled violently, fears were for some time entertained as to the safety of the inside travel- lers. They were eventually extricated, and the injured re- moved to the hospital. One young man, unknown, and three others, were less seriously injured. INDISPOSITION OF Mn GLADSTONE.—The Press Associa- tion is enabled to state that Mr. Gladstone has been some- what indisposed for the last few days. Late on Thursday evening Sir Andrew Clarke, his medical adviser, paid him a long visit, and again saw Mr. Gladstone on Friday morning, remaining with him Sons time in D )wning.street. Mr. Gladstone, on Friday evening, attekled a Cabinet Council, at which all the Ministers were present except Letci r,P.'neer and Sir Charles Dilke. The council lasted from a quarter-pit four until nearly seven o'clock, and was then only adjourned until next day, when Sir C. Dila will be able to join his colleagues at the council table. The circumstances under which the Cabinet Council was sum- moned, and the lengthy deliberations of Ministers, have caused considerable stir in political circles.

div.head: BOILER EXPLOSION AT OLDII/01.-TEKREE
div.p: BOILER EXPLOSION AT OLDII/01.-TEKREE
MEN KILLED.

At two o'clock on Friday afternoon a boiler at Stanley Mill Lees, near Oldham, exploded with terriac force, killing three men outright, and injuring many others—some it is feared fatally. The mill had been stopped for a month for repairs, and work had been re-commenced only on Friday morning. All the men killed, and nearly all those injured, were bricklayers who were at work making a new flue to the boiler next to the one that exploded. ANOTHER DYNAMITE EXPLOSION. The Central News learns that a serious explosion, be- lieved to be due to dynamite, occurred last evening at Gower-street Station on the Metropolitan Railway. A number of persons are believed to have been injured. The explosion occnrrea about 9-30, between Gower-street and Kings Cross Stations. The sound is described as deafen- ing, and caused quite a panic amongst the passengers in a passing train; nearly every window in the carriages were smashed, the lights were extinguished, and several persons injured by the falling glass. The matter is now being in- vestigated by the police. Official opinion is divided as to. whether the explosii was due to the explosion of gas or to j dynamite. I ATTEMPTED MURDER OF TWO CHILDREN.

At Richmond, Surrey, on Friday, Ida Emily Redstone, was charged with attempting to murder two little girls named Weir, the children of her mistress, and with attempt- ing to commit seicide. It seems that the young woman was a servant to Mrs Weir, and had taken the two children out for a walk. On reaching the river she said she would go no further, but woeld throw them in, and this they say she did, after which it would seem that she attempted to drown herself also. Her strange conduct has apparently been brought about 3•57 a quarrel with her mistre.., who was from house at the time the children were taken out, and on returning found that almost every article of value in the house had been broken te pieces. The only witness called was William Hednott, a waterman, who deposed that ha was standing by Mr Maynard's boathense, Chiswick, when he heard children's screams on the opposite side of the river. Ile afterwards heard a splash, and ran for a boat. With the assistance of his mate, Barntam. he rowed to the spot whence the soueele came. They turned the boat's head to the tow path, when they saw a black object in the water. Witness caught hold of it, and found it to be the prisoner, whom he pulled into the boat. About six yards lower down he saw something else in the water.svhich he ascertained to be a female child, and he pulled her out also. Still further on he saw another child in the water, and this one he rescued also. The three appeared to be dead. He called for assistance, and Mr Maynard and his two sons came. They got the prisoner and the two children ashore, and sent for medical aid. After a long time they revived. The prisoner, who said she did not wish to ask witness any questions, was then remanded for a week. SHOCKING MURDER IN LIVERPOOL.

A shocking murder was committed on Friday morning in one of the low parts of Toateth Park, Liverpoolrthe victim being a Norwegian sailor named Sever Olouaves Jonsone, who resided in a house in Langley-st. About one o'clock a woman went into the house followed by a man named Tag- gart. Jansone objected to his presence and put him out of the house, but was then himself pulled into the street by Taggart, who butted him with his head and knocked him down. At this moment another man came, and, taking off his belt, twisted one end round his hand; and with the

buckle began to beat Jonsone about the head and body. A large crowd quickly gathered around, and the screams of the females attracted the attention of police officers, who were told that a man had been kiLed. On going into the house, they found Jonsone lying in an insensae condition. He was conveyed to the institution, where Dr. Dixon pro- nounced life to be extinct. The inspector having received the assistance of some constables, proceeded to another house in Langley-street, where he apprehended Taggart and a man earned Kavanagh, and also a stepson of the latter named Nl`Namara, alleged to have taken part in the outrage, and they were locked up. They will be brought before Mr. Raffles to-day (Saturday) morning, by which time Inspector Hamilton will have pursued his inquiries sufficiently to present the case in court. It appears that tha deceased and a woman who claims to be his wife occupied the house and had five female lodgers. Taggart had entered the house 1 with one of these women, but, whether his money was stolen from him or for some other reason, he commenced to quarrel with her. Jonsone. the "keeper of the house, with the assistance of the woman, pitched him into the street. Taggart, however, returned with the other two men, and, entering the house, they commenced an attack tin Jonsone with belts, while one of them struck him on the temple with a bottle. ..rionsone was about forty five years of age, and had only recently returned from sea. FRANCE AND CHINA.

Pears, FRIDA.Y.—The French naval forces in Chicose waters are te be further augmented. Four additional cruisers have been ordered to prepare for service, and as aeon as they are equipped, they will be sent to loin the fleet under Ad- miral Courbet.
FIGHTING IN ASHANTEE. FORTY KILLED.

CAPE COAST CAS7T.L-ti- -(v1;:-.1.17,7;;R-P-OOL), PEO. 9.—On the 12th November Prince Rookie and his son, with a strong party of Ashantees, attacked Marsu, a town of some impoitance, lying north of Coomassie. They were defeati,d with a loss of 40, hilled and many prisoners, among the latter being Boarkie and his son Quasie Karsah. The King of Mansu is Low awaiting the arrival of a commissioner from Governer -Young to inquire into the cause of this at- tack of the Ashantees, and.unless this is satisfactorily ac- complished thore is little doubt Boarkie and the other pri- soners will be put to death. Boarhie was the ambasaalor who was sent to the late Governors Sir Samuel Rowis, by the late Kiag Mersab, He bears a had reputatien,
